<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-07-settings-authority/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-07-settings-authority.md) -->

# Desktop settings have one native ABP authority

Status: accepted architecture, implementation staged. Contract version 0.1.0.

Desktop appearance and layout belong to a headless `settingsd` authority. Settings
controls, Mix operators and agents submit validated batches through native ABP.
Applications and compd/Quoin consume complete accepted snapshots through shared
headless `settings` contracts and one theme adapter per UI layer. Closing a
Settings page does not stop delivery. Other services retain their own hardware
and operational settings; discovery does not create a distributed transaction.

The shared library has multiple external owners from its first commit:
settingsd, applications and compd. The plain component names `settings` and
`settingsd` describe their public contracts. Config remains independent of Bus;
the UI toolkit layer remains independent of settings transport. No COSMIC implementation
or GPL/MPL code is incorporated.

Settings behaviour has one shared implementation per concern: `settings`
consumer ordering/recovery and render-domain comparison; one theme adapter
projecting settings onto the UI toolkit; shared reusable controls and
role/default builders; and one shared event-loop activation/invalidation path.
Applications retain their service lifetime, content and deliberate overrides.
Compd owns output geometry, work areas, Wayland configuration and presentation.
Standard widgets inherit current defaults without copied app palettes, font
captures or settings handlers. Extract repeated components during migrations;
keep headless crates independent of renderers and the UI layer independent of Bus.

Each profile has one exclusive writer. Authored settings, revision and bounded
operation receipts share a durable strict-data replacement. A no-op persists a
receipt without changing semantic revision. The durable store incarnation fences
restores; broker sequence is delivery order, not settings revision. Caller access
remains open across the trusted mesh. Correct target/revision binding and
canonical publisher ownership do not require the operator to own the session.

Native calls/events use existing ABP/noded, preserving frozen framing and
identity constants. External toolkit D-Bus adapters are later compatibility
boundaries inside the independent MixOS session. Retained broker snapshots are
presentation/recovery aids, not a durable offline store. Recovery is driven by
lifecycle/connection/loss events, without an idle settings polling loop.

Consumer application and frame presentation are separate evidence. Compositor
geometry/input updates remain coherent while Wayland configure/ack/buffer changes
complete asynchronously. No global same-vblank guarantee is made.

The authority/store and shared consumer primitives are implemented; consumers
adopt them as they enter this tree. Full widget geometry/resources, panel reconfiguration, native
frame/first-map acceptance, named profiles, previews, replication and compatibility
remain in development. This decision establishes ownership; individual fixtures
do not close full desktop acceptance. See the [initial contract](../spec/settings/README.md).

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-08-mix-programs-and-documents/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-08-mix-programs-and-documents.md) -->

# Decision — `.mix` programs and `.mx` documents

Status: accepted 2026-10-08. Target of the **next major Mix binary refactor and
deployment**; implementation and filename migration are pending. The release
number is assigned during implementation, not inferred from this decision.

## The decision

| Family | Canonical extension | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mix program | `.mix` | Executable Mix with its ordinary language capabilities and caller authority |
| Mix document | `.mx` | Strict declarative data consumed and validated by a defined reader/schema |

Macros, scene behaviours, services, installers, tests and modules are roles of
ordinary Mix programs. They introduce no separate grammar or extension. Themes,
configuration, specifications, manifests, catalogues and scenes are document
purposes. Different schemas do not make different script languages.

An `.mx` document cannot contain general executable Mix. A schema may allow
the existing restricted, side-effect-free expression subset in precisely defined
fields. Scene bindings remain permitted under their current limits; function
calls, assignment, process/file effects and Bus operations remain refused.

The first migration preserves existing strict-data and scene-envelope syntax.
This decision unifies file families and execution rules, not every document's
grammar. Changing the scene envelope later is a separate schema migration, not
a prerequisite or excuse to add another parser now.

## Enforcement and evolution

1. Ordinary program execution and executable file/module loading refuse `.mx`,
   including serve/reload paths. A malformed document never falls back to the
   full interpreter or shell. Extension checks complement strict parsing; they
   are not a malware detector or sandbox for intentionally run programs.
2. Generic documents use strict parsing. App-owned documents also validate their
   schema, supplied by the owning reader and/or declared in the document. A
   schema can be a Rust type/validator; it need not be another file.
3. Data strings stay literal except at schema-declared restricted binding fields.
   A document describing commands does not gain execution authority by being
   data; running those actions is an executable program responsibility.
4. New purposes use existing Mix programs or versioned document schemas. A new
   family, suffix or evaluation mode requires an accepted decision explaining
   why existing facilities fail, authority/resource limits, negative tests and
   compatibility. There is no macro or workflow dialect to introduce.
5. Legacy `.conf.mix`, `.spec.mix`, `.data.mix`, `scene.mix` and other inventoried
   data names remain readable during a measured migration. They are transitional
   spellings, not additional permanent families. Accepting this decision does
   not make current binaries recognise or enforce the new extension.
6. Install upgraded readers before switching files/writers. Preserve user data,
   expose conflicts between old/new files, and retain a tested binary-plus-data
   rollback. Frozen Cosmix deployments are not silently upgraded or renamed.
   No frozen ABP bytes or cross-node transport contracts change.

Canonical examples are `behaviour.mix`, `report_selection.mix`, `settings.mx`,
`scene.mx` and `authority.mx`. Keep script homes from the macro decision:
app-local `config/macros/` and global `/opt/mixos/mix` hold executable macros;
documents remain in their owning component/app directories.

The [file-family contract](../spec/mix/2026-10-08-programs-and-documents.md)
specifies boundaries and acceptance. The [Mix guide](../../mix/README.md) distinguishes
current behaviour from the target. This decision updates the source-layout
file conventions and the macro contract's planned data-fixture spelling while
preserving their existing compatibility obligations.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-09-chrome-family-and-schemes/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-09-chrome-family-and-schemes.md) -->

# Decision — the chrome family and chrome schemes

Status: accepted 2026-10-09.

## The decision

- **A typed `chrome` family in the design.** Application chrome (title bars,
  menus, tabs, panels and controls) is described by one closed set of colour
  roles, such as `chrome`, `card`, `field`, `hover`, `text_dim`, `accent` and
  `caption_close`. Each role names a colour primitive.
- **Chrome colours are exact.** No contrast adjustment, recipe or derivation
  applies to a chrome role: it renders exactly as authored. Colours are
  written as OKLCH at nine decimals, which round-trips every 8-bit sRGB value
  (the design crate tests the full cube).
- **Coverage is explicit.** A design that authors the chrome family must
  author every role, and an unknown role or primitive is a compile error.
- **Three chrome schemes**, `pro`, `studio` and `classic`, join the six hue
  schemes. Their light and dark modes step the interface brightness:

  | scheme | dark | light |
  |---|---|---|
  | `pro` | Pro | Pro Medium Gray |
  | `studio` | Studio | Studio Light |
  | `classic` | Classic | Classic |

- **Semantic pairs keep their guarantees.** In the chrome schemes the semantic
  pairs (`base`, `card`, `popover` and the rest) take the neutral `mono`
  palette for the mode, so every contrast rule still holds for components that
  read pairs. The egui toolkit draws the chrome schemes from the chrome family.

## Why

A desktop whose applications sit side by side should look like one desktop,
down to the pixel. Exact chrome roles make that a matter of values, not
adjustments, while the semantic pairs keep their accessibility guarantees.

## Consequences

- `Scheme::is_chrome_scheme()` tells consumers which styling path applies.
- Tests that pinned the six revision-one schemes iterate `Scheme::REVISION_ONE`;
  the chrome schemes carry their own exact-value tests.
- Components that read semantic pairs, such as the compositor's own panels,
  move to the chrome family over time.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-09-icons-and-type/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-09-icons-and-type.md) -->

# Decision — icons and type

Status: accepted 2026-10-09.

## The decision

- **Icons are Lucide.** Every icon in MixOS applications and the desktop
  comes from the [Lucide](https://lucide.dev) set: 24 px grid, round caps and
  joins, a single stroke colour. Icons are taken unmodified from a pinned
  upstream release and ship with Lucide's licence (ISC, with MIT for the
  icons derived from Feather) and a `NOTICE` line. A component ships only the
  icons it uses.
- **Type is Inter and JetBrains Mono.** Interface text is Inter; numbers,
  code and JSON are JetBrains Mono. Both are SIL OFL 1.1 and ship as
  unmodified static faces from their upstream releases.
- **The shipped desktop sizes** are Inter Regular at 12.5 px for body text,
  10.5 px for small text, Inter SemiBold at 15 px for headings, Inter Medium
  for emphasis, and JetBrains Mono at 12 px.
- **Weight is a design token.** Each typography role names a weight, and the
  renderer selects the static face of that weight (300 Light, 400 Regular,
  500 Medium, 600 SemiBold). A light profile, with body text at 300, is a
  change to the design's weights and nothing else.
- **Icon stroke is a design token.** The design metric `icon.stroke_width`
  sets the stroke every icon is drawn with (default 1.5, the approved
  baseline; a session choice may override it, see
  [session icon stroke and type](2026-10-14-session-icon-stroke-and-type.md)), so a
  lighter icon set accompanies a lighter type profile without new assets.
- **Colour comes from the theme.** Icons take the colour of the text around
  them; no icon carries a colour of its own.

## Why

One icon family and one type family give every MixOS application, and the
external applications that run alongside them, the same look. Making weight
and stroke tokens keeps the visual weight of the whole desktop adjustable in
one place.

## Consequences

- `libs/toolkit` embeds the faces and icons and applies them from the theme.
- A new icon is added by copying its SVG from the pinned Lucide release into
  the component that uses it and listing it there.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-10-mix-components/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-10-mix-components.md) -->

# Decision — Mix components

Status: accepted 2026-10-10. Amends [the source layout](2026-10-04-source-layout.md)
(AGENTS.md §2 and §10).

## The decision

- **A component may be written entirely in Mix.** It lives where its kind
  says (`services/<role>d/`, `apps/<name>/`, `cli/<name>/`, `libs/<name>/`)
  and follows every naming rule. It has no Cargo package.
- **Its identity is `component.mx`** at the top of the component, a
  strict-data document (schema 1) with the fields a Cargo package carries
  in `[package.metadata.mixos]`, plus the name, version and principal
  program:

  ```text
  {
    schema: 1,
    name: "releasesd",          -- = directory = component
    component: "releasesd",
    kind: "service",            -- matches the kind directory
    layer: "desktop",           -- bus | mix | core | desktop
    contract: "public",         -- none | public
    version: "0.1.0",           -- the component's own MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
    program: "scripts/releasesd.mix"
  }
  ```

- **A component is one or the other.** A directory with both `Cargo.toml`
  and `component.mx` is refused.
- **Layout inside the component:**
  - programs in `scripts/`, modules they `require` in `scripts/lib/`;
  - units in `units/`, calling `/opt/mixos/bin/mix` by absolute path;
  - tests in `tests/*_test.mix`.
- **Install location:** a Mix component's `scripts/` tree installs to
  `/opt/mixos/lib/<component>/`, read-only like the binaries in
  `/opt/mixos/bin`. `/opt/mixos/share` stays for data.
- **Shared Mix test helpers** live in `tests/lib/`. The first is
  `private_bus.mix`, which starts a throwaway, owned noded broker for Bus
  tests of serve citizens.
- **Gates.** `tools/component_index.mix` reads both identity sources,
  applies the same identity, layer and contract rules to each, and checks
  that `program` names a `.mix` file inside the component. Names are unique
  across both kinds. A Mix component has no Cargo dependency closure, so its
  declared layer is checked at review: it may use only the `mix` binary, the
  Bus and the verbs of components at or below its layer.
- **Versions and contracts.** A Mix component carries its own version, since
  there is no workspace package to inherit one from. With
  `contract: "public"`, its Bus verbs and document schemas are registered
  like any other (`docs/docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix`, `docs/docs/spec/<topic>/`).

## Why

Mix is the system's own language. A service that is mostly glue (talking
HTTP, checking hashes, moving files, answering the Bus) is shorter, clearer
and easier for an agent to change in Mix than in Rust, and Mix already has
the primitives. Until now every component had to be a Cargo package, so such
a service had a choice of being rewritten in Rust to fit the layout, or
hidden in another component's `scripts/`, where it has no owner, no index
entry and no gate. Neither is honest.

`component.mx` keeps the one rule that matters (directory = component =
name, with a declared kind, layer and contract), so the component index stays
the agent's single map of the tree.

## Consequences

- The first Mix component is `services/releasesd` (upstream application
  releases).
- The generic line-JSON bridge for external applications (AGENTS.md §4.1)
  will land the same way.
- `tools/component_install.mix` installs Mix components: `scripts/` to
  `/opt/mixos/lib/<component>/` and `units/` to `/etc/systemd/system`. It
  writes an install record, keeps one previous tree for rollback and has a
  `--check` for drift. `--root` targets an image or container tree. Units of
  Rust components still wait for the unit collector.
- Rejected: a separate top-level directory for Mix programs. It would
  classify by language, not by kind of artefact.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-10-scheme-and-style-axes/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-10-scheme-and-style-axes.md) -->

# Decision — scheme and style are separate axes

Status: accepted 2026-10-10.

## The decision

- **Scheme and style are separate choices.** The scheme picks the colours:
  one of the nine palettes. The style picks the chrome's forms and lengths:
  `plain`, `pro`, `studio` or `classic`. A theme context has a scheme, a
  style, a mode and a contrast. A style of "none" means the scheme's own
  style, which keeps every existing selection exactly as it was.
- **Any palette takes any style.** A chrome style draws from the chrome
  colour roles. The `pro`, `studio` and `classic` palettes author those
  roles. Every other palette derives them from its semantic pairs, through
  a typed and documented mapping in the design (`families.chrome.derive`).
  For example, the bar is the `base` surface, cards the `secondary`
  surface, and selections and the menu highlight the `accent` pair. A
  colour a palette does author always wins over the derivation. In the
  other direction, the plain style draws any palette through its semantic
  pairs, which every palette has.
- **The contrast rules still hold.** The pairs keep their WCAG checks.
  Derived text roles sit on surfaces of the same pair, or close to them,
  and the design tests that text on derived chrome meets AA (4.5:1) in
  every hue palette, mode and contrast. The authored chrome palettes stay
  exact, as before.
- **Light or dark base comes from the palette.** Whether the chrome sits
  on a light or a dark base is read from the lightness of its own `chrome`
  colour, not from the style. A light palette in a style first designed
  for a dark one is still drawn light.
- **Decorations and caption side sit beside the axes.** They change no
  colour or length, so they are not part of the design context:
  - `csd`: the application draws its own title bar, as before;
  - `ssd`: the compositor decorates the window, and the application shows
    its menus and right-hand controls in a menu-bar row;
  - caption side `right` (the default) or `left`. On the left the order is
    Close, Minimize, Maximize, with Close in the corner, and the menus
    follow the captions.
- **Every surface takes the axes.** Settings has `appearance.style`,
  `appearance.decorations` and `appearance.caption_side`. The shared theme
  file has `style:`, `decorations:` and `caption_side:`. Each application's
  View → Theme menu has a Style group and a Decorations group. An app's own
  choice persists, and older saved state loads with the defaults.

## Why

Palette and style answer different questions. Tying them together meant a
colour preference forced a layout, and a layout preference forced colours.
As separate axes, each new palette works in every style and each new style
works with every palette.

## Consequences

- Every scheme, style, mode and contrast combination compiles; the design
  tests compile them all.
- A new palette needs no chrome colours to work in a chrome style. It can
  still author any of them where the derived colour is not the one wanted.
- The style family's binding from each scheme to its own style remains.
  It is what "the scheme's own style" resolves to.
- The style family no longer carries a base token. The light or dark base
  is the palette's, as described above.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-10-style-tokens-as-data/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-10-style-tokens-as-data.md) -->

# Decision — style tokens as data

Status: accepted 2026-10-10.

## The decision

- **A typed `style` family in the design.** The chrome family says which
  colours the chrome is. The style family says which forms it takes and
  how big they are. Every choice a renderer used to make by asking which
  scheme it was drawing is now one token:
  - forms, such as a tab strip or cards for panel groups, a checkbox or a
    switch for on/off controls, bevels or outlines, a ringed, plain or block
    slider knob, and pill or rounded push buttons;
  - lengths, such as the title-bar height, the menu row padding, the bar
    and dock sizes, the push-button height and the corner radii;
  - the renderer base: pair-based or chrome widgets, and a light, dark or
    mode-following base palette.
- **Tokens are typed and closed.** Each token is a named choice, a flag or a
  number with a declared range. Every style must author every token. A
  missing, unknown or ill-typed token is a compile error, as is a scheme with
  no style or one bound to a style that does not exist.
- **Styles are named and bound per scheme.** `styles` holds named token
  sets, and `schemes` gives every scheme exactly one of them. The shipped
  design has four styles: `pro`, `studio` and `classic` for the chrome
  schemes, and `plain` for the six hue schemes. `plain` writes down, as data,
  the geometry those schemes used to derive from their pair-based style. A
  style does not vary by mode or contrast, and modifier blocks cannot alter
  it.
- **Renderers read the resolved style, never the scheme.** The egui toolkit
  builds its chrome from the compiled style. No component branches on a
  scheme any more. A design that authors no style family takes the embedded
  design's style for its scheme.

## Why

The chrome styles should be values a designer can edit and compare, not
branches a programmer has to find. With the style family, a new style is a
new token set in the design, with no renderer change. Moving every decision
across changed no pixel: the toolkit's and the applications' snapshots
render the same images before and after.

## Consequences

- This lays the ground for a separate style axis, where any palette can be
  combined with any style. Today the binding from scheme to style is fixed
  in the design; a later decision can make the style its own selection.
- `Scheme::is_chrome_scheme()` now only groups schemes, for example in theme
  menus. The style's `widgets` token decides which styling path applies.
- A form the token set cannot express yet, such as a new tab shape, still
  needs code once: a new choice for the token and the code that draws it.
  After that, any style can select it.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-compd-module-layout/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-compd-module-layout.md) -->

# Decision — compd's module layout on entry

Status: accepted 2026-10-11. Amends [the source layout](2026-10-04-source-layout.md)
(AGENTS.md §4, Rust modules).

## Context

AGENTS.md §4 forbids new `mod.rs` and `foo/foo.rs` files and says code
transplanted from elsewhere is renamed on entry. The compositor's crates
arrive written in an older layout: about 570 `mod.rs` files and about 270
self-named module files (`foo/foo.rs`, each the file of a module `foo::foo`).

## The decision

- **Every `dir/mod.rs` becomes `dir.rs` on entry.** Rust resolves `dir.rs`
  with its children in `dir/`, so the rename changes no module path. An
  explicit `#[path]` resolves against the directory of the file that holds
  it, so each one in a renamed file is rewritten (for example
  `#[path = "encode/dialog_unavailable.rs"]` in `graphics`).
- **Self-named module files stay, as a standing exception.** Each is the
  canonical file of a module `foo::foo`; removing it renames the module at
  every caller, which is churn a transplant should not carry. No lint can
  gate them either way (`clippy::self_named_module_files` enforces the
  opposite, `mod.rs` style).
- **The exception shrinks and ends.** It covers only the compd crates, and
  each crate leaves it when it is next substantially edited: its self-named
  modules are dissolved into their parents in a change of their own. No new
  self-named module file is added to any crate.
- **No `mod.rs` can come back.** Every compd crate carries
  `[lints.clippy] mod_module_files = "deny"`, as the rest of the workspace
  does, and clippy runs as a gate.

## Consequences

- The transplant stays a near-zero semantic change, so its tests prove the
  same behaviour they proved before.
- Readers of compd will meet `foo::foo` paths for a while.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-executed-commands/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-executed-commands.md) -->

# Decision — executed commands are published

Status: accepted 2026-10-11. Amends [egui applications](2026-10-09-egui-applications.md)
(AGENTS.md §4.1).

## The decision

- **Every application publishes each command it runs.**
  - The topic is `<app>.command.executed`, where `<app>` is the
    application's Bus service name.
  - An event means the command registry accepted the invocation and the
    command's handler returned.
  - A command that is unknown or disabled is refused, and nothing is
    published.
  - The event does not report the outcome of work the handler queued, such
    as a save that later fails. Outcomes travel by the application's own
    verbs and topics.
- **The body:**

  ```text
  {
    v: 1,
    run: "5f0c…",           -- this process: a UUID drawn once at start
    seq: 812,                -- per run, from 1, assigned in execution order
    at_ms: 1760160000123,    -- integer ms since the Unix epoch, at handler return
    id: "file.open",         -- the command's stable id
    origin: "menu",          -- menu | shortcut | palette | ui | bus | macro
    dropped: 0               -- events this run lost since the last one published
  }
  ```

- **`seq` and `dropped`:**
  - **Numbering.** `seq` is assigned when the event is created, before it
    is queued, so the published stream may have gaps.
  - **Loss.** When the queue is full the oldest queued event is dropped and
    a loss counter grows. The next event that is actually published carries
    the counter in `dropped`, and the counter resets. A gap in `seq` always
    equals the sum of the `dropped` values that explain it.
  - **Ordering.** `seq`, not `at_ms`, orders a run's events: the wall clock
    can move.
  - **A new run.** A different `run` means the application restarted, and
    `seq` starts again at 1. Consumers key a sequence by the publishing
    service (and node) together with `run`; `run` is opaque.
  - **Reconnects.** Events that could not be published while the Bus was
    away count as dropped.
  - **Unknown outcomes.** A publish whose outcome is unknown (the
    connection failed after the frame went out, or no answer came) may have
    reached subscribers, so it is assumed delivered and not counted. If it
    was in fact lost, a subscriber sees a gap that `dropped` does not
    explain, the same as its own missed deliveries. Exact accounting there
    would need a broker receipt per event.
  - **Subscriber loss.** A subscriber that misses deliveries detects it from
    `seq` gaps that `dropped` does not explain.
- **`origin` is the mechanism that reached the registry**, not an earlier
  cause:
  - `menu`: a menu row, including one chosen through synthetic input;
  - `shortcut`: a key binding, including a synthetic key press;
  - `palette`: the command palette or Help search;
  - `ui`: any other control in the window, such as a toolbar button;
  - `bus`: `<app>.execute` (or another verb whose documentation says it runs
    a registry command);
  - `macro`: the shared macro runner. This value is reserved until
    applications have a Macros menu.
- **No arguments.** Registry commands take none. A command whose effect
  depends on a choice made later, such as a path picked in a dialog, is
  recorded here only as having run. Replay needs those choices, and the
  [recording spec](2026-10-11-rec-and-play.md) defines how applications
  publish them before `rec` is built.
- **Publishing never blocks the application.**
  - Events go through a bounded queue on the application's existing effect
    path.
  - The topic is not retained.
  - Events still queued when the application exits are lost, and nothing
    counts them: the next run starts afresh.
- **It will be implemented once.** The toolkit's command registry will take
  the origin at dispatch and record each run. The shared Bus connection (the
  `citizen` library, or an application's own connection until it moves to
  `citizen`) will publish the records. An application will not write its own
  publisher.

## Why

Every action is already a command with a stable id, and agents already reach
every command over the Bus. Until now the commands a person ran by hand
stayed inside the process. Nothing could watch them, record them or learn
from them. Publishing each run closes that gap with one hook, and it is the
first half of how [`rec`](2026-10-11-rec-and-play.md) writes a person's work
as a script.

## Consequences

- AGENTS.md §4.1 gains the rule.
- `Registry::execute` gains an origin, and the existing call sites state
  theirs.
- Each application gets a test proving that a menu command and a Bus command
  are both published with the right origin and consecutive `seq`, and that
  a refused command publishes nothing.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-keymaps-in-settings/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-keymaps-in-settings.md) -->

# Key bindings are desktop settings

Status: accepted. Settings contract 0.4.0 (additive). Widens
[Desktop settings have one native ABP authority](2026-10-07-settings-authority.md),
whose scope was the desktop's appearance and layout.

## Context

Every egui application offers its actions as commands with optional
shortcuts ([egui applications](2026-10-09-egui-applications.md)). Before
this decision each application kept its key bindings its own way:

- dopus read an overlay file, `keymap.conf.mix`, in its config directory,
  once at start-up;
- ced had a fixed table of Notepad++-style defaults;
- BusViewer and Prefs had shortcuts written into their command lists;
- each parsed chord text in its own way (`ArrowLeft` in dopus, `Left` in
  ced).

So a person changing a key had to know which application kept it where, an
agent could not change one over the Bus, and nothing could show every
binding in one place.

## Decision

1. **The user's bindings live in settingsd.** The authored desktop profile
   gains `keymaps`: per application id, per action id, the list of chords
   the person chose. An empty list unbinds the action. An action that is
   not listed keeps the application's default.
2. **Defaults stay with the application.** An application's default chords
   ship in its code, beside the actions they run, so a new action arrives
   with its key and an application without settingsd still has its keys.
   settingsd stores only what the person changed.
3. **One chord grammar.** A chord is modifiers then one key, joined by `+`:
   `Ctrl`, `Alt` and `Shift`, in any order, then a key name. Key names are
   egui's (`ArrowLeft`, `PageDown`, `F6`, `Delete`, `Num1`), a single letter
   or digit, or one of the short forms `Up`, `Down`, `Left`, `Right`, `=`,
   `-` and `/`. `Ctrl` is the platform's command key. One stroke per chord.
   settingsd checks the grammar; the application checks the key name, and
   reports and skips one it does not know.
4. **Edited by the existing transaction.** `settings.apply` takes
   `keymaps.<app>` (the whole map, or null to drop every change for that
   application) and `keymaps.<app>.<action>` (a list of chords, or null to
   return that action to its default). Limits: 16 applications, 256 actions
   each, 4 chords per action, 32 bytes per chord.
5. **Followed live.** The summary (`settings.get {view: summary}` and the
   summary topic) carries `keymaps`, omitted while empty. Each application
   applies its own entry whenever the profile's revision changes, so a new
   binding works at once, without a restart.
6. **How an application applies them.** The toolkit's command registry keeps
   the defaults it was built with. Applying a profile entry starts from
   them:
   - each listed action takes exactly its listed chords: the first is its
     menu accelerator, the rest also run it;
   - a chord the person bound takes precedence over a default, and the
     default loses that chord;
   - an unknown action or key is skipped and reported in the application's
     log.
7. **The record format is unchanged.** `keymaps` is authored and omitted
   while empty, so every stored profile re-serialises byte for byte and its
   seal still verifies. It has no effect on the resolved design, so the
   effective digest and design revision do not move when only a binding
   changes.

## Consequences

- dopus no longer reads `keymap.conf.mix`. No such file existed on the
  running session, so nothing needed migrating.
- `<app>.commands` reports each command's effective shortcut and its further
  chords, so an agent can read what a key does before and after a change.
- A shell that decodes the full snapshot (`deny_unknown_fields`) must be
  rebuilt before a profile carries `keymaps`. The portal is one; it is
  rebuilt with this change.
- A Keyboard Shortcuts page in Prefs can follow: it reads each application's
  commands over the Bus and writes `keymaps.<app>.<action>`.

## Not covered

- The compositor's own bindings (workspace and window keys) are not an
  application's commands; they stay in the compositor for now.
- Multi-stroke chords, and keys an editor widget handles itself (Cut, Copy,
  Paste and the cursor keys in ced's editor).

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-rec-and-play/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-rec-and-play.md) -->

# Decision — rec and play

Status: accepted 2026-10-11. Amends [the source layout](2026-10-04-source-layout.md)
(AGENTS.md §3.4).

## The decision

- **One Rust command-line tool, `cli/recplay`, installed as `rec` and
  `play`.** The binary is `recplay`. `rec` and `play` are links to it,
  added at install time in `/opt/mixos/bin`, and it chooses its behaviour
  from the name it was started as. Run as `recplay`, it prints help for both.
- **`play` puts something on the desktop.**
  - A file or URI opens with the handler the desktop already knows. That
    means shared-mime-info for the type, desktop entries' `MimeType=` and
    `mimeapps.list` for the handler. MixOS ships no table of its own and
    names no application.
  - A `.mix` program is performed when the person runs `play x.mix`
    themselves.
  - An `.mx` document is read by its schema and never executed.
  - `play` has **no media decoders.** It describes and previews a foreign
    format only through a handler's own command-line tool, named in a
    per-user document that ships empty.
- **`play` is the one resolver.**
  - `play --serve` answers `play.open`, `play.resolve`, `play.info`,
    `play.handlers` and `play.perform` on the Bus. The file manager and the portal's OpenURI
    use it, so every way of opening a file reaches the same handler.
  - Opening a `.mix` over the Bus shows it in the editor. Only
    `play.perform` runs it, and every perform is logged.
- **`rec` writes an editable Mix script** from what happens on the desktop.
  It builds on [executed commands](2026-10-11-executed-commands.md), [verb
  classes](2026-10-11-verb-classes.md) and the broker's observation stream.
  Runs of lines to one application are grouped in `address … end`, and a
  script never waits with a sleep.
- **A recording spec comes first.** `docs/docs/spec/recording/` is written and
  accepted before `rec` is built. It settles what these sources alone
  cannot:
  - **Replay arguments.** The broker does not show the payloads of a native
    session's calls, and a command event carries no arguments. Each
    application declares a recording surface: the committed actions it
    publishes with the arguments needed to repeat them, such as the path a
    dialog returned.
  - **One record per action.** A Bus call that runs a command shows up both
    in observation and as a command event. A causal identifier, or a rule
    for which source is authoritative, keeps exactly one.
  - **Per-verb replay rules.** Targets are resolved stably instead of being
    dropped (a tab, a buffer). Fencing values are made fresh on replay
    (revisions, operation ids). Deliberate waits such as `ced.wait` are kept
    as conditions, never turned into sleeps.
  - **Sensitivity.** Each owner marks what is sensitive, including text
    embedded in other values. A recording that lacks a required argument
    says so and is marked incomplete. It never guesses.
- **`rec` and `play` are accepted name collisions.** Both names belong to
  sox, which installs `/usr/bin/rec` and `/usr/bin/play` (checked
  2026-10-11 in Arch Linux and Debian trixie, where sox is the only owner).
  - MixOS installs to `/opt/mixos/bin`, which comes first in its PATH, so a
    MixOS session's `play` is this one.
  - sox's commands stay reachable by full path.
  - MixOS's own units and scripts call `/opt/mixos/bin/play` by absolute
    path.
  - `recplay` itself collides with nothing.

## Why

Opening a file and recording what a person does are two halves of the same
contract, the desktop's verbs. One resolver means the file manager, the
portal, the command line and agents never disagree about which application
opens a file. Using the freedesktop data that applications already install
means MixOS learns a new format the moment an application that handles it
is installed, without a MixOS change.

A recorded script is ordinary Mix. It can be read, edited, shared and
performed on another machine, and it shows exactly how the work was done.

The two names are the plain words for the two actions. sox's tools of the
same names are audio utilities that a MixOS session does not ship. The cost,
calling them by full path, falls on few people and is easy to pay.

## Consequences

- AGENTS.md §3.4 lists the accepted collisions: `mix` (Elixir), and `rec`
  and `play` (sox).
- `play`'s Bus verbs, the per-user handler document and the Bus snapshot
  document schema are registered as contracts when they land.
- The file manager stops spawning `xdg-open` and calls `play.open`.
- Rejected: a MixOS MIME-to-application table. It duplicates what every
  application already installs, and it would have to name applications.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-settings-authority-stays-a-service/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-settings-authority-stays-a-service.md) -->

# The settings authority stays a separate service on noded

Status: accepted. Builds on
[Desktop settings have one native ABP authority](2026-10-07-settings-authority.md).

## Context

The question came up whether settingsd should be merged into noded, since
every settings read and publication already passes through the broker.

- noded is the Bus broker: every service and application on a node
  depends on it, and the ABP wire is frozen.
- settingsd is a domain authority. It owns a durable, sealed settings
  store, compiles design sources into projections, and answers
  `settings.apply` and `settings.get`.
- noded retains settingsd's last publication, so an application starts
  with the right look while settingsd is stopped or restarting.

## Decision

1. **settingsd stays its own process and unit**, a client of noded like
   editd, portald and releasesd. It is not merged into noded, and noded
   gains no settings logic beyond what any service gets: topic
   reservation for the registered owner, retention and owner stamping.
2. **The reasons are failure isolation and least privilege, not
   convenience:**
   - a settingsd crash, restart or upgrade must not drop the Bus;
     retained topics carry consumers through it;
   - design compilation is CPU work. One apply once took about 370 ms of
     compile time; inside the broker that would stall every message;
   - noded listens on the network; the settings store is written only by
     settingsd's service account;
   - noded is generic plumbing and runs on headless nodes with no desktop
     settings at all.
3. **The costs are accepted and handled where they arise:** start order
   (settingsd starts after noded is reachable, and the session target
   upholds it), one Bus hop per read, and changes that touch both, such as
   a new reserved topic, ship together.

## Consequences

- A proposal to fold another service (editd, portald, releasesd) into
  noded meets the same test and is refused for the same reasons unless a
  decision says otherwise.
- Bus-level improvements that help settings, such as publisher stamps for
  plain clients or conditional reads, belong in noded as generic features
  available to every service.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-settings-snapshot-schema-2/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-settings-snapshot-schema-2.md) -->

# Settings snapshot schema 2 sends each design once

Status: accepted. Settings contract 0.3.0 (additive), snapshot schema 2 beside
schema 1. Follows [plain followers read a summary](2026-10-11-settings-summary-reads.md).

## Context

A snapshot carries one compiled design projection per effective context:
the desktop and each native app. With the embedded design every context
shares one projection, so a 499 KB schema 1 snapshot holds seven copies of
one 71 KB projection. Native consumers (the portal, the compositor's scene
host and applications on the shared `settings` consumer) need those
projections, receive the snapshot as a retained topic delivery and read it
again to confirm, so each of them moves about 1 MB per change.

Several of those consumers belong to applications still awaiting their port
to this tree's egui toolkit. They carry their own copy of the settings
library and must keep working, unchanged, until each is ported.

## Decision

1. **Schema 2 is a wire form.** `settings::compact::CompactSnapshot` holds
   each distinct projection once under `designs`, keyed by its digest; each
   context's `design` is a digest naming one. `compact::decode` expands
   schema 1 or 2 into the same in-memory `Snapshot`, so the consumer,
   reducer, cache and effective digests do not change. A context naming an
   unknown design, or a design no context names, is refused. Digests are
   opaque keys to the decoder.
2. **Asked for, never assumed.** `settings.get` (full view) and
   `settings.appearance.get` take `schema`: 1 is the default and is never
   sent; 2 answers in the compact form; any other is refused with
   `unsupported_schema`.
3. **A compact topic.** settingsd publishes the retained snapshot on three
   topics, in order: `settingsd.desktop.changed.<profile>` (schema 1),
   `settingsd.desktop.compact.<profile>` (schema 2), then the summary. A
   revision is published once all three are; a failure retries all three.
   noded reserves the compact topic for settingsd as it does the others.
4. **Ported consumers move now.** The shared native consumer
   (`settings::native`) follows the compact topic and reads schema 2, and
   the portal asks for schema 2. Measured with the embedded design, the
   compact snapshot is about 72 KB where schema 1 is 499 KB.
5. **Unported consumers move with their port.** An application or service
   still on its own copy of the settings library keeps following the schema
   1 topic and reading schema 1. Each moves when it is ported, by using the
   shared consumer. Nothing in an unported consumer changes for this
   decision.

## Retiring schema 1

The schema 1 topic and default stay while any consumer still uses them.
Publishing schema 1 costs a full snapshot per change, so once the last
consumer has moved, a later decision stops publishing it and makes schema 2
the default read. The library keeps decoding schema 1 for caches and old
retained state.

## Not chosen

Deltas between revisions, compression and local compilation are discussed
in the summary decision. Schema 2 removes duplication without changing what
a consumer holds; local compilation (no projection on the wire) remains the
next step once consumers can pin the design source by digest.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-settings-summary-reads/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-settings-summary-reads.md) -->

# Plain settings followers read a summary, not the snapshot

Status: accepted. Settings contract 0.2.0 (additive). Builds on
[Desktop settings have one native ABP authority](2026-10-07-settings-authority.md).

## Context

The settings snapshot carries the profile's complete effective design: one
compiled projection per context (the desktop and each native app). Measured
on a running session with the embedded design source:

- a `settings.get` reply is 499 KB of JSON, 498 KB of it `effective`: seven
  byte-identical 71 KB projections, 62 KB of each a button table;
- settingsd publishes that whole snapshot as the retained payload of
  `settingsd.desktop.changed.<profile>`;
- an application following the session look on a plain Bus connection
  (`settings::follow::Follower`) cannot verify a delivery's publisher, so it
  treats the delivery as a hint and reads `settings.get` again. It uses only
  the profile's identity, revision and appearance names.

One appearance change therefore moved about 0.5 MB to every plain follower
twice (the delivery and the re-read), and each parsed it. Idle traffic is
zero; the cost is per change. Native consumers (the portal, the compositor's
scene host and applications using the shared `settings` consumer) do use the
projections, from owner-stamped deliveries.

## Decision

1. **A summary topic.** settingsd also publishes a retained
   `settingsd.desktop.summary.<profile>` whose payload is a
   `settings::Summary`: schema, binding, incarnation, revision, design
   revision, source digest, the appearance names and `custom_source`. It
   never carries the projections or a custom design source. noded reserves
   it for settingsd exactly as it reserves the snapshot topic: only the
   registered `settingsd` service may publish or clear it, and inner routing
   headers are canonicalised. A revision counts as published once both
   topics are; a failure retries both.
2. **A summary read.** `settings.get` takes an optional `view`: `full` (the
   default, the complete snapshot as before) or `summary` (the same
   `Summary` under `summary`, with the usual status fields). An unknown view
   is refused like any unknown field. A request without `view` reads exactly
   as it did under 0.1.0, and the field is never sent at its default.
3. **Plain followers move to the summary.** The `Follower` subscribes to
   the summary topic and reads the summary view; Prefs does the same. A
   follower still treats a delivery only as a hint: this decision does not
   change how deliveries are trusted.
4. **Native consumers are unchanged.** The snapshot topic and the full view
   keep their schema and behaviour for every consumer that uses projections.

Measured on the same session after the change, one appearance change sends
a plain follower a 566-byte summary delivery and a 587-byte summary read,
where it had a 542 KB delivery and a 542 KB read. The remaining large
transfers belong to native consumers: the snapshot publish, the portal's
`settings.appearance.get` and the compositor scene host's full read, each
about 542 KB. They are the subject of the deduplication step below.

## Rollout

The summary topic is new, so the order matters: noded (the reservation),
then settingsd (publishes and serves the summary), then the followers. A
follower that reaches a settingsd without the summary view is refused
(`unknown field`) and keeps its last look, and it hears no hints from a
settingsd that does not publish the summary topic. Roll back in the reverse
order.

## Considered and deferred

- **Deduplicating `effective` by content digest** (one copy per distinct
  projection, contexts naming a digest) would make the full snapshot about
  72 KB. It changes snapshot schema 1, which native consumers decode and the
  optional cache stores, so it needs a schema 2 negotiated per request and
  the consumer, reducer and cache moving together. It is the next step for
  native consumers.
- **Compiling projections locally from the summary.** A projection is a
  function of the pinned source and the selected axes, and native consumers
  already link the design library: they could compile instead of
  transferring, at a few milliseconds per context. It needs the source
  pinned by digest and a compiler-version check, which the cache already
  records.
- **Immutable artifacts fetched by digest** remain the planned path for
  settings too large to inline (the 960 KiB snapshot ceiling).
- **Deltas between revisions** are not worth it: a scheme change rewrites
  most colour values in a projection, so a JSON delta is nearly the size of
  the projection. A summary is already smaller than any delta of it.
- **Compression** under the frozen ABP framing would mean base64 bodies;
  WebSocket permessage-deflate is not available in the Bus's WebSocket
  library and its window is too small for repeated 71 KB projections.
- **Trusting summary deliveries** (dropping the re-read) needs the
  publisher stamp noded already records to reach plain clients. It is a
  separate change to the Bus client API.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-verb-classes/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-verb-classes.md) -->

# Decision — verb classes

Status: accepted 2026-10-11. Amends AGENTS.md §5 (Bus verbs are wire
contracts).

## The decision

- **The verb registry moves to schema 2.** Every entry in
  `docs/docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix` gains a `class`, one of:

  | class | Meaning | Examples |
  |---|---|---|
  | `intent` | Changes what an application or service holds, or what another caller would see, at someone's request | `<app>.open`, `<app>.execute`, `<app>.refresh`, `settings.apply`, `releases.notes` (it fetches when nothing is cached), `<app>.quit`, `<app>.window` |
  | `query` | Changes nothing another caller could observe. The one allowance: it may write the artefact it was asked for and returns, such as a screenshot | `<app>.ping`, `.info`, `.state`, `.commands`, `.ui.tree`, `.ui.capture`, `.window.state`, `settings.get`, `ced.wait` |
  | `input` | Synthetic low-level input, standing in for a person's hands | `<app>.ui.click`, `.ui.pointer`, `.ui.scroll`, `.ui.key`, `.ui.type` |
  | `system` | Session plumbing. The single-instance activation verb `<app>.show` is `system` even when something calls it directly | `<app>.show` |

- **The class describes the verb, not one call.** A verb that both reads and
  changes state is `intent`.
- **When in doubt, it is `intent`.** Dropping a real action is worse than
  keeping a read.
- **A verb an application describes as `read_only` is a `query`.** Each
  application's registry test checks this. The reverse need not hold:
  `.ui.capture` writes a file, so it is not read-only, but it is still a
  query.
- **The registry gate** (`tools/verb_registry.mix`) refuses:
  - a schema other than 2;
  - an entry that is not in the canonical one-line form;
  - an unknown or missing field;
  - a bad name, owner, status or version;
  - a duplicate;
  - a class outside the four.

## Why

Tools that watch the Bus need to know what a verb is for:

- a recorder keeps intent and drops reads;
- a live traffic view colours them differently;
- an agent asked "what changed?" looks only at intent.

Without a declared class, each tool guesses from verb names, and the guesses
drift apart. The registry already declares every verb's owner, version and
status, so its purpose belongs there too.

## Consequences

- Every existing entry is classified in one change, together with the gate.
- A new verb is registered with its class from its first commit.
- Classes are about purpose, not replay. A recorder still needs each owner's
  replay rules ([rec and play](2026-10-11-rec-and-play.md)), for example
  that `ced.wait` is a deliberate ordering point.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-hostd/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-hostd.md) -->

# Decision — hostd, the host service

Status: accepted 2026-10-12.

## The decision

- **One service, `hostd`, runs as root on each host.** It has two jobs:
  information about the host (hardware, OS, the MixOS mode, network
  management state, devices, power) and privileged actions on the host.
  It is the host agent of the VT-native design: the only MixOS code on the
  host besides `mix`.
- **No generic exec.** No verb runs a caller-supplied command, script or
  shell string. Each verb does one job, checks its arguments against a
  schema and does the work natively (writes the file itself, calls
  networkd, resolved, logind or iwd over Varlink or D-Bus).
- **Written in Rust.** Mix is the client. A root process that interprets
  scripts is too much attack surface.
- **A verb that can't be reversed is not added.** Exception: the two desk
  power verbs, `desk.restart` and `desk.stop` (see Amendments).
- **Every new verb is reviewed on its own,** and the verb list stays short.

### Callers and transport

- **Local callers** use a Unix socket. Identity comes from the kernel
  (`SO_PEERCRED`) and the caller's cgroup, never from the request.
- **Reads are also served on the Bus,** like any other service's.
- **Writes from other nodes** are accepted only when signed by a controller
  key listed in that host's policy, over the target node, a nonce and an
  expiry. Mesh trust alone never authorises a write. A host with no listed
  controller accepts no remote writes. Enforcement is on the receiving
  host.
- **Ports below 1024 are not hostd's job.** A service that binds one gets
  `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` in its own unit.

### Tiers

| Tier | Examples | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| read | host info, network state, devices | caller identity |
| reversible | Wi-Fi connect, link configuration, device bind, suspend | a standing grant, plus a dead-man check or a kept previous state |
| reversible, wide blast radius | firewall, host package upgrade, reboot | a grant, a second signature from an independent reviewer, and a rate limit |
| irreversible | — | no verb exists |

### Autonomy within limits set in advance

- **Standing grants,** not per-call prompts. A grant names the caller (from
  the kernel), the verbs, argument limits and an optional expiry. Only
  creating or widening a grant needs a person, confirmed through physical
  input that no Bus caller can synthesise.
- **Reversible by construction.** A verb applies its change, runs a health
  check, and reverts unless the check passes in time. It keeps the previous
  state (the previous file, or a filesystem snapshot) behind a receipt that
  `hostd.undo` restores.
- **Limits:** a rate limit per caller and verb, a circuit breaker after
  repeated rollbacks, and a `freeze` that drops hostd to reads only.
- **Audit:** one journal record per call.

### Files hostd owns

hostd writes only files it names itself (networkd files are
`/etc/systemd/network/50-hostd-*`) and never edits a file it didn't write.

## Why

- Agents need to change host configuration (network, WireGuard, power,
  devices) without `sudo` from a session, and without a person approving
  each call.
- MixOS core has no polkit. hostd is the mechanism and its policy in one
  small binary, with rules as data instead of scripts.
- Closed verbs make a stolen credential worth far less than a root shell.

## Consequences

- Session code never shells out to `sudo`; a missing host action is a new
  hostd verb.
- Write verbs arrive one reviewed verb at a time. The first is
  `net.link.apply`; the verbs, grants and refusals are documented in the
  [host service manual](../../hostd/README.md).
- **Root on the host** means uid 0 in hostd's own pid and user namespaces,
  proven through a pidfd. Root inside a container is never root on the
  host, with or without uid remapping.

## Amendments

### 2026-10-13: desk power verbs are an exception to "no irreversible verbs"

`desk.restart` and `desk.stop` restart or power off one desk machine. A
powered-off desk cannot be put back by hostd, so no undo can exist. The
desk must still be able to restart or stop itself, so the two verbs are
admitted as exceptions to the irreversibility rule. They are not a pattern
for other verbs.

Reversibility is replaced by these limits, which apply to both verbs:

- **One desk per grant.** The verb takes no machine name. The grant's
  `desks` limit must name exactly one valid machine, and that machine is the
  only one the verb can touch. A caller with no desk, or two, is refused.
- **The host is never powered.** The verbs run `machinectl reboot` or
  `machinectl poweroff` on the named machine only.
- **A standing grant, rate limited.** Nothing runs without a grant, and a
  grant carries a rate limit and an expiry.
- **Freeze applies.** `hostd.freeze` refuses both verbs.
- **Every call is recorded,** as a receipt and in the audit journal. `hostd.undo`
  refuses both verbs.

Deferred (Mark, 2026-10-13): the second signature from an independent reviewer
that the reboot tier requires is not built for `desk.*`. Security gates are
added once the desktop is ready for daily use, where they are needed. Until
then, the grant's rate limit and expiry are the only second check.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-non-root-install-and-service-ports/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-non-root-install-and-service-ports.md) -->

# Decision — non-root install, per-service users, mesh-first ports

Status: proposed 2026-10-12. Builds on
[one repository, install profiles](2026-10-12-one-repository-install-profiles.md)
and the one-system-binary design (every headless daemon a personality of
`mix`, chosen by `argv[0]`), which needs its own decision record.

## The question

The server programs (maild, webd, dnsd and the rest) are moving into MixOS,
headed for one `mix` binary. Updates already reach desktop users through
releasesd, which by rule never changes anything as root. Can a whole node,
servers included, be installed and kept current without root, and how do
unprivileged daemons serve ports 25, 53, 443, 465, 587 and 993?

## Where these servers run

The usual MixOS server is a node on its owner's own WireGuard mesh, a /24
of their machines. Mail, web and DNS are served to that mesh, not to the
internet. A server that must take connections from outside the mesh (an MX
on public port 25, a public website on 443) is the exception. This record
covers the mesh case and states what it does not settle for the public one.

## The decision

### 1. Root installs once; updates never need it

- **Bootstrap (root, once per node, and again only when units change):**
  create the system users, install the unit, socket, sysusers and tmpfiles
  files, and hand the server prefix to the `mixos` user.
- **The server prefix `/opt/mixos` is owned by the system user `mixos`.**
  A releasesd instance running as `mixos` keeps it current, with the same
  checks as a desktop install (GitHub digest and `SHA256SUMS`, staged
  unpack, previous version kept for rollback). It uses releasesd's existing
  layout through its environment: `MIXOS_RELEASES_ROOT=/opt/mixos`, so
  releases land in `/opt/mixos/opt/<app>/<version>` and their programs are
  linked into `/opt/mixos/bin`. The unit paths (`/opt/mixos/bin/<daemon>`)
  do not change.
- **Desktop installs stay per user** in `~/.local`, as today.
- Binaries are readable and executable by everyone and writable only by
  `mixos`. No daemon runs as `mixos`.

### 2. Every daemon runs as its own user

- Each server daemon runs as its own system user (`maild`, `webd`, `dnsd`
  and so on), declared in its component's sysusers fragment. Never as root,
  never as a login user, never as `mixos`.
- Each daemon's state lives in its own `StateDirectory=`, which no other
  service user can read. A compromised webd cannot read mail, keys or the
  login user's home.
- Units use systemd's sandboxing (`NoNewPrivileges=yes`,
  `ProtectSystem=strict`, `ProtectHome=yes`, `PrivateTmp=yes` and a
  `CapabilityBoundingSet=` that names only what the daemon needs), and each
  component's units are reviewed against that list.

### 3. Privileged ports come from systemd

- **Socket activation is the target.** A system `.socket` unit binds the
  privileged ports as root and passes the open sockets to the daemon
  (`LISTEN_FDS`). The daemon never holds a capability. Socket activation
  also keeps the listening socket open across a restart, so an upgrade
  drops no connections that are still queued.
- **Interim:** a daemon that cannot take inherited sockets yet gets
  `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` with
  `CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` in its unit. Taking
  inherited sockets is part of each port's definition of done (maild,
  webd, dnsd).
- **Not file capabilities.** The kernel clears them whenever the file is
  replaced, so every update would silently lose the ports. In the one
  binary they would also give the `mix` shell, and every script, the right
  to bind 443.
- **Not lowering `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` by default.** It
  applies to every user on the node. A node owner may still choose it for a
  single-user machine, but MixOS does not do it for them.

### 4. Mesh first

- Server daemons listen on the node's mesh address by default, never on
  every address. The `.socket` units name the mesh address
  (`ListenStream=<mesh-ip>:25`, with `FreeBind=yes` so the socket can be
  bound before the WireGuard interface is up).
- Listening on a public address is an explicit per-node configuration,
  never a default and never part of an install profile.

### 5. Applying an update without root

- releasesd (as `mixos`) moves `current` and records the transition in
  `meta.json`. A root-owned systemd `.path` unit watches that file and
  starts a root service that restarts only the units whose component
  version or hash changed in the release manifest. The `mixos` user
  triggers the restart but never controls which units restart or how.
- A release whose units, sysusers or tmpfiles fragments changed cannot be
  applied by `mixos`. releasesd installs the binaries, reports that the
  bootstrap step is needed, and leaves the running services on the
  previous version until a root user runs the installer.

### 6. What still needs root at run time

- **nspawnd:** `systemd-nspawn` needs root. It stays a root service in its
  own profile, outside this model.
- **noded:** reading network state needs nothing; changing it needs
  `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, granted in its unit the same way as the interim port
  capability, only if that node uses the feature.
- **compd:** none. Seat, input and display access come through logind and
  libseat, as today.

## Not settled: servers open to the internet

A daemon that accepts connections from outside the mesh (an MX on public
port 25, a public website on 443) faces hostile traffic. Running it as its
own sandboxed user, with the port granted by systemd, is still the baseline.
It is not shown to be enough: rate limits, DoS behaviour, TLS and ACME
exposure, whether the public listener should be its own process or node, and
firewall policy all belong to a separate decision before any public
listener ships as a supported configuration.

## Why

- **Updates without root** are what make the releasesd model work for a
  whole operating system: no package manager, no distribution repository,
  and no root shell for routine updates.
- **Per-service users** limit what one compromised daemon can reach. Running
  every daemon as the login user would have been simpler, but would have
  handed a mail-server bug the owner's SSH keys and secrets.
- **Ports from systemd** grant the right per service and per port, survive
  updates, and keep capabilities away from the shell that shares the
  binary.
- **Mesh first** matches how MixOS servers are used, and keeps the
  internet-facing case visible as the exception it is.

## Alternatives

- **Everything as the login user** (user units with lingering, plus the
  sysctl). Rejected: no isolation between daemons or from the owner's home.
- **File capabilities on `mix`.** Rejected: lost on every update, and
  granted to every script.
- **Root installs through a package manager.** Rejected: it is the
  dependency that releasesd removes.
- **Root-run releasesd for the server prefix.** Rejected: releasesd's trust
  rule (never act as root) is what makes a bad release unable to take over
  the node. A fixed `.path` unit for restarts keeps root's part small.

## Consequences

- Each server component ships a sysusers fragment, its units with the
  sandboxing list, and `.socket` units for its ports. The install-profile
  resolver lists them, as that decision already requires.
- maild, webd and dnsd learn to take inherited sockets as part of their
  ports.
- releasesd gains a server instance (`mixos` user, `/opt/mixos` root) and a
  "units changed" result. The restart service and its `.path` unit are new
  work, alongside the installer the install-profiles decision calls for.
- The bootstrap installer is the only routine root step, and it runs again
  only when a release changes units.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-one-repository-install-profiles/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-one-repository-install-profiles.md) -->

# Decision — one repository, install profiles

Status: accepted 2026-10-12; amended 2026-10-12 after review. AGENTS.md
§2.3 (identity and metadata), §2.5 (Mix components) and §10 (the
checklist) are amended in the same change that adds the `profiles` field
and its gate.

## The question

MixOS has two audiences: a desktop (the compositor, the apps and their
settings services) and servers (mail, web, blobs, DNS and the mesh daemons
on headless nodes). The server programs have not moved into this
repository yet. Should they get a repository of their own?

## The decision

- **Everything stays in this repository and its one Cargo workspace.**
  Desktop, server, command-line and library code alike. There is no second
  MixOS source repository for server programs.
- **The split is an install split, not a source split.** Every shipping
  component declares the **install profiles** that include it:

  | Profile | Meaning |
  |---|---|
  | `base` | On every MixOS system: the shell and the Bus node |
  | `server` | What a headless node may run |
  | `desktop` | The desktop session: compositor, apps, their services and the session's own wiring |

- **Composition.** `server` and `desktop` each include `base`: resolving
  either one yields its own components plus `base`'s. A system may install
  both. A resolved set is the union of its profiles, each component once.
- **Who declares.** A component's *principal* package declares `profiles`:
  the package whose name is its component (the directory under `apps/`,
  `services/` or `cli/`), or a Mix component's `component.mx`. The list is
  non-empty, has no duplicates and names only the three profiles. The field
  is absent on libraries, on a component's private crates (whatever `kind`
  they inherit from their owner), and on `tool` and `test` packages.
  Libraries are never installed on their own; they are linked into what
  needs them. The session's targets and wiring (`session/`) belong to
  `desktop`; when the `session` kind lands, it declares `profiles` like any
  other shipping component.
- **Where it is declared.** A Rust component adds `profiles` to its
  `[package.metadata.mixos]`:

  ```toml
  [package.metadata.mixos]
  component = "webd"
  kind = "service"
  layer = "core"
  contract = "public"
  profiles = ["server"]
  ```

  A Mix component adds the same `profiles` list to its `component.mx`.
- **Naming.** Install profiles are unrelated to Cargo's build profiles
  (`release`, `release-fast`) and to any service's own settings profiles.
  Prose says "install profile"; tools take `--install-profile`, beside
  `--cargo-profile` and `--target`, never a bare `--profile`.
- **The profile gate** is new, workspace-wide work. Today's closure and
  layering gates check compd's own crates only; they do not protect other
  components. The profile gate:
  - refuses the declaration errors above;
  - refuses a `base` or `server` component that itself declares the
    `desktop` layer;
  - resolves the normal and build dependency closure of each `base` and
    `server` principal, for every feature set its profiles build, and
    refuses any `desktop`-layer workspace package in it, and any upstream
    GUI crate (smithay, egui, eframe, wgpu, winit, Bevy and the like) even
    though those carry no MixOS metadata;
  - for a Mix component, which has no Cargo closure, refuses a `desktop`
    layer in a `base` or `server` component; what it calls on the Bus is
    checked at review, as AGENTS.md §2.5 already says.

  The component index ([`/docs/components/`](../components.md)) shows each component's
  profiles.
- **Resolving, installing and activating are separate.**
  - **Resolve:** one tool answers "what is in `server`?" from the metadata,
    deterministically. Its output covers the packages to build, the Mix
    components, and each component's runtime artefacts: units by class
    (system or session), `sysusers` and `tmpfiles` fragments, and assets.
    Build scripts, images and installers never keep their own lists.
  - **Install:** places those files. Rust components go to an installer
    that gives binaries and units the record, rollback and drift check
    `tools/component_install.mix` gives Mix components (separate work that
    follows this decision); Mix components go to that existing installer.
  - **Activate:** which services a particular node runs, with what
    configuration, is that node's decision, not the profile's. Installing
    `server` makes a service available; it does not start every server on
    every node.

### The first assignment

| Component | Profiles |
|---|---|
| `mix-shell` (the `mix` binary), `noded` | `base` |
| `compd`, `settingsd`, `portald`, `editd`, `releasesd`, `busviewer`, `ced`, `dopus`, `prefs` | `desktop` |

`server` starts empty: the server programs join it as they move in (mail,
web, blobs and the rest). `releasesd` is a per-user session service and
`editd` serves the session's editors, so both are `desktop`. A headless
mode for either would be its own decision, with suitable supervision,
before it joins `server`.

## Why

- **The two sides share their foundation.** The Bus, noded, Mix, the config
  and props libraries and logging sit under both, and they change almost
  daily. A second repository could pin them as Git dependencies rather than
  wait for releases, but every foundation change would still mean a
  coordinated upgrade on the other side, and consolidating duplicated code
  across the boundary would mean moving it between repositories.
- **Changes cut across both.** The verb registry's move to classes changed
  the registry, its gate and every application in one commit. Across two
  repositories that is coordinated pull requests that can drift apart.
- **The separation that matters can be enforced here.** Headless code
  never needing a GUI stack is a property of a dependency closure, and the
  profile gate checks exactly that for every `base` and `server` component.
  A repository boundary would enforce it less precisely: it says nothing
  about which features or which programs a node gets.
- **This was decided once already.** The
  [source layout decision](2026-10-04-source-layout.md) rejected one
  repository per component so that one dependency graph can be gated,
  shared code consolidated, and changes made atomically. A desktop/server
  split is the same proposal in two pieces, and nothing it relied on has
  changed.
- **What people actually need separated is the build and the install.** A
  mail server should never compile or install the compositor. Profiles say
  that precisely, from data, in one place.

## Alternatives

- **A second repository for server programs.** The strongest case for it:
  an independent lockfile, toolchain and release pipeline, so desktop
  dependency churn never touches a server build and a server fix never
  waits on the desktop. That isolation is real; it loses to the shared,
  fast-moving foundation and the consolidation still to do. A split would
  be the right call if the server side ever needed a different licence,
  private code, its own team or its own release cadence. None of these
  applies. Private deployment detail already lives outside this repository.
- **Cargo features or a second workspace in this repository.** Rejected. A
  second workspace means two lockfiles and two dependency graphs, which is
  what AGENTS.md §0 rules out. Features select code inside a crate, not
  which programs a system gets.
- **A top-level `server/` directory.** Rejected: the top level is
  classified by kind only (AGENTS.md §1). A web server is a service like
  any other; which systems it belongs on is data.

## Consequences

- One `Cargo.lock`: a dependency bump for the desktop also moves the
  servers' resolved versions, and a server fix ships from the same tree as
  that day's desktop work. Each component's tests and the gates catch a
  break; the alternative was version drift between repositories.
- Building a server set compiles only that set's closure (`cargo build -p`),
  so headless builds stay small. A server build host still checks out the
  whole tree, desktop vendor forks included.
- AGENTS.md §2.3 and §2.5 gain the `profiles` field, and §10's checklist
  asks for it.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-one-system-binary/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-one-system-binary.md) -->

# Decision — one system binary

Status: accepted 2026-10-12. Amends [the source layout](2026-10-04-source-layout.md)
(AGENTS.md §2.3, §3.4, §6 and §9).

## The decision

- **One binary, `mix`, carries the shell and every headless daemon.** It is
  built by a new host component, `cli/system` (package `system`, kind `cli`).
  The host's only code is the dispatcher and the global allocator.
- **A daemon is a personality, chosen by the name the binary was started
  as.** `noded`, `maild`, `webd` and the rest are symlinks to `mix` in
  `/opt/mixos/bin`. Each still runs as its own process, under its own unit
  and journal identity, because the kernel names a process after the name it
  was executed by. There are no daemon subcommands under `mix`: the shell's
  first-argument namespace stays the shell's.
  - `mix --personalities` lists what the binary contains, with each
    component's version.
  - An unknown name exits 2 and prints that list.
  - The shell's self re-execution passes `mix` as its name, so a re-exec from
    a daemon personality comes back as the shell.
- **Components keep their identity.** Each daemon keeps its own crate, tests,
  units, metadata, version and verb registry. Its library exports
  `pub fn main() -> ExitCode`; its own `[[bin]]` stays for development
  builds. `cli/mix-shell` becomes a library with no binary.
- **What goes in:** the shell, `noded`, and every headless base and server
  daemon as it arrives, including the headless desktop-profile services.
  **What stays out:** anything with a GUI stack (compd, the applications),
  and any daemon whose dependencies dwarf the rest. The install-profile
  gate's closure check enforces the first.
- **One personality per process.** No setup happens at link or load time.
  The async runtime, TLS provider, signal masks, panic hook and logger are set
  up in the personality's own `main`, never in a shared library's
  initialiser. Each personality passes its own logging identity and records
  its own build provenance. Every personality uses one allocator, mimalloc.
  A test starts every personality and checks its identity.
- **Fleet builds are static.** The shipped binary targets
  `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, fully static, so one file runs on every
  supported distribution regardless of its C library.
- **Shell tests test the shipped binary.** The shell's process-level tests
  live in `cli/system/tests/` and run `mix` as built by the host.

## Why

Every daemon links the same core: the async runtime, serialisation, the Bus,
the Mix evaluator, logging. Linked separately, each carries its own copy, and
every release links that core once per daemon. Measured on the first
two-personality build (the shell and `noded`), the combined binary was 11%
smaller than the two separate ones and its release link took 40% less time.
Both gains grow with each personality. A static musl build cost nothing in
size, startup or evaluator speed, and the same file ran on both
distributions tested.

One file also means one artifact per architecture, one hash to verify and one
version on every node. Running daemons keep the old file's inode, so an
upgrade restarts only the units whose component changed.

Memory is not part of the case: different personalities run different code,
so they share little.

## Consequences

- AGENTS.md §2.3: `cli/system` builds the `mix` binary. `cli/mix-shell` is
  the shell's library and builds no binary.
- AGENTS.md §3.4: a daemon may be installed as a personality, a symlink named
  after its component; units name the symlink.
- AGENTS.md §6: `cli/system` is the one package allowed a non-dev dependency
  on `kind = "cli"` packages.
- AGENTS.md §9: the bootstrap is `cargo build --profile release-fast -p system`.
- Build scripts that built `-p mix-shell` to get `mix` build `-p system`.
- The installer creates each node's personality symlinks from its install
  profiles, keeps the previous binary for rollback, and restarts only changed
  units. The release archive's manifest lists each personality with its
  component version.
