<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-scene-strings/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-scene-strings.md) -->

# Decision — scene strings until Mix reads Fluent

Status: accepted 2026-10-12. Bounds AGENTS.md §4's i18n rule for Mix Scenes content until the gap below is closed.

## The problem

AGENTS.md §4 says user-visible strings come from Fluent catalogues
(`<component>/i18n/<lang>/<component>.ftl`) and that new GUI code does not
hard-code them. Mix Scenes content, the panel, launcher, calendar, notes
and settings scenes in `share/scenes`, is written in Mix, and **Mix has no
Fluent loader**. A scene cannot read a catalogue today. Its strings ("Apps",
the calendar's month names, the launcher's category labels, and the
panel's hover tips) are English literals in Mix.

That is a gap in Mix, not a reason to work around it (AGENTS.md §0).

## The decision

- **Until Mix reads Fluent, a scene library keeps its user-visible strings
  in one table** — the English source — and builds every string through one
  lookup. `share/scenes/lib/models.mix` does this for the panel's hover
  tips: `$TEXT` holds them, `text(key, vars)` fills `{name}` placeholders
  and `counted(n, none, one, many)` chooses the plural form.
- **No new scattered literals.** New user-visible scene strings go into
  such a table, never inline in the model code.
- **The table is the seam.** When Mix gains a Fluent reader, each table
  becomes `share/scenes/i18n/en/<scene-library>.ftl`, keyed exactly as the
  table is, and the lookup reads the session's language with English as
  the fallback. The callers do not change.
- **Older literals** ("Apps" in the panel template, `CATEGORY_LABELS` and
  the month names in `lib/data.mix`) move into tables when their scenes are
  next edited, not as a drive-by.

## Closing the gap

The Mix work is a Fluent reader (parse `.ftl`, resolve a message with
arguments and plural selectors, choose a locale with fallback), added to
`libs/mix` as a builtin or a standard module. This decision is superseded
when that lands and the scene tables are converted.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-screenshot/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-screenshot.md) -->

# Decision — screenshot

Status: accepted 2026-10-12; amended 2026-10-13 (saved shots are named
`YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.png`, as Spectacle can name them, instead of
`Screenshot YYYY-MM-DD HH-MM-SS.png`). Amends
[the source layout](2026-10-04-source-layout.md) (AGENTS.md §3.4).

## The decision

- **The screenshot and annotation app is `apps/screenshot`.** Its package,
  binary and directory are `screenshot`, its app id is
  `dev.mixos.screenshot` and its Bus service and verbs are `screenshot` and
  `screenshot.*`. "Screenshot" is exactly what the app does, and it is the
  word a person looks for in a launcher.
- **It supersedes Cap.** Cap was the iced screenshot app (`apps/cap`,
  `dev.mixos.cap`, verbs `cap.*`) that lived outside this tree. The egui
  port brings its behaviour across under the new name:
  - the engine moves into the `annotation` crate: the immutable capture,
    the editable objects with undo, one painter for preview and export,
    and no-clobber PNG publication;
  - the iced shell is rewritten on the toolkit, with every action a
    registry command.

  Cap's names are retired and stay reserved (§3.5): the binary `cap`, the
  app id `dev.mixos.cap` and the verbs `cap.ping`, `cap.info`,
  `cap.capture`, `cap.cancel`, `cap.open`, `cap.annotate`, `cap.move`,
  `cap.delete`, `cap.crop`, `cap.undo`, `cap.redo`, `cap.export`,
  `cap.show` and `cap.quit`. They are entered in the retired-names
  registry when it lands. None of them was ever registered here.
- **Print Screen starts it.** compd's bindings, in both profiles:
  - Print takes a region;
  - Shift+Print takes the whole output;
  - Alt+Print takes the window that had the keyboard.

  compd launches `screenshot --comp SERVICE --capture MODE`, naming its own
  Bus service (so a nested compd's key captures through that compd) and,
  for a window capture, the window that had the keyboard at the key press.
  There is one window and one headless instance per compositor:
  `screenshot` and `screenshot-headless` for `comp`, `screenshot-<comp>`
  and `screenshot-headless-<comp>` for another when the name fits in 31
  bytes, else `screenshot--<hash>` and `screenshot-headless--<hash>`; a
  window name never starts with `screenshot-headless`. If that window is already running, the new
  process hands the request to it over the Bus (`screenshot.take`) and
  exits. Unsaved annotations are never discarded by a key press: the window
  comes forward and asks first.
- **Saved shots go to the screenshots folder.** Save (Ctrl+S) writes
  `XDG_PICTURES_DIR/Screenshots/YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.png` (local time) with no
  dialog. A taken name gets `_2`, `_3` and so on, and nothing is ever
  replaced. Every save is published on `screenshot.saved` and recorded, so
  an agent gets the latest shots from `screenshot.recent` without being
  told a path.
- **`screenshot` is an accepted name collision.**
  - Arch Linux's `extra/nwg-shell` installs `/usr/bin/screenshot`, a helper
    for that shell. It was the only owner found on 2026-10-12, checked with
    `pacman -F`.
  - In Debian trixie no package installs a `screenshot` in a binary
    directory. The name appears only inside private directories (a GIMP
    plug-in, the Qt examples), checked with the packages.debian.org
    contents search.
  - Fedora was not checked: it has no public file search that works
    without a Fedora host.
  - MixOS installs to `/opt/mixos/bin`, which comes first in its PATH, so a
    MixOS session's `screenshot` is this one. compd launches it from its
    own directory, and the desktop entry names it by absolute path.

## Why

The plain word is the right name for the plain job, and `cap` said
nothing to someone who did not already know it. The collision costs
little: nwg-shell's helper is internal to nwg-shell and is not run by name
inside a MixOS session.

Handing a shot to an agent should need no typing. A fixed folder, a name
that sorts by time, a topic on every save and a query for the latest shots
give the agent the file without the person saying where it is.

## Consequences

- AGENTS.md §3.4 lists the accepted collisions: `mix` (Elixir), `rec` and
  `play` (sox), and `screenshot` (nwg-shell).
- The `screenshot.*` verbs and its drive verbs are registered in
  `docs/docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix`.
- compd's binding table gains Print, Shift+Print and Alt+Print. No bare
  F1–F12 key is bound: those belong to the person.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-system-dialogs/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-12-system-dialogs.md) -->

# Decision — shipped system dialogs

Status: accepted 2026-10-12. Widens the scene loader's v1 rule that only
the Scene Editor may be a dialog.

## The problem

The scene host has one dialog seat. A dialog takes it when it loads, keeps
it while loaded, takes the keyboard when it shows and gives it back when it
hides. The loader therefore refused `window.kind: "dialog"` for every
installation except the Scene Editor, so no other part of the desktop could
ask a short question, such as the name for a workspace.

## The decision

- **A system dialog** is a shipped scene template that:
  - is marked `hidden: true` in its shipped `template.conf.mix`;
  - declares `window.kind: "dialog"` in its shipped `scene.mix`;
  - is installed under its own template name.

  The loader allows it to load as a dialog. The permission is read from the
  shipped files under the templates root, never from the user-editable
  installed copy. A shipped dialog that is not hidden, a system dialog
  installed (or forked) under another name, and any other scene edited into
  a dialog are all still refused. The installed copy of a system dialog is
  the person's own, like any installed scene, and keeps the permission its
  name carries.
- **Hidden templates stay out of the gallery**, so people still see one
  dialog scene, the Scene Editor.
- **A system dialog holds the seat only while it shows.** Its owner installs
  it disabled and enables it to ask. The dialog disables itself once its
  dialog is hidden by Save, Cancel or Esc, or by another dialog taking the
  seat.
- **The Scene Editor.** By default the Scene Editor is a native application
  window, not a dialog scene. It never uses the dialog seat, so it and a
  system dialog can both be open. The legacy scene frontend
  (`SCENES_EDITOR_APP=0`) is a dialog scene and keeps priority:
  - opening it pre-empts a system dialog;
  - it holds the seat for as long as it is loaded, hidden or not, so a
    system dialog asked for meanwhile is refused (`DIALOG_BUSY`) and its
    owner says so;
  - unloading it (`scenes.editor.close {unload: true}`) frees the seat.
- **One system dialog at a time.** A dialog asked to show for something else
  while it is already showing (another workspace) refuses until it is saved
  or cancelled. A failed start is rolled back (the scene is disabled again),
  and the dialog releases the seat only when the host's current state shows
  it hidden, never on a stale notice.
- **Focus.** A dialog takes the keyboard when it maps and gives it back when
  it hides. Its `window.autofocus` field gets focus as it opens.

The first system dialog is `share/scenes/workspace-rename`. Right-clicking a
pager button opens it for that workspace, and it names the workspace through
`comp.workspace.rename`.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-13-bundled-font-licences/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-13-bundled-font-licences.md) -->

# Bundled fallback font licences

**Status: accepted, 2026-10-13.**

MixOS uses Inter and JetBrains Mono for its application typography and retains
egui's bundled fallback fonts for additional glyph and emoji coverage.
The pinned `epaint_default_fonts` 0.36.2 package declares
`(MIT OR Apache-2.0) AND OFL-1.1 AND Ubuntu-font-1.0`.

The dependency checker permits those licences only for that exact package
version. The general permissive code-dependency allowlist is unchanged.
Updating the font bundle version requires reviewing the exception and the
shipped licence files together. This does not change MixOS's own MIT OR
Apache-2.0 licence or replace its primary typefaces.

The bundled font notices and complete upstream licence texts are recorded in
`libs/toolkit/assets/fonts/fallbacks/`. Their hashes, the primary-font licence
texts and the Lucide licence are pinned in the toolkit's licence manifest.
`libs/toolkit/scripts/install_licenses.mix` verifies that manifest and installs
the notices under `share/licenses/toolkit/`. Desktop release archives and the
native image builder invoke this same installer.

The font licences permit embedding and redistribution subject to their
conditions, including preservation of copyright and licence notices and
restrictions on renaming modified fonts. We keep the upstream font files
unmodified. References: [SIL OFL 1.1](https://openfontlicense.org/open-font-license-official-text/)
and [Ubuntu Font Licence 1.0](https://canonical.com/legal/font-licence).

Lucide SVGs supply interface icons. Noto Emoji remains a text/emoji fallback;
removing Material Symbols does not remove emoji coverage.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-13-desk-and-deskd/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-13-desk-and-deskd.md) -->

# Decision — desk and deskd

Status: accepted 2026-10-13. Follows the multi-call precedent of
[rec and play](2026-10-11-rec-and-play.md); within the naming rules of
[the source layout](2026-10-04-source-layout.md) (AGENTS.md §3).

## The decision

- **`desk` is the desktop's applications in one binary.** The GUI apps
  (busviewer, ced, dopus, prefs, screenshot, backdrop, and term when it
  lands) build into one executable, `desk`. Each app's name is a link to
  it in `/opt/mixos/bin`, and the binary runs the app it was started as.
  `desk <app> [args]` does the same, and `desk` alone lists the apps.
- **`deskd` is the desktop's session services in one binary**, by the same
  rule: the services a desktop session runs and a headless host does not
  (portald, settingsd, editd). Each keeps its name as a link and its own
  unit.
- **What stays separate:**
  - `mix` (the shell, on every host);
  - `noded` (the broker, on every host, desktop or not);
  - `hostd` (the host's information and privilege service, on every
    host). It runs as root and is the one way to elevate: it never shares
    a binary with `deskd` or anything else that runs as the session
    account;
  - `compd` (the compositor: its robustness and its dependency set are
    its own).
- **Each app and service is still its own process.** A crash ends one app,
  not the others; units, desktop entries and scripts keep calling
  `/opt/mixos/bin/<name>`.
- **Each crate keeps a `run` entry point and its own `main`**, so
  `cargo run -p ced` and every per-app test work as before. The multi-call
  crates only dispatch. Identity (build info, app ID, version) is passed by
  each app's `run`, never taken from the multi-call crate's package.

## Why

Every egui app links its own egui, wgpu, naga, fonts and icons: about
22 MB of each binary is that shared runtime, and an app's own code is 1 to
3 MB. A measured prototype put six apps (backdrop, busviewer, ced, dopus,
prefs, screenshot; release profile, fat LTO) in one binary: 128.7 MB
separately, 29.4 MB together. Link-time optimisation removes the
duplicates, and running apps share one mapped executable, so the runtime
is in memory once.

Rust dynamic libraries were rejected: there is no stable Rust ABI, libstd
would ship as a shared library, LTO stops at the boundary, and generic code
is still copied into each app. A C-ABI wrapper around egui would be a
second UI API.

## The names

- `desk` and `deskd` are plain nouns, a pair in the `<role>d` convention
  (§3.1, §3.4), unique in the dependency graph, and installed by no Arch
  package (checked 2026-10-13; the other distributions' file lists are
  checked before first use).
- The layers read in order:
  - **MixOS** is the system.
  - **mix** is its shell and language.
  - **noded** is the broker on every host.
  - **hostd** is the host's information and privileged actions, as root,
    on every host.
  - **compd**, **desk** and **deskd** are the desktop.

  A headless host runs `mix`, `noded` and `hostd`; a desktop adds the
  other three.
- A machine running the desktop is "a desk"; numbered instances (a desk
  and its number) are names of machines, not of these binaries.

## Not decided here

When each app and service moves in, the install layout of the links, and
how `component_install.mix` and the unit collector treat a multi-call
binary. Those land with the implementation.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-13-instance-verb-families/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-13-instance-verb-families.md) -->

# Instance verb families (schema 3)

Status: accepted, 2026-10-13.

## Context

Some Bus verbs are not one name. A bridge serves one service per instance it
runs, so a verb such as `<instance>.status` exists once for each running
instance, and the instances are known only at runtime. The verb registry
(`docs/docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix`, checked by `tools/verb_registry.mix`) listed
only concrete names, so there was no place to record these verbs or to check
that a name could not be taken by an instance.

## Decision

1. **Schema 3 is additive.** The `verbs` list is unchanged from schema 2, and
   its entries stay concrete in this migration. A new `families` list follows
   it. A family does not stand in for a concrete verb, in the registry or in
   code. This decision does not settle whether a concrete verb may later be
   expressed as a family; that would take its own decision.

2. **Schema 2 takes no families.** A schema 2 file with a `families` key is
   refused, empty or not, so an unvalidated list cannot pass as legacy data.
   Schema 1 stays refused. Schema 3 requires a `families` list, even an empty
   one.

3. **Family fields** are exactly `pattern`, `owner`, `members`, `version`,
   `status`, `class`, in that order, one entry per line, written
   `pattern:"…"` (never `name:"…"`). The fields are validated like the verb
   fields: release versions, the statuses and classes below, and component
   names for the owner.

4. **Pattern.** It is `<app>.<suffix>`, where the literal `<app>` stands for
   the instance name and the suffix is one or more lower identifier segments
   (`call`, `ui.tree`). Catch-all patterns are refused, and each pattern is
   unique across all owners.

5. **Members.** `members` is either `"instances"`, meaning the members are
   runtime instances and are not listed, or a nonempty list of unique Bus
   service names.
   - Families of one owner may share a listed member, so one service can
     implement several families (for example `<app>.call` and `<app>.status`).
   - A listed member used by families of two owners is refused.
   - A listed member may equal the first segment of concrete verbs only when
     every such verb has the family's owner, and the expanded wire name
     (`member.suffix`) is not itself a concrete verb. An exact concrete
     duplicate is always refused.
   - Any other collision is refused, not resolved.

6. **Class semantics** are those of
   `docs/docs/decisions/2026-10-11-verb-classes.md`. A family records its class as
   written; the gate checks that it is one of the four classes and does not
   infer it from the handler. The `bridged` families are classed:
   - `<app>.call` and `<app>.execute` are `intent`.
   - `<app>.commands`, `<app>.inspect` and `<app>.status` are `query`.
   - `<app>.screenshot` is `intent`. A capture alone would be a query (a query
     may write the artefact it returns), but its `focus` option can bring the
     window forward, which another caller sees. A family has one class, so the
     verb is intent whether or not `focus` is set.

7. **Family ownership.** A family with `"instances"` belongs to its owner
   component only. The source check accepts an `on @.<suffix>` declaration
   only from the component whose `"instances"` family has that suffix. Every
   such family must be declared at least once in its owner's runtime code.
   Another component declaring the same suffix is refused as a wrong owner.

8. **Declarations come from the native parser.** The source check reads the
   handler metadata of the native `mix lint --json` (lint schema 2). There is
   no fallback reader.

## Checks and their limits

- **Source check (`--source ROOT`).** The gate reads the `.mix` files under
  `apps/`, `services/`, `cli/` and `libs/`. It skips `tests/`, `test/`,
  `benches/`, `fuzz/`, and `*.conf.mix`/`*.spec.mix` files. The declarations
  come from the native parser: each file is passed to `mix lint --json FILE`,
  and every handler whose command starts with `@.` is a declaration. The
  handler metadata is the parsed AST, so nested and duplicate declarations
  count, and text inside quotes, heredocs and comments does not. The source
  is never executed.
  - **Feature detection.** The lint document is schema 2, with a `handlers`
    list. A Mix that answers without it fails with `native Mix lacks parsed
    handler metadata; rebuild current Mix`. There is no fallback parser.
  - **Fail-closed.** A file that does not lint (nonzero exit), output that is
    truncated, a document that is not valid JSON, a wrong `tool`, `files` or
    `summary`, or a handler with a bad `command`, `file` or `line` each make the
    check fail. An unreadable source root or nested source directory fails the
    check too. Diagnostics and source text are never printed.
  - **Walk.** The gate lists each directory with the native `ls` and reads each
    entry with `stat`, recursing by hand. The native `glob` and `walk` skip an
    unreadable directory without an error, so they are not used to prove an
    absence. Test, bench and fuzz directories are skipped before the recursion.
    The source root and each kind directory must be a plain directory (a
    symlink is refused). Trailing slashes are dropped before that check, so a
    symlink named with one is refused too. Only the last component of each such
    path is checked without following links; a symlink in a directory above it
    is followed, as any path is. A symlink anywhere else in a kind's tree is
    refused, and so is a directory that cannot be listed.
  - The check is **structural**. It proves that a handler for the suffix sits
    in the owner's code, not that it registers at runtime. The owner's Bus
    suite tests the runtime registration.
- **Instance check (`--instances DIR`).** Each `*.conf.mix` file stem in DIR
  is checked against the Bus name rule, the reserved names (the `mixos-`
  prefix, `noded` and `noded-*`, the broker's session-name shape), the first
  segments of concrete verbs and the listed family members. A name that is a
  concrete prefix or a listed member is refused whatever its owner. DIR must be
  a plain directory (a trailing slash does not get a symlink past this), and an
  unreadable DIR fails the check. Any path may hold glob characters, since `ls`
  takes a name, not a pattern. Configs are flat by design: the gate lists the
  top level only, dot files included. A `*.conf.mix` entry in a subdirectory,
  and any other file, is ignored; none of them is a runtime config, and the gate
  neither recurses into them nor reads their contents. Symlinks, directories and other non-regular files named
  `*.conf.mix` are refused, and so are configs when the registry has no
  instances family. Config contents and tokens are never read.
- **Offline.** Neither check touches the network or a running broker. A name
  that passes here is a name the Bus will accept, as far as the Bus's own
  rules go. A runtime refusal (for example, a broker that has already
  registered the name) is still possible and is not this gate's concern.
- **Mesh exposure is unchanged.** Nothing in the gate or the registry changes
  what any mesh peer can reach. The families describe names; a service's own
  configuration decides what it serves.

## Consequences

- Schema 2 files stay valid as long as they carry no families.
- The source check needs a Mix whose `mix lint --json` reports handler
  metadata (lint schema 2). An older Mix fails the source check until it is
  rebuilt; the gate does not fall back to another reader.
- A new instance family needs a family entry, and an `on @.<suffix>` handler
  in its owner's code, in the same change.
- Public examples use only the neutral fixture names `fakeapp`, `demod` and
  `otherd`. No runtime instance name belongs in this repository's docs.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-14-session-icon-stroke-and-type/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-14-session-icon-stroke-and-type.md) -->

# Decision — session icon stroke and type

Status: accepted 2026-10-14. Extends
[icons and type](2026-10-09-icons-and-type.md) and the
[keymaps in settings](2026-10-11-keymaps-in-settings.md) precedent.

## The decision

- **Four optional session choices** join the profile's appearance:
  `appearance.icon_stroke` (1.0 to 3.0 in quarter steps, on Lucide's 24-unit
  grid), `appearance.font_family`, `appearance.font_weight` (100 to 900 in
  steps of 100) and `appearance.mono_family`.
- **None means the design's own value**: the `icon.stroke_width` token (the
  approved 1.5 baseline), Inter, the scheme's own weight, and JetBrains Mono.
- **The stroke baseline stays 1.5.** It is the approved baseline (hub plan
  `2026-10-13-lucide-panel-icons`), and the shipped token matches it.
- **A user weight replaces the weight locked by the chrome schemes.** Body
  text takes the chosen weight; headings keep their design offset above it.
- **System fonts are runtime data.** A chosen family is read from the host's
  font files when it is available. Nothing is embedded, so the bundled-font
  licence obligations in
  [bundled font licences](2026-10-13-bundled-font-licences.md) are unchanged.
  A missing or still-scanning family falls back to the bundled Inter, which
  stays behind any system font as glyph fallback.
- **Carried by the existing carrier.** `settings.apply` takes the new keys,
  `prefs.appearance.set` is the Prefs front verb, and every app follows the
  summary topic as it does for the scheme. No new verb.

## Why

The icon stroke and the typeface are the two things a person most often
wants to tune, and they are session-wide, so they belong in the profile and
not in each app. Making them optional keeps every existing profile's digest
valid, so nothing is migrated.

## Digest and rollback

- The new `Appearance` fields are omitted when unset, like `style`,
  `decorations` and `caption_side`. A profile that sets none of them
  re-serialises byte for byte.
- The store is format 3. A profile that sets any of the four keys will not
  load in a format-2 build, because `Appearance` denies unknown fields. Roll
  back by resetting the keys first, with `settings.reset` or a null value.

## Scope

- **Apps following the session look** (busviewer, ced, dopus, screenshot)
  pick the choices up through `session_look` and `toolkit::install`, with no
  edits beyond the overlay.
- **Prefs** builds its own theme from its draft; it is updated alongside.
- **backdrop** draws textures only, with no text or icon widgets, and
  installs once at startup. It is out of scope.
- **compd's title bars** use their own theme builder and an embedded-only
  font database. They follow in a later slice, once the contract is proven
  nested; the `Effective` and `ChangePlan` fields are already in place.
- **Profiles that name their own design source** receive no session look,
  so they keep their design's own values. The choices are still saved.

## Consequences

- `libs/settings` 0.6.0 and store format 3. The change is additive for every
  profile that does not set a choice.
- `libs/toolkit` gains a theme overlay applied by `session_look`, a stroke
  precedence (overlay, then token, then `DEFAULT_STROKE` 1.5), a weight
  override that beats the chrome lock, and a background scan of the host's
  font files.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-16-monitord-and-monitor/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-16-monitord-and-monitor.md) -->

# Decision — monitord and Monitor

Status: accepted 2026-10-16.

## The decision

- **`monitord`** (`services/monitord`, kind service, layer core) runs once
  per host as its own unprivileged user. It samples the system and its
  processes, keeps recent history in memory and longer history in SQLite,
  and answers read verbs on the Bus. It runs headless; a mesh node with no
  desktop is a first-class host.
- **`Monitor`** (`apps/monitor`, binary `monitor`, app id
  `dev.mixos.monitor`) is the egui task manager: processes, performance
  graphs, apps, services and users, in the shape people know from Windows
  Task Manager and GNOME Mission Center. It reads everything through
  monitord's verbs, never from `/proc` itself, so the same window shows any
  node on the mesh (`monitord.<node>.bus`).
- **monitord observes; it does not act.** No verb signals, renices or
  stops anything.
  - The `monitord` command line acts locally as the person who runs it:
    `monitord signal` and `monitord renice` make the system call directly
    and the kernel decides, exactly like `kill` and `renice`.
  - Acting across users or across the mesh is hostd's job, as closed verbs
    behind grants ([hostd decision](2026-10-12-hostd.md)), added one
    reviewed verb at a time.
- **A personality of the system binary.** monitord's library exports
  `main`; `cli/system` carries it
  ([one system binary](2026-10-12-one-system-binary.md)). The unit runs
  `/opt/mixos/bin/monitord serve`.

### History

| Tier | Resolution | Kept | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| live | the sample interval (1 s) | 10 minutes | memory ring |
| short | 1 minute (avg, min, max) | 7 days | SQLite |
| long | 1 hour (avg, min, max) | 1 year | SQLite |

- SQLite (`rusqlite`, already in the system binary through the shell)
  holds only system-wide series: CPU, memory, swap, load, pressure, and one
  series per network interface and disk. Per-core and per-process series
  live in memory only; they are too many to keep.
- The database is `/var/lib/monitord/history.db`, owned by monitord. It is
  a cache: deleting it loses history, nothing else.
- Retention is configuration, so a small node can keep less.

### Sampling

- System-wide sampling runs all the time at 1 s. It reads a handful of
  `/proc` files and costs next to nothing.
- The process table is sampled only while someone is reading it: a
  `monitord.processes` call holds the process sampler on for 30 s. An idle
  mesh node does not walk `/proc` every second. A cold call samples twice,
  a short interval apart, so CPU percentages are never zero by default.
- monitord reads what an unprivileged user can read. A process's I/O
  counters and some of its details are readable only for monitord's own
  processes; elsewhere those fields are absent, never guessed. Wider reads
  are a later, reviewed capability (`CAP_SYS_PTRACE` or a hostd verb).

### On the Bus

- Read verbs (all queries): `monitord.status`, `monitord.snapshot`,
  `monitord.processes`, `monitord.process`, `monitord.series` and
  `monitord.history`. The verbs and their bodies are documented in the
  [monitord manual](../../monitord/README.md).
- A retained topic, `monitord.summary`, carries a small system summary
  every 5 s, so a dashboard of the whole mesh subscribes instead of
  polling.
- The reply bodies are a public contract (`contract = "public"`), versioned
  in monitord's changelog. Monitor depends on the JSON, not on monitord's
  Rust types. If a second component needs those types, they are promoted to
  a library by review (AGENTS.md §2.2).

### What it is built from

- **Phase 1 reads the kernel directly.** `/proc` and `/sys` parsers are
  small, and each one reads from a root directory, so tests run against a
  fixture tree, the way hostd's do. No collection crate is needed yet.
- **Later phases use permissive crates,** each checked against `deny.toml`
  when it enters:

  | Area | Crate |
  |---|---|
  | NVIDIA | `nvml-wrapper` (MIT OR Apache-2.0) |
  | AMD | `libamdgpu_top` (MIT) |
  | Intel, and GPU use per process on every vendor | `qmlib` (Apache-2.0) |
  | systemd units, login sessions | `zbus_systemd` (MIT OR Apache-2.0) |
  | battery | `starship-battery` (ISC) |
  | graphs, tables (Monitor) | `egui_plot`, `egui_table` (MIT OR Apache-2.0) |

- **Code may be lifted** from bottom (MIT) and systemd-manager-tui (MIT),
  with its notice kept (AGENTS.md §4).
- **GPL and other copyleft monitors are reference only:** Mission Center
  and magpie, Resources, nvtop. Nobody copies or translates their code.
  Where one of them shows *what* to read, the reader is written fresh from
  the kernel's documentation.

### Phases

1. monitord: CPU, memory, swap, pressure, load, disks, network interfaces,
   the process table and tree; history; the Bus verbs and topic; the command
   line, with local `signal` and `renice`.
2. Monitor: the egui window over phase 1, any node on the mesh.
3. GPUs: NVIDIA, AMD and Intel, with use per process.
4. systemd services and the Apps view (processes grouped by application).
5. Sensors, fans, battery, power.
6. Privileged readings (per-process network bytes over eBPF, SMART, RAPL
   energy, DMI) through a reviewed capability or hostd verbs.

## Why

- Every node on the mesh should be able to say what it is doing, in one
  shape, to any agent or window that asks, without ssh.
- The split between a headless sampler and a window is already the right
  one in Mission Center (magpie and its GTK frontend), but that code is
  GPL-3.0 and MixOS is MIT OR Apache-2.0. Permissive Rust crates cover
  most of the same ground, and what they don't cover is small.
- Keeping monitord read-only keeps it unprivileged, so it can run
  everywhere. Killing a process is already a kernel-checked system call for
  the local user; across users or nodes it is a privileged change, and
  those go through hostd.

## Consequences

- noded's built-in `mon` module (`mon.status`, `mon.processes`,
  `mon.props.*`) is superseded. Its verbs were never registered and nothing
  in the tree calls them. It is removed once monitord is installed on the
  mesh.
- monitord adds a system user, `monitord`, and the state directory
  `/var/lib/monitord`.
- Monitor's graphs and tables record their performance workloads (a
  2,000-process table, a 64-core grid) before they are optimised
  (AGENTS.md §4.1).

## Amendments

### 2026-10-16: Monitor's End task and Kill, and its widgets

- **Monitor acts on this node's processes the way the command line does.**
  End task (SIGTERM) and Kill (SIGKILL) are local system calls made as the
  person running Monitor, and the kernel decides. They are off while
  another node is shown, and no Bus verb of monitord's is involved. Acting
  on another node, or as another user, stays hostd's.
- **Phase 2 adds no graph or table crate.** The graphs are painted
  directly: a 64-core grid is 64 graphs a frame, which a plotting widget
  per graph would make heavy. The process table is `egui_extras`'
  `TableBuilder`, already in the tree. `egui_plot` and `egui_table` stay
  candidates for when a view needs what they add (zoom, axes, ragged rows).

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-16-site-url-layout/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/decisions/2026-10-16-site-url-layout.md) -->

# Decision — site URL layout

Status: accepted 2026-10-16, after review by two independent reviewers.

## The question

mixos.dev serves two readers from the same files. A person in a browser
gets a static HTML page, and nothing needs JavaScript to render. An agent
or script on any machine fetches the same page as Markdown and starts from
`/llms.txt`. MixOS will grow to hundreds of apps, services, libraries and
tools over the next few years. How should the URL space be organised, so
that an address, once published, never has to change?

## The decision

### Two namespaces

- **Each component's documentation is at the top level, under the
  component's name.** Examples: `/mix/`, `/term/`, `/compd/`, `/hostd/`,
  `/noded/`.
- **Everything that is not a component lives under `/docs/`.** That covers
  guides such as `/docs/try/` and `/docs/drive/`, plus
  `/docs/decisions/`, `/docs/spec/`, `/docs/dev/`, `/docs/releases/`, and
  the generated indexes below. The site's global navigation has a Docs
  entry that leads there.

### Component names

- A component's name is the `component` declared by its principal package
  in `[package.metadata.mixos]`, or by its `component.mx`. Component names
  are already plain, unique across the workspace and never reused (see
  [source layout](2026-10-04-source-layout.md)), so an address can be
  built from the name alone.
- A component name starts with a lowercase letter and contains only
  lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.
- **Two names are reserved: `docs` and `v`.** The component metadata gate
  refuses them, so a forbidden name is caught when the component is
  created, not when the site is built.
- Site machinery uses names no component can take. Generator inputs and
  assets live in `_build/` and `_web/` (renamed from `build/` and `web/`),
  and root files (`index.html`, `404.html`, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`,
  `sitemap.xml`, `robots.txt`, `CNAME`, the favicons) all contain a dot or
  start with an underscore.
- **Mix's names.** The `mix` component is the language library, so `/mix/`
  is the Mix language manual and the same pages `mix man TOPIC` reads. The
  `mix` binary's component is `system` (`/system/`), and the shell is
  `mix-shell` (`/mix-shell/`). Each links to the others.

### Where pages come from, and their addresses

The path of a source file relative to the site root (the repository's
`docs/` directory) determines its address. The table gives every
mapping:

| Source | HTML | Markdown |
|---|---|---|
| `docs/<name>/README.md` | `/<name>/` | `/<name>/README.md` |
| `docs/<name>/<page>.md` | `/<name>/<page>/` | `/<name>/<page>.md` |
| `docs/docs/<page>.md` | `/docs/<page>/` | `/docs/<page>.md` |
| `<component dir>/CHANGELOG.md` (mirrored) | `/<name>/changelog/` | `/<name>/changelog.md` |
| Generated index pages | `/docs/<index>/` | `/docs/<index>.md` |

- **The Markdown is published at its source path.** Relative links inside
  it therefore resolve correctly under ordinary URL resolution. An agent
  builds a component's Markdown address as `/<name>/README.md`. The
  generator checks every relative link in both formats.
- **Hand-written component documentation lives in `docs/<name>/`.** That
  is its one canonical copy. The component's own directory keeps a short
  `README.md` that points to the page, so someone browsing the source
  finds it.
- **`CHANGELOG.md` stays beside the code**, where releases update it. Only
  the principal package's changelog is published. The published copy is
  generated and never edited. Relative links in it are rewritten to the
  source on GitHub. A component with no changelog has no changelog page.
  `changelog` is therefore a reserved page name inside every component.
- **The doubled `docs/docs/`** is accepted. It keeps the rule that the
  source path determines the address, without a rename table.
- **Generated pages have a Markdown twin** like every other page.
- **HTML is the canonical address.** Each HTML page names its Markdown as
  `<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown">`. `sitemap.xml` lists HTML
  only.

### Navigation from metadata

- **The URL never encodes kind, layer or install profile.** These change
  over a component's life: a library is promoted, or a desktop service
  becomes useful headless.
- `/docs/desktop/` and `/docs/server/` are generated index pages listing
  components by their declared install `profiles`. A component in both is
  listed in both, with one page. Components in the `base` profile are
  listed under a reader-facing heading such as "Core components". The word
  `base` stays in the installation docs.
- `/docs/components/` is the one complete, generated component index,
  giving each component's name, kind, profiles, source path and page. It
  replaces the hand-run `docs/docs/dev/components.md` (formerly
  `docs/dev/components.md`).
- Until `profiles` is declared everywhere, the indexes list undeclared
  components as unclassified. They never guess from `layer`.

### Agents

- `/llms.txt` lists every section, with absolute Markdown URLs: one line
  per component (with its kind and profiles) and one per page under
  `/docs/`. Every published document can be reached from it.
  `llms-full.txt` remains an optional single file.
- Every page states that it describes the current `main` branch.

### Every component has a page

- The principal package of every component (app, service, cli or lib) and
  every Mix component must have `docs/<name>/README.md`. Private crates and
  `tool` and `test` packages are excluded.
- **A component without a page fails the site gate.** While existing
  components are being documented, the ones still missing are named in an
  exception list in `site.conf.mix`. That list may only shrink, and a new
  component cannot be added to it.

### Addresses are permanent

From the day this decision is accepted:

- A profile change or a source move never changes an address.
- An address that goes away keeps working in both formats: an entry in
  `site.conf.mix`'s `redirects` for browsers, plus a short Markdown page at
  the old `.md` address that names the new one, because an agent fetching
  Markdown does not follow an HTML redirect.
- A split leaves a page that links to its successors. A retired component
  keeps a retirement page, which stays listed in `/llms.txt`, and its name
  is never reused.

### Versions

`/v/` is reserved for versioned copies of the site. How they work is
decided before the first stable release.

## Why

- **One namespace for components, one for everything else.** An address
  either names a component or starts with `/docs/`. Only two names are off
  limits for components.
- **Names are the most stable thing a component has.** The source-layout
  decision rejected splitting the source tree by desktop, server or core,
  because a component could plausibly sit in either of two places and
  moves between them. Putting that axis into URLs would have recreated the
  problem where a move is most costly.
- **It matches what already works.** `/mix/` and the existing component
  pages (`/hostd/`, `/noded/`, `/prefs/`, `/backdrop/`, `/screenshot/`,
  `/dopus/`) are already at the top level, and `mix man` already fetches
  `/mix/<topic>.md` and `/mix/README.md`.
- **One canonical copy.** Keeping hand-written docs in `docs/` rather than
  beside the code relaxes the source-layout principle that a component is
  self-contained. That is deliberate: documentation for readers has one
  home, one navigation and one gate. Code, tests and changelogs stay with
  the component.

## Rejected

- **Mirror repository paths** (`/apps/term/`, `/libs/bus/`). The address
  is predictable, but it encodes kind, and it moves when a component moves
  in the source tree.
- **Sections by install profile** (`/desktop/term/`, `/server/maild/`,
  `/base/noded/`). Profiles are deployment data that change, a component
  can be in two, and `server` is empty today. A profile change would move
  a public URL.
- **A component prefix** (`/c/term/` or `/components/term/`). It protects
  the component namespace, but `/docs/` does the same job from the other
  side, with shorter, more readable component URLs.
- **Docs beside the code, mirrored into the site.** That makes two copies,
  needs a freshness gate and a mapping table, and splits navigation.
- **A `/<name>.md` alias for each component page.** Relative links in it
  would resolve against the wrong directory.
- **Mapping `/docs/` to a differently named source directory** (for
  example `docs/guides/`). It avoids `docs/docs/`, but it adds a permanent
  rename table.

## Consequences

- Nobody depends on the current URLs, so this one move keeps no old
  address. The permanence rules apply from acceptance.
- The root pages that are not components move under `docs/docs/`: `try`
  and `drive`, plus `decisions/`, `spec/` and `dev/`.
- Root pages that describe a component become its page
  (`docs/hostd.md` becomes `docs/hostd/README.md`, and so on). Four were
  named after a topic rather than their component, and take the
  component's name: `edit` becomes `editd`, `portal` becomes `portald`,
  `bridge` becomes `bridged` and `releases` becomes `releasesd`. (The
  first draft of this record listed `edit`, `bridge` and `releases` as
  non-component pages; each documents one service.)
- The component READMEs beside the code move into `docs/<name>/README.md`,
  leaving a pointer behind. The CHANGELOGs stay where they are.
- `docs/build/` and `docs/web/` become `docs/_build/` and `docs/_web/`.
- The component metadata gate gains the name grammar and the reserved
  names.
- `gen-site` gains the output-collision check (every HTML, Markdown, asset
  and generated output), the changelog mirror, the generated indexes and
  their Markdown twins, the alternate links, the missing-page gate with its
  exception list, and a grouped `llms.txt`.
- Every link to a moved page is updated, including in AGENTS.md and the
  decision records.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/spec/bridge/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/spec/bridge/README.md) -->

# Bridge contract

Status: draft, version 0.2.0. Machine-checkable fixture:
[`bridge.spec.mix`](bridge.spec.mix). Verified by
`services/bridged/tests/bridge_core_test.mix` (the config contract against
the fixture, the wire protocol against a stand-in app) and
`services/bridged/tests/bridged_test.mix` (every verb over a private broker).

`bridged` puts an external application on the Bus. The application offers a
line-delimited JSON control channel on loopback TCP; one `bridged` instance
per application maps six Bus verbs onto it. This page fixes the control
channel an application must offer, the instance config schema, the serve-name
rule and the Bus verbs.

## The control channel an application offers

| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Transport | TCP on the loopback interface, one port per application. The bridge keeps one connection open and reuses it. |
| Framing | One JSON object per line, UTF-8, `\n`-terminated (a trailing `\r` is ignored). A line is at most `max_line` bytes. |
| Auth (`auth: "token"`) | The first line on every connection is `{"id":"auth","method":"auth","params":{"token":"<64 hex>"}}`. The application replies `{"id":"auth","ok":true,...}` or refuses and closes. The bridge sends nothing else until that reply is ok. |
| Auth (`auth: "key"`) | As `token`, with `params.key`. The application writes the 64-hex secret to the key file after it starts, and may rotate it; the bridge reads the file on every connect, before any bytes are sent. |
| No auth (`auth: "none"`) | Requests start at once. An application that receives an `auth` line it does not expect should refuse it and close. Any local process can use such a port while it is open. |
| Request | `{"id":N,"method":"<name>","params":{...}}`, `N` a number the bridge increments per request. |
| Reply | `{"id":N,"ok":true,"result":<any JSON>}` or `{"id":N,"ok":false,"error":"<text>"}`, matched to the request by `id`. Lines that are not JSON or carry another `id` are skipped. A reply without a boolean `ok` is a transport failure. |
| Port squatting (residual) | Loopback TCP cannot prove who listens. If the application dies, a local process that binds its port before it returns receives the token on the bridge's next reconnect, and can then impersonate the application to the bridge and use the token on the real one. A unix-socket control channel checked by owner would close this; it is a possible future protocol option. |
| Methods the named verbs use | `engine.commands`, `engine.execute` (`{command, params}`), `ui.inspect`, `ui.screenshot` (`{path?, focus?}`). An application without one of them answers `ok:false`; `<app>.call` reaches any other method. |

## Bus verbs

An instance started with `--name <app>` answers under its own name.

| Verb | Body | Sends | Reply on rc 0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<app>.call` | `{method, params?}` | `<method>` with `params` (default `{}`) | the app's `result` |
| `<app>.commands` | — | `engine.commands` | the app's `result` |
| `<app>.execute` | `{command, params?}` | `engine.execute {command, params}` | the app's `result` |
| `<app>.inspect` | — | `ui.inspect` | the app's `result` |
| `<app>.screenshot` | `{path?, focus?}`, or empty | `ui.screenshot` with only those keys | the app's `result` |
| `<app>.status` | — | nothing | `{service, connection, host, port, auth, instance, connects, failures, calls, last_error, last_latency_ms, retry_after_s}` |

`connection` is `never-connected`, `up` or `down`. `status` never contains
the token.

| rc | Meaning | Body |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | The app replied `ok:true` | its `result` as JSON |
| 10 | The app replied `ok:false` | its `error` text |
| 11 | Connect, auth, transport or timeout failure, or backing off after one | text saying which |
| 12 | A bad request from the caller (missing field, body not a JSON object, an encoded request over `max_line`) | text naming the problem |

Every call has one transport deadline, `timeout_s`, starting when the call
does. Connect, the auth line and its reply, and the request and its reply
all draw on that one budget: each write gets the time left as `tcp_send`'s
`{timeout}`, which bounds the whole send, and each read gets the time left
too. So a peer that stops reading or reads too slowly cannot hold a call
past it: the write fails, the call answers rc 11 and the connection is
dropped. A budget already spent before a write fails the same way without
sending.

The budget bounds transport, not local work. Encoding the request
(`json_encode`) and Mix's scheduling run on the same clock but cannot be
interrupted, so they can take a call past `timeout_s`; the next transport
step then fails at once without touching the network. For example, a
32 MiB request with `timeout_s` 0.001 spends tens of milliseconds encoding,
then is refused before writing. This needs Mix >= 0.112.1; on an older Mix
the bridge refuses to start (`RUNTIME`).

After a transport failure, or a reply without a boolean `ok`, the connection is dropped and no new one is tried for
`backoff_s`; calls in that window answer rc 11 at once.

The token never appears in a reply: any occurrence of it, in any letter case,
in an app's error text, in a result, or in `last_error`, is replaced by
`[redacted]`.

**Registration.** The six verbs are an instance family, `<app>.<verb>` with
owner `bridged` and `members: "instances"` (runtime members, not listed). They
are declared in `docs/docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix` (registry schema 3). The static
gate `tools/verb_registry.mix` checks the family's owner and suffix;
`tools/verb_registry.mix --instances DIR` checks private file-stem naming and
collisions only and reads no config token. The runtime guard reads the verbs
and families lists but does not enforce the full canonical format. Installing
the registry is a separate deployed prerequisite: the scripts and the registry
come from the same revision, at `/opt/mixos/share/bus/verbs.conf.mix` or the
`BRIDGED_VERBS` override.

**Classes.** `<app>.call` and `<app>.execute` are `intent`; `<app>.commands`,
`<app>.inspect` and `<app>.status` are `query`. `<app>.screenshot` is `intent`,
because its `focus` option can bring the window forward, a change another
caller sees, even though the verb otherwise only captures. The reasoning is in
the [decision](../../decisions/2026-10-13-instance-verb-families.md).

## Instance config, version 0.2.0

A strict-data document (`load_data`; never executed).

**Path:** `$BRIDGED_CONFIG` when set; otherwise `<etc>/bridge/<app>.conf.mix`,
where `<etc>` is `$MIXOS_ETC` when set, else `/etc/mixos`. The file stem is
the serve name.

```text
port: 47801,
token_file: "/home/user/.config/fakeapp/control.token",
timeout_s: 20
```

| Key | Type | Default | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| `port` | integer | required | 1–65535 |
| `host` | string | `"127.0.0.1"` | `"127.0.0.1"` or `"localhost"`, which is connected to as `127.0.0.1` (never `::1`); anything else is refused |
| `auth` | string | `"token"` | `"token"`, `"key"` or `"none"`; an explicit `nil` is refused |
| `token_file` | string | — | required with `auth: "token"` or `"key"`, refused with `auth: "none"`; a leading `~/` expands to `$HOME`. With `key` it is the key file, read on every connect; a missing or unusable key is rc 11 before any connect, and the next retry after `backoff_s` reads it again |
| `timeout_s` | number | 5 | (0, 300]: the whole-call deadline |
| `connect_timeout_s` | number | 2 | (0, 300]: the connect step, within the deadline |
| `backoff_s` | number | 2 | [0, 300]: the pause after a transport failure |
| `max_line` | integer | 1048576 | 64–16777216 bytes per line, both ways: a longer reply is a transport failure (rc 11); a longer request is refused before it is sent (rc 12) |
| `instance` | string | — | 1–64 of `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`; echoed by `status` so a launcher can recognise its own bridge |

Unknown keys are refused, so a typo never falls back to a default. The token
file holds exactly 64 hex characters (one trailing newline allowed) and has
no group or other permission bits (`chmod 600`). Errors name the file, never
its content.

## Serve name and the start checks

The name must match `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,30}$`, the Bus's own rule for a
service name, and must not start with `mixos-` (`mix --serve` strips that
prefix before registering, so the checked name and the Bus name would
differ). The broker's own names are refused as noded refuses them: `noded`,
`noded-*`, and the session-name shape `<t|c><1-7 of [a-z0-9]>-<22 of
[a-z2-7]>`. It must also not be the first segment of a verb the registry
already gives to another component, so an instance can never answer, say,
`settings.status`. The registry read is `$BRIDGED_VERBS`, else the installed
`/opt/mixos/share/bus/verbs.conf.mix`:

| Registry entry | Reserves |
|---|---|
| `verbs: [{name, ...}]` | the first segment of `name`, whatever the status (retired names stay reserved) |
| `families: [{pattern, members: "instances"}]` | nothing (runtime members, such as bridged's own family) |
| `families: [{pattern, members: [names]}]` | each listed name |
| `families: [{pattern}]` with a literal first segment | that segment; an `<app>` or `*` first segment reserves nothing |

The guard fails closed: a missing or unreadable registry, one without a
`verbs` list, an entry without a `name` or `pattern`, or an unknown `members`
form refuses the start. `families` is optional, so the schema-1 registry and
later schemas with families both read.

A refused start prints `bridged: refusing to start: CODE: message` and exits
2. Codes: `RUNTIME` (Mix older than 0.112.1), `NAME_INVALID`, `NAME_RESERVED`,
`REGISTRY`, `CONFIG`, `TOKEN`.
`mix bridged.mix --check <app>` runs the same checks without joining the Bus
and exits 0 when the instance may start; an unexpected error at start exits 3,
never 2.

The unit runs `mix bridged.mix --start <app>`. That process runs the same
checks in process, before the name reaches the Bus, and exits 2 on a
documented refusal without starting anything. Otherwise it runs
`mix --serve bridged.mix --name <app>` as its child (no shell) and exits with
the child's exit code. Mix has no process-replacing exec, so the parent and
child pair is deliberate; the unit's control-group kill stops both. The unit
never restarts on exit 2 (`RestartPreventExitStatus=2`); every other non-zero
exit, including a missing or unreadable script (exit 1), is a failure,
restarted under `Restart=on-failure` and rate-limited by
`StartLimitBurst=5` in `StartLimitIntervalSec=60`. A clean stop exits 143:
systemd signals both processes, and Mix records the SIGTERM the parent gets
and exits 143 whatever the child returned, so the unit lists
`SuccessExitStatus=143`. `$BRIDGED_MIX` overrides the mix binary the child
runs under (default `/opt/mixos/bin/mix`); it exists for tests.

Starting `mix --serve bridged.mix --name <app>` directly, not through
`--start`, registers the name on the Bus before the checks run, so a
refused name holds a free Bus name for a moment before the process exits.
`--start` (the unit) is the supported path. The reverse collision, a verb
registered later whose first segment is an instance already running, is
the verb-registry gate's to refuse, not the bridge's: the bridge checks only
at start.

The unit is sandboxed: no capabilities or new privileges, the file system
read-only with private `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` (config and token files must
live elsewhere), address families limited to IPv4, IPv6 and unix sockets,
and IP traffic to loopback only (`IPAddressAllow=localhost`,
`IPAddressDeny=any`). A Bus endpoint off loopback needs a drop-in adding its
address to `IPAddressAllow`. The IP filter is cgroup BPF: enforced on hosts
that support it, ignored where they do not, and not proven by the offline
`systemd-analyze security` score.

`--start` outside systemd has no parent-death protection: killing the
`--start` process alone can orphan the serve child. Run it under the unit,
whose control group holds both. `BRIDGED_MIX` and the instance's `.env` file
must be administrator-controlled: anyone who can change them picks the code
that runs as `mixos`.

## Changes

- 0.2.0 (2026-10-13): additive `auth: "key"` (`params.key`, secret read from
  `token_file` on each connect). Token and none modes are unchanged.
- 0.1.0 (2026-10-10): first version.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/spec/handler-closure-capture/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/spec/handler-closure-capture.md) -->

# Handler closure capture

Lambdas defined inside an `on` handler capture its local variables by value,
including callbacks passed to `map` and `all` and nested callbacks. Those
locals remain available if the closure escapes the handler. Global variables
continue to be read live; capturing handler locals does not freeze globals.

Each handler invocation has its own local frame. A closure retains the locals
of its defining invocation, rather than reading another invocation's locals.
Assignment inside a closure continues to bind a function-local variable.

# Mix program and document file-family contract

Status: accepted target contract, version 1.0.0, 2026-10-08. Planned for the next
major Mix refactor/deployment; no current-binary conformance is claimed. Authority:
[programs and documents decision](../../decisions/2026-10-08-mix-programs-and-documents.md).

## 1. Families, not dialects

`.mix` is executable Mix. `.mx` is a declarative Mix document. Macro, behaviour,
module, task, installer and resident citizen are executable roles; configuration,
theme, spec, catalogue, manifest, policy and scene are document schemas/purposes.
The public API vocabulary is program/document, not safe/unsafe script flavours.

The same interpreter and program grammar serve every executable role. Full
language access remains subject to caller OS permissions and existing host
capability policy; it does not imply privileged execution. Schema binding
evaluation uses the existing pure expression implementation, never a second
general interpreter or a quietly expanded builtin allowlist.

Canonical new data filenames end in `.mx`, for example `node.mx`, `settings.mx`,
`theme.mx`, `scene.mx`, `template.mx` and `authority.mx`. Stems follow existing
repository naming rules and describe purpose where useful; no new compound
suffix is required to select a trust class. Executable test gates remain `.mix`;
their declarative fixtures become `.mx`.

## 2. Program/file admission

All file-based program entry points refuse `.mx` before evaluating any content:

- Direct CLI program execution, `--serve`, interactive file execution and every
  serve initial load, reload candidate and committed generation.
- `source`, `include`, `require`, prelude/startup file loading and any equivalent
  executable file reader in the library or an embedder.
- App macro runners, scene behaviour launchers and automation dispatchers.

Provide a stable structured refusal code and diagnostic saying that the file is
a document and requires a document reader. Exact code registration occurs with
the implementation. `--no-lint` and normal script flags do not bypass admission;
there is no general execute-document override.

Check both the requested path and resolved file target, including symlinks, with
one shared policy used across callers. `.MX` is also refused on executable paths;
writers emit lowercase `.mx`. Filename admission is not a comprehensive security
boundary: renaming, explicit source-string evaluation and intentionally running
a program remain under the caller's authority. Strict parsing is what keeps
document consumption non-executing.

Anonymous program source (`-c`, stdin, library source-string APIs) remains
explicitly executable input, with existing capability policy. Document readers
must never pass document bytes to those APIs or reclassify a failed parse as
program source. Do not disable ordinary stdin/REPL workflows to simulate content
provenance that the runtime cannot establish.

Document checking/linting is non-executing. CLI `--check`/check/lint handling of
`.mx` must validate as a document, or return a clear unsupported-schema/kind
diagnostic. It must never report executable syntax checks as document validation.
The implementation must define this UX and its machine-readable output, without
silently guessing an executable fallback.

## 3. Document readers and schemas

Generic `.mx` documents use the existing strict parser: literals, lists, maps,
comments and the existing round-trip encoding. It refuses variables, calls,
command substitutions, interpolation, statements and executable separators.
`load_data` remains a data-only API and is documented for `.mx`; parsing failure
is terminal for that load. It does not invent filenames or dispatch script code.

Application/service-owned documents additionally validate their owning schema.
The caller may supply schema identity and version, or the document may declare
them; if both do, disagreement is refused. Generic literal data need not carry
an app schema. Schema identity/version are semantic, not another filename family.
Existing numeric `schema` fields do not have to be converted to strings merely
to rename files. Migration must preserve each owning schema's version semantics.

Scene `.mx` documents retain their current `---` header envelope and fenced
strict-data widget map in this first refactor. The existing scene reader handles
that structure; the generic strict reader does not become a scene interpreter.
A consumer explicitly selects its document reader/kind. An unknown kind/schema,
invalid envelope, malformed widget map or invalid binding produces a document
error. No candidate reader is ever the executable parser.

Do not couple extension migration to a rewrite of scene metadata or layouts.
If a common strict-data scene envelope is useful later, version it and provide
a migration independently. Existing layout, model, action-name, diff and source
round-trip contracts must remain intact in this release.

## 4. Restricted bindings and action authority

Only schema-declared fields can interpret restricted expression strings. In all
other fields the identical string is literal data. The scene binding compiler
retains its model/item roots, allowed operations, dependency tracking and size,
time and aggregate list-row limits. Calls, assignments, shell forms, process
launches, file writes and Bus requests cannot be smuggled in through a binding.

Data may name an action implemented by a trusted application/program, but cannot
supply a general executable action body. A workflow document or rule catalogue
is not a bypass for the normal activation/authority of the program consuming it.
Do not introduce automatic command-string evaluation, executable includes or
download-and-run behaviour into document readers.

Non-executing is not synonymous with consequence-free: schemas must still bound
resource use and validate referenced paths/assets/settings according to their
own contracts. The file-family change does not promise that every configuration
value or action reference is appropriate for every consumer.

## 5. Legacy compatibility and migration

Inventory every data consumer and producer, not just files with recognised
suffixes. Include generated runtime state, embedded include_str fixtures, startup
configuration, tests, asset manifests, scenes, watched paths, install collectors,
public guides and private hub automation. Distinguish code/data from its actual
reader; names such as `data.mix` can be executable helper modules and must not be
renamed blindly. No bulk suffix replacement or executable grammar change.

Use explicit rollout phases:

1. Readers gain `.mx` support and legacy data compatibility. Program paths refuse
   `.mx`. Record capability/version evidence on every deployment target.
2. Migrate source fixtures and literals, install collectors and app/service path
   resolvers. Deploy coupled binary/script bundles while retaining legacy files
   needed by unmigrated callers.
3. Switch owning writers to canonical `.mx` only after their readers are ready.
   Migrate user files explicitly and retain recoverable originals and a receipt.
4. Remove legacy spellings only after every supported consumer and tested rollback
   is accounted for, through a documented compatibility-removal release.

Generic `load_data(path)` uses the literal supplied path; it must not silently
rewrite arbitrary `.mix` filenames. Owning configuration/scene resolvers may
support old/new alternatives explicitly. If both exist, compare typed semantic
values under the owning schema: equivalent copies get a visible migration
diagnostic; differing copies are a conflict requiring explicit resolution. A
malformed canonical file does not cause a quiet fallback to an old file.
Declared precedence or explicit operator selection must be observable.

Migration tools run in Mix through native facilities, with a preview/report,
idempotent apply, ownership checks, originals and bounded failure recovery. Do
not rewrite schema versions, erase comments, overwrite user edits or convert
operational identities without a specific migration requirement. Preserve state
and registry format identities, hashes/signature domains and frozen ABP bytes.
Any affected signed artefact is reissued through its existing native authority;
renaming a signed path is not permission to edit signed content in place.

## 6. Component integration and deployment

`libs/strict`, `libs/expr` and `libs/scene` keep their headless separation from
the full Mix interpreter. `libs/mix` and `cli/mix-shell` share program admission;
`libs/config` and owning services/apps handle document paths/schema validation.
Use existing install collectors and native deployment/lifecycle facilities. No
new broker, alternate node-control transport or duplicate parser is introduced.

This is a coordinated binary/library/consumer refactor, not a stand-alone CLI
rename. Build provenance must identify the exact revision, language/library and
binary versions, enabled features, test receipts and installed document formats.
Select the actual release number and compatibility window in its release record.
The current source baseline is language 0.109.1 / binary 0.109.4; that is not the
new release or evidence about every installed target.

Qualify an isolated native target before any working desktop, then roll through
explicitly selected native targets. Stage readers before documents and writers;
verify the real ABP path, loaded scenes/configuration and executable macros. The
self-contained VT-native image carries all readers, interpreter and documents.
It must not depend on host packages or host desktop/session resources.

Rollback includes compatible binary, consumer scripts and document/state copies.
Restoring only the previous binary after a filename migration is insufficient.
Candidate reload failure must preserve the accepted evaluator and managed children.
Frozen Cosmix nodes keep their old spellings until separately migrated; no broad
fleet deploy or production restart follows merely from accepting this spec.

## 7. Required acceptance matrix

| Boundary | Required evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Program admission | Valid and malicious `.mx` refused by direct CLI, serve/reload, REPL file launch, source/include/require, macro and library file APIs before a marker effect occurs; cover symlinks, uppercase and `--no-lint` |
| Strict data | Valid `.mx` round-trips; variables, calls, interpolation, substitutions and statements refuse; errors cannot enter executable fallback |
| Scenes | Existing fixtures renamed without semantic change; pure bindings resolve, effectful bindings refuse, resource bounds and layout/model diffs still pass |
| Schema selection | Known versions work; unknown/mismatched schema/kind, invalid fields and malformed canonical files refuse visibly |
| Legacy coexistence | Old/new readers, generated writers, equal/conflicting duplicate files, missing paths, idempotent migration and interruption recovery behave as specified |
| Native applications | Ced macro/undo remains executable `.mix`; all six app consumers, Quoin scenes and relevant service configuration load through their real native path |
| Packaging/identity | New image has required documents/readers; signed path changes use the native authority; freeze checks confirm no ABP wire/domain-byte changes |
| Deployment/recovery | Exact candidate build runs on isolated target; selected-target rollout reports loaded formats and final state; old binary-plus-data rollback actually restores service/scene/macro behaviour |

Implement declarative fixtures as `.mx` and executable integration gates as `.mix`.
Use negative tests with observable marker effects rather than tests that merely
check an extension helper. Successful docs builds, renamed files or mock readers
do not establish runtime conformance. No extra script families may be introduced
as a shortcut around these boundaries.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/spec/portal/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/spec/portal/README.md) -->

# Settings portal contract

Status: accepted, version 0.1.0. The cbc2 verification of `services/portald`
passed on the commit that carries it (dcd2f1a). The verbs and wire shapes below
are fixed by the XDG portal specification.

`portald` implements the Settings interface of the XDG desktop portal, on the
session bus, for the `org.freedesktop.appearance` namespace. The machine-checkable
key table is in [portal.spec.mix](portal.spec.mix).

## Bus identity

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Bus name | `org.freedesktop.portal.Desktop` (requested without queueing) |
| Object path | `/org/freedesktop/portal/desktop` |
| Interface | `org.freedesktop.portal.Settings`, version property 2 |
| Error prefix | `org.freedesktop.portal.Error` |

## Methods and signal

- `Read(s namespace, s key) -> v`: the value in one extra variant layer,
  deprecated form.
- `ReadOne(s namespace, s key) -> v`: the value in a single layer.
- `ReadAll(as namespaces) -> a{sa{sv}}`: globs matched against namespaces.
  An unmatched glob yields no namespace entry. An empty array or any empty
  filter matches all namespaces. Up to 64 filters of 256 bytes each are accepted;
  larger requests return `org.freedesktop.portal.Error.InvalidArgument`.
- `SettingChanged(s namespace, s key, v value)`: emitted only when a key's value
  changes.

An unserved namespace or key on `Read` or `ReadOne` returns
`org.freedesktop.portal.Error.NotFound`.

## Keys

| Namespace | Key | Wire type | Values |
|---|---|---|---|
| `org.freedesktop.appearance` | `color-scheme` | `u` | 1 dark, 2 light |
| `org.freedesktop.appearance` | `contrast` | `u` | 0 normal, 1 high |
| `org.freedesktop.appearance` | `accent-color` | `(ddd)` | sRGB 0 to 1; absent when the source has no accent |

Defaults before any projection: `color-scheme` 1 (dark), `contrast` 0, no
`accent-color`.

## Source and identity

- Source verb: `settings.appearance.get`, read-only, from `settingsd`.
- The reply carries the atomic snapshot evidence alongside the projection.
  The shared settings Consumer checks the evidence and manages subscription,
  initial reads, lifecycle generations, delivery loss and bounded recovery.
- Trigger: authenticated retained topic `settingsd.desktop.changed.<profile>`.
  A publication also triggers a read when settingsd restarts at the same revision.
- A projection is identified by binding, incarnation and revision. A projection
  older than the held one within the same incarnation is refused and counted as
  stale. An equal identity changes nothing. A new incarnation is adopted.
- The authority's projection schema is `APPEARANCE_SCHEMA = 1`. An unknown
  schema is refused.

## Startup

1. Load the validated binding-specific cache at
   `<state directory>/<instance>/<profile>/appearance.json`, else defaults.
   A mismatched binding and the old unpartitioned cache are ignored.
2. Request the bus name without queueing immediately. A held name refuses a
   second instance. Authority work runs asynchronously.
3. Answer Read within 250 ms of process launch, tested with the production binary
   and configuration against a silent authority, including cache and profile switch.
4. Serve, and back off on source failure from 250 ms to 30 s. Transport recovery
   remains alive through initial broker failure.

The name is never held waiting on the source.

## Verbs

`portald.status` (read-only) is registered in `docs/docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix`.

## Compatibility

Version 2 of the interface is the one served. A breaking change to a method
shape, key type or key value needs a new interface version, and both versions
must be served during the deprecation period.

## Deferred

- The FileChooser interface.
- Accent as a settings field. The current projection carries the design's
  resolved accent through settingsd's in-memory sidecar, outside the sealed
  snapshot.
- Caller identity and sandboxed app IDs.
