# Releases contract

Status: accepted, version 0.3.0 (0.3.0 adds optional `category` metadata;
0.2.0 adds `exec_wrapper`). Verified by
`services/releasesd/tests/releases_test.mix` (offline logic) and
`services/releasesd/tests/releasesd_test.mix` (every verb over a private
broker).

`releasesd` follows GitHub repositories named in a per-user catalogue and
installs their Linux release tarballs for that user. This page fixes the
catalogue schema, the Bus verbs and the on-disk layout that other tools may
rely on.

## Bus identity

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Service | `releases` (`mix --serve releasesd.mix --name releases`) |
| Verbs | `releases.status`, `.list`, `.check`, `.notes`, `.install`, `.update`, `.rollback`, `.remove`, `.link` |
| Bodies | JSON objects; `{}` or an empty body where no field is required |
| Success | rc 0, JSON reply |
| Refusals | rc 10 bad request, rc 14 unknown app, rc 15 the operation failed; body `{error_code, message}` |

Error codes: `USAGE`, `ROOT`, `UNKNOWN_APP`, `CATALOGUE`, `NO_RELEASE`, `NO_ASSET`,
`AMBIGUOUS_ASSET`, `DOWNLOAD`, `DIGEST`, `UNVERIFIABLE`, `LAYOUT`,
`NO_PREVIOUS`, `PENDING`, `BUSY`.

| Verb | Body | Reply |
|---|---|---|
| `releases.status` | — | `{catalogue, apps, installed, root, share, bin, state, authenticated, arch}` |
| `releases.list` | `{apps?}` | rows from the last check |
| `releases.check` | `{apps?}` | rows after asking GitHub |
| `releases.notes` | `{app}` | `{app, tag, published, url, notes}` |
| `releases.install` | `{app, tag?}` | result |
| `releases.update` | `{apps?}` | results; default every installed app |
| `releases.rollback` | `{app}` | result |
| `releases.remove` | `{app}` | result |
| `releases.link` | `{apps?}` | results |

A row is `{app, repo, category, category_label, installed, latest, published, checked, status}`, with
`category` the catalogue's optional group and `category_label` its display label
(null when absent), and
`status` one of `current`, `update`, `not installed`, `unchecked` or
`error: <text>`. A result is `{app, action, version?, previous?, verified?,
links?, skipped?, error?}`; `verified` is `{asset, sha256, proofs, tag}`.

## Catalogue, schema 1

The optional top-level `categories` map supplies display labels for supported
groups, for example `{creative: "Graphics"}`. Labels must be non-empty strings
of at most 64 characters without control characters. Labels are projected onto
rows so Prefs can use catalogue terminology without knowing external products.

A strict-data document, by default `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/mixos/releases.mx`
(`~/.config/mixos/releases.mx`). A missing file is the default catalogue,
MixOS itself: `mixos-desktop` and `mixos-server`, both from `markc/mixos`. It
is re-read on every request.

```text
{
  schema: 1,
  apps: [
    {name: "example", repo: "owner/example"},
    {name: "other", repo: "owner/other", asset: "(?i)linux-x86_64-full\\.tar\\.gz$"}
  ]
}
```

| Field | Rule |
|---|---|
| `name` | `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}$`, unique; it becomes a directory name |
| `repo` | `owner/name` on GitHub |
| `asset` | optional regex choosing the tarball when the default is wrong or ambiguous |
| `category` | optional `mixos-desktop`, `mixos-server`, `creative` or `other`, used by Prefs to group rows; omitted entries remain in Other, with legacy MixOS bundle identifiers recognised |
| `exec_wrapper` | optional list of 1–32 non-empty strings without control characters, the first an absolute path without `=`; see below |

**`exec_wrapper`.** When `link` writes the app's desktop entries, every
`Exec=` becomes `Exec=<wrapper…> -- <the entry's own Exec>`. The entry's own
Exec keeps its field codes (`%F`, `%U` …) and is made absolute as usual.
Each wrapper argument is written per the Desktop Entry Specification: `%` is
doubled; an argument with a reserved character is double-quoted, with
`"` `` ` `` `$` `\` escaped inside the quotes; then every backslash is
escaped once more as a string value. The literal `--` separates the wrapper
from the app's command, so a wrapper can always fall back to running that
command as it stands. Every `Exec` is wrapped, Desktop Actions included,
with whitespace before the key and around `=` allowed. The main group and
every Desktop Action must have a non-empty `Exec`, or the entry is refused
(`LAYOUT`). An install, update or rollback checks this before the version
becomes current, so a refusal changes nothing. If a wrapper is added while
an install or rollback is interrupted and the target cannot be wrapped, the
retry abandons that change: `current` returns to the other recorded version
(if that one passes), `previous` is cleared, and `meta.json` records
`abandoned: {op, target, reason}`. A rollback that does this reports it as
its result. A wrapped entry gets `DBusActivatable=false`, since D-Bus
activation would start the app without its `Exec`. `TryExec` stays the
app's real program. The entry is
rebuilt from the app's own copy on every link, so it is never wrapped twice.
The link manifest records the final content. Removing the field unwraps the
entry on the next link.

The default asset is the one release file matching `linux[-_.]<arch>.tar.gz`
(`x86_64`, `amd64` or `x64`; `aarch64` or `arm64`), excluding web builds.

## Verification

An install proceeds only if every checksum source the release publishes
matches, and at least one exists: the asset's API `digest`, and a
`SHA256SUMS`/`checksums` file (itself matched to its own API digest) that
lists the tarball exactly once. Anything else refuses with `DIGEST` or
`UNVERIFIABLE`, and nothing changes on disk.

## Trust rules

- **Never as root.** Every operation that changes files refuses with `ROOT`
  when run as uid 0, before taking any lock or creating any file. Installs
  are per user, by that user.
- **The release is checked before use.** It is unpacked into a stage without
  owners, special permissions, ACLs, extended attributes or file flags, then
  refused (`LAYOUT`) if any symlink does not lead, step by step and through
  no other symlink, to an existing file or directory inside the release; if
  it holds a special file; or if any file is setuid or setgid. Desktop entries are read
  only when they are regular files inside the release.
- **Downloads are bounded.** The tarball may not exceed its published size
  (2 GiB when none is given), a checksum file 1 MiB, and each file must
  arrive within 30 minutes.
- **A manifest is evidence, not permission.** Each entry is `{path,
  states}`, every state a link target or a sha256. A path is replaced or
  removed only if it is inside this target and still in one of its states;
  anything else is left and reported (`skipped`, `kept`). Before changing
  anything, a relink publishes an intent manifest listing each path's old and
  new state, so an interrupted relink is recognised and finished.
- **Only managed versions are touched.** A version directory is managed when
  it carries `.verified-<version>.json`. Pruning and removal touch nothing
  else; an app directory holding anything unmanaged is kept. `current` and
  names ending in `.json` are never versions.
- **A retry finishes the job.** Before `current` moves, `meta.json` records
  the new version and previous one plus `pending: {op, target}`, cleared once
  the links are done. A later install, rollback or link first resumes a
  pending transition exactly: a resumed rollback is the rollback asked for; a
  resumed install is finished before a new rollback starts from it. Several
  link targets may share one opt directory (a session seeing it read-only):
  `pending` records its originating target by a random id kept in the
  target's own `<share>/mixos/releases/.target-id` (never by path: two mount
  namespaces can show different directories at one path). Only that target
  resumes and clears it, another target's `link` only reconciles its own links, and its
  install, rollback or remove refuses with `PENDING` until the origin has
  finished.
  Installing the version that is already current reconciles its links.
- **Serialised, in one order.** Locks are always taken installation first
  (`<root>/opt/.releases.lock`, shared by every target using that opt
  directory, whatever its state directory), then target
  (`<share>/mixos/releases/.lock`). Install, update, rollback and remove hold
  both. A link holds its target and, when it can open it, the installation;
  through a read-only opt it cannot, and it then only reconciles its own links
  and never resumes a pending transition. The service also handles requests in order:
  while an install downloads, other requests wait, so callers allow minutes
  for `install` and `update`.

## Layout

Root defaults to `~/.local`.

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `<root>/opt/<app>/<version>/` | the release prefix: `bin/`, `share/` |
| `<root>/opt/<app>/current` | symlink to the active version |
| `<root>/opt/<app>/meta.json` | `{name, repo, version, previous, verified, installed_at, pending?, abandoned?}` |
| `<root>/opt/<app>/.verified-<version>.json` | the proof of each kept version |
| `<share>/mixos/releases/<app>.links.json` | what was made in this target: `[{path, states: [{link} or {sha256}]}]` |
| `$XDG_STATE_HOME/mixos/releases/<app>.json` | the last check: ETag, latest release |

The current and previous versions are kept; older ones are pruned. Links:
`bin/*` into `<root>/bin`; desktop entries into `<share>/applications` with
`Exec`/`TryExec` made absolute through `current`; hicolor icons and MIME
packages as symlinks. A path that is not in the target's manifest is never
replaced or removed.

## Environment

`MIXOS_RELEASES_ROOT`, `MIXOS_RELEASES_VIEW` (the root as the apps see it,
for installs into a container), `MIXOS_RELEASES_SHARE`, `MIXOS_RELEASES_BIN`,
`MIXOS_RELEASES_CATALOGUE`, `MIXOS_RELEASES_STATE`, `MIXOS_RELEASES_API`
(default `https://api.github.com`) and `GITHUB_TOKEN` (else `gh auth token`).
The token is sent only to `https://api.github.com`.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/docs/spec/settings/ (source: https://mixos.dev/docs/spec/settings/README.md) -->

# Desktop settings contract

Status: accepted authority contract, version 0.4.0 (0.2.0 added the summary
topic and read view, [decision](../../decisions/2026-10-11-settings-summary-reads.md);
0.3.0 added snapshot schema 2, [decision](../../decisions/2026-10-11-settings-snapshot-schema-2.md);
0.4.0 adds key bindings, [decision](../../decisions/2026-10-11-keymaps-in-settings.md)). Full desktop consumer
integration remains in development. No frozen ABP wire bytes change.

`settingsd` serves one explicitly initialised profile in the initial slice.
`settings` provides shared headless types, resolver, consumer and snapshot reducer;
`design::DesignReadProjection` is render data that cannot construct an accepted
design or fork compiler apply lineage. Consumers are the desktop applications
and compd's Quoin shell.

## Served verbs

All trusted mesh operators can invoke these verbs. Requests carry JSON bodies;
responses preserve ordinary ABP rc conventions: 0 for handled results and 10 for
refusal, invalid input or unknown verbs. Domain status is structured in the body.

| Verb | Input and result |
| --- | --- |
| `settings.describe` | No mutation; version, fields, ranges, defaults, limits and implemented/deferred capabilities |
| `settings.get` | `{binding:{instance,profile}, view?, schema?}`; `view` `full` (default): complete accepted snapshot under `snapshot`, in `schema` 1 (default) or 2 (each distinct design projection once under `designs`, contexts naming it by digest; other schemas refused with `unsupported_schema`); `summary`: the profile's `Summary` (schema, binding, incarnation, revision, design revision, source digest, appearance names, `custom_source`, `keymaps` when any are set, and `terminal` when any value is set; never projections or a source) under `summary`; both with publication/recovery status |
| `settings.appearance.get` | `{binding:{instance,profile}, schema?}`; read-only appearance projection (`mode`, `contrast`, sRGB `accent`) tagged with incarnation and revisions; the reply also includes the atomic `snapshot` (in `schema` 1 or 2, as for `settings.get`) for shared Consumer validation; `wrong_target` on a foreign binding |
| `settings.validate` | Fenced apply-shaped body; resolve/compile candidate without a write or receipt; valid with current base identity or diagnostics/conflict |
| `settings.apply` | Fenced batch described below; durable changed/unchanged receipt |
| `settings.reset` | Apply-shaped body with empty changes and explicit reset paths; same transaction semantics |
| `settings.status` | Binding plus optional operation_id; accepted/published revision and retained receipt or unknown_operation |

The profile identifier and instance use 1–64 ASCII letters, digits, dash or
underscore. Operation IDs use the same character set, up to 128 bytes. Revisions
are canonical decimal u64 **strings**, including on strict-data boundaries;
numeric, overflowing, signed and leading-zero representations are refused.
Panel thickness accepts a whole numeric value such as 48 or 48.0, within its
declared range; Mix data numbers use floating representation. Fractional values,
numeric strings and overflow are refused before acceptance.

```json
{
  "binding": {"instance": "example", "profile": "default"},
  "expected_incarnation": "authority-readback-uuid",
  "expected_revision": "1",
  "operation_id": "example-batch-1",
  "changes": {
    "appearance.mode": "light",
    "ui.text_scale": 1.1,
    "shell.panels.bottom.thickness": 48
  },
  "reset": []
}
```

An optional request_digest is checked against BLAKE3 of the canonical serde JSON
representation of the typed request, with request_digest set to null. Object
maps are sorted; reset-list order remains part of the request. Use the shared
request digest API rather than hashing arbitrary JSON text. Reusing an operation
ID with different input is refused. Receipt lookup/deduplication precedes expected
revision conflict, after target/incarnation checks. An old retained operation can
retrieve its original receipt after subsequent edits.
Retry the identical request to recover its receipt. Updating a fence changes the
digest and requires a new operation ID. Validation checks the present fence;
another writer may still win before a later apply.

Retain at most 128 receipts, inside the accepted document. A no-op writes its
receipt durably without increasing desktop revision or publishing a new snapshot.
Missing/evicted IDs return unknown_operation: opaque IDs have no expiry order,
and the initial contract cannot prove expired_operation. Resolve ambiguity by
readback and a newly fenced operation; exactly-once is not promised beyond
retention. Restores establish a new incarnation and clear foreign-history
receipts. Status includes publication_pending and recovering separately from
durable acceptance; a changed result can remain unpublished after broker failure.

## Initial data and resolution

The schema covers appearance scheme/style/mode/contrast, window decorations
(csd or ssd) and caption side (right or left) plus embedded or complete
strict-data design source; UI density/text scale/reduced motion; named panels
with edge/mode/thickness; ordered shell pages; and whole app override records
with scheme/mode/contrast/text scale. Describe supplies exact ranges. Unknown
fields/scopes are refused. Field reset restores a package default; removing an
app override restores profile inheritance. Per-field authored provenance beyond
these initial concrete profile values is later work.
The package source is pinned in accepted storage at profile creation. Null
appearance.source selects that pinned source, including after binary upgrades;
it does not silently adopt the upgraded binary's embedded defaults. Adopting a
new package source requires an explicit mutation with a new revision.
The accepted effective digest also fences compiler interpretation drift. A
changed interpretation requires explicit migration rather than changing the
same accepted identity on reload.

The accepted record carries a format number (absent in format 1; now 2). On
open the record's seal is verified as stored, in its own format, so tampering
is still refused. An older record is then upgraded by one rule: everything
authored is kept, the effective interpretation is resolved again from the
authored desktop and the pinned source (derived data is never trusted across
formats), both digests are sealed at the current format, and the backup and
then the primary are replaced atomically. A second open changes nothing. An
authored field added later is omitted at its default, so older records still
verify; a change to the effective interpretation bumps the format.

Validate the whole candidate and all advertised app contexts before acceptance.
Compilation checks the source's claimed contexts. App overlays affect their
context alone; profile high contrast takes precedence. A custom source is at
most 256 KiB. Encoded requests are at most 384 KiB. Inline snapshots are at most
960 KiB, reserving 64 KiB for ABP/broker envelope overhead under the current 1 MiB
retained limit. Larger settings are refused until native immutable artifact
delivery is implemented. Required fonts/assets and runtime live capability are
not yet advertised.

Snapshot schema 1 includes binding, incarnation, desktop revision, resolved-design
generation, source digest, complete desktop and effective per-app/desktop design
projections. The resolved-design generation is owned by the authority and
survives restart; it is not a broker sequence or a reconstituted compiler apply
handle. Clients must confirm an incarnation change through fresh bound readback
before installing it. Work tickets fence superseded asynchronous completion.
Conflicting payloads at the same incarnation/revision trigger a fresh read;
if the bound authority confirms the contradiction, report it and preserve the
installed values rather than enter an endless readback loop.
Fresh decoded topic deliveries use Reducer.observe. Captured tickets are for
asynchronous completions; a new delivery can advance the state while an older
bound read is pending, and that read cannot roll the revision back.

The settings library API is now 0.5.0; authority verbs are 0.3.0. Snapshot
schema 1 is the default; schema 2 is its compact wire form, decoded into the
same in-memory snapshot. The shared native consumer follows the compact topic
and reads schema 2; consumers on their own library copy stay on schema 1 until
ported. The shared consumer performs subscribe-before-get over the host's
existing supervised Bus connection through its optional native executor. It
owns no transport/task/incoming receiver. Hosts feed connection generations,
deliveries and explicit queue loss, execute at most one current action, and
cancel superseded work. Bootstrap buffers one latest candidate; loss coalesces
one later full read. A bounded history suppresses repeated rejected confirmation
candidates. Transport recovery has one pending backoff from 250 ms to 30 seconds;
success/disconnect cancels it. Protocol/target/schema refusal is visible and
quiescent until a new event or explicit refresh. Every native call is bounded
to one second; the host must also cap the combined initial bootstrap to one
second and show a labelled fallback while recovery continues.
Use the same initial deadline with `native::execute_until` for subscribe and
read. Recovery exposes an absolute deadline, preserved during malformed-event
storms; arrivals cannot restart or bypass it. Canonical app/shell constructors
choose `app:<id>` or `desktop` contexts. Captured read tickets and baselines
distinguish real same-incarnation rollback from a valid read racing a newer
publication. Cancel old executor futures when their current work ticket changes.

One context-specific change plan separates paint, text, layout, resources, motion
and optional shell geometry. Source/provenance/revision-only changes advance
evidence without rendering work. Received accepted data is distinct from staged
and applied data. Prepare all resources, then on the renderer event loop check
the stage ticket immediately before synchronous activation and acknowledgement,
without an intervening await. Old connection, consumer and stage completions
cannot claim application. Hosts must fence the actual swap as well as its report.
Identical render inputs need no swap; application never proves presentation.
`Consumer::evidence()` reports binding, context, connection generation,
confirmation, presentation kind, accepted (`current`) and UI-acknowledged
(`applied`) identities, plus normal and fallback faults. Each identity carries
incarnation, canonical string revision, design revision and source digest.
Absent identities are null. Losing confirmation demotes installed current data
to LastGood; an installed fallback is never an authority fence. The shell
exposes this same evidence at `shell.props.get` path `settings`, including root
and dotted reads such as `settings.applied.revision`, behind its existing caller
and connection checks. Evidence does not assert a broker participant record or
frame presentation. `settings_cache` supplies the shared host's persistence
identity, cache fault and fallback diagnostics. The persistence identity is
historical and must match current applied evidence to describe that capture.
Quoin uses the shared worker's service-owned persistent cache while its existing
Bus supervisor starts; terminal refusal preserves offline resources, and only
explicit initial rejection permits a configured scene service override.
`compd.truth.slots.<id>.decided` independently reads the
geometry owner's decided size, or null when absent, without falling back to
committed client geometry. The native desktop geometry gate compares these
readbacks with real client configures and captured pixels.
DTO field additions require explicit classification in the shared comparison;
source/provenance exclusions are deliberate rather than wildcard omissions.
Shared fallback preparation tries validated retained bootstrap data, then local
cache, then current embedded defaults. The host supplies readiness checks for
every reference used by its context and shell capability on its worker. A fenced
completion produces the same immutable UI stage; it never seeds the authority
reducer or mutation fences. Installed data has explicit Current, Retained,
Cached, LastGood and Embedded labels. Identical fresh authority data can promote
cache/embedded evidence without a redundant swap.

Optional `settings/cache` stores applied authority/retained generations in an
existing isolated absolute cache directory. Its versioned JSON envelope binds
instance/profile, context, shell capability, interpretation and content digest.
Bounded directory-relative regular-file reads refuse symlinks in every path
component and cannot block on FIFOs. Before reuse, complete projections must
match current compilation of their authored inputs; unavailable old pinned
package sources and compiler drift are refused visibly. Exact JSON float
round trips preserve these checks. Digests detect corruption, not file origin;
valid cache data still supplies no authority evidence. A stable locked serial
writer fences superseded applied-generation saves, permits retry of the latest
failed attempt and reports ambiguous post-rename failure. All I/O belongs off
the UI loop. Cache failure preserves usable applied data. Real font/asset loading,
artifact preparation and GUI fallback/first-map timing remain pending.

## Shell panel preferences

Quoin prepares appearance and the global panel policy together, then installs
both on the compositor loop before acknowledging the settings revision. Each
record's explicit edge selects one of four panels on every current and future
output; the record ID is provenance, independent of a connector or page name.
`dock`, `overlay` and `hidden` map to runtime docked, pinned and hidden modes.
The default profile owns the bottom panel in dock mode, requesting 40 logical
pixels. An edge without pages draws nothing and reserves no work area.

Thickness is requested logical pixels. Runtime edge ranges, the active page's
minimum and the output/opposite-edge budget fit the request. A bottom page with
a 52-pixel minimum therefore presents 52 pixels for the default 40-pixel
request. Panel rows include a nullable `settings` object with the record ID,
`requested_px`, `fitted_px`, `presented_px`, `reserved_px` and constraint names.
Output shrinkage fits the panel; regrowth recovers the request. Page selection
and registration use the existing carousel and panel model.

Settings owns the mode and thickness of each declared edge. Conflicting legacy
panel writes refuse `SETTINGS_MANAGED` before changing interaction state; exact
current mode or settled-size requests are no-ops. Transient show/hide and page
selection remain available. Persistent toggles cannot undock managed panels.
For managed edges Toggle changes transient visibility only while hidden; docked
or pinned modes treat it as a successful no-op. Corner-menu mode entries are
disabled while managed; activating a disabled selection is an inert action.
Removing a profile record
restores that edge's captured local mode and settled thickness. Saving a page
selection keeps those local values, so profile preferences do not leak into the
local state file. Thickness or appearance updates retain interaction holders;
an actual transition to hidden retires invalid keyboard/menu holders.

Duplicate records targeting one edge and non-empty `shell.page_order` lack a
runtime identity mapping and fail whole shell preparation. The authority's
schema can accept them, but Quoin reports the preparation fault and retains
the last good appearance and panel policy. Correct them through a new fenced
settings mutation. This is consumer capability validation, not a rollback of
the accepted authority revision. Empty page ordering preserves local order.

Requested maximised windows keep their owning output and follow only changes
to their desired content rectangle; removal chooses an available output while
retaining the original unmaximise geometry. Scene reservations are reconciled
after settings activation and before frame work, including without the comp
Bus port. An unchanged target does not emit another maximise configure while
the client is slow to acknowledge or replace its buffer. The compositor's
decided slot remains authoritative during these transitions; older legally
acknowledged buffers do not undo a newer target. Existing aspect-preserving
fit and inverse input mapping remain in use.

Fullscreen continues to use the whole output. Its compositor record, pending
protocol intent and committed state fence work-area reconfiguration through
delayed entry/exit commits. After fullscreen releases ownership, the next normal
dispatch restores the latest maximised content rectangle, even if the work-area
map has not changed again. Window geometry changes schedule redraw and retarget
the human Wayland pointer, respecting grabs. This does not by itself prove
stationary hover or scene bounds before/after rendering.

The protocol fixtures exercise actual xdg configure/ack/buffer commits using
the production geometry executor. Their headless output has no renderer; native
Bus delivery fixtures and protocol fixtures do not establish their composed
rendered settings-to-frame behaviour. Persistent tiling, new maximise intent
with no outputs, native window/input/frame evidence and VT latency acceptance
remain outstanding. Current text scale changes the title font, while decoration
extents continue to come from the selected style's fixed height and border.

## Key bindings

The profile's `keymaps` holds the person's key bindings: per application
id, per action id, the chords chosen. An empty list unbinds the action; an
action not listed keeps the application's own default, which ships with the
application. The field is omitted while empty, so profiles written before it
keep their seals, and it does not affect the resolved design.

- **Apply:** `keymaps.<app>` takes the whole map (null drops every change
  for that app); `keymaps.<app>.<action>` takes a list of chords (null
  returns the action to its default). Action ids are dotted: everything
  after the app id is the action id.
- **Chords:** `Ctrl`, `Alt` and `Shift`, each at most once and in any
  order, then one key: a name of ASCII letters and digits (`ArrowLeft`,
  `F6`, `PageDown`, `B`, `1`) or `=`, `-`, `/`. settingsd checks this
  grammar; the application checks that it knows the key.
- **Limits:** 16 applications, 256 actions each, 4 distinct chords per
  action, 32 bytes per chord, 64 bytes per action id.
- **Followers:** the summary carries `keymaps`, and each application applies
  its own entry when the revision changes (`toolkit::Registry::rebind`).

## Terminal

The profile's `terminal` holds the term's preferences. Each default is the
term's behaviour before the group existed, except padding (8 px instead of
1 px) and the focus ring: `accent` at strength 0.25 gives a quiet tint from
the current theme accent. `neutral` remains available; `accent` at strength
0.5 matches the earlier half-accent ring. Each value is omitted at its
default, so older profiles keep their seals. It does not affect the resolved
design. Terminal colours are not a setting: they follow the session theme.

| Field | Type and range | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `terminal.font.family` | string or null, 1–128 bytes, no control characters | null: `appearance.mono_family` |
| `terminal.font.size` | number 6–48 | the design's UI type size |
| `terminal.font.weight` | integer 100–900, step 100 | 400 |
| `terminal.padding` | integer 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 (px) | 8 |
| `terminal.scrollback.lines` | integer 0–1000000 | 1000 |
| `terminal.scroll.speed` | integer 10–200 (rows per wheel line, scaled by speed/40; touchpad travel in cell heights at that scale) | 40 |
| `terminal.border.width` | integer 1–4 (px) | 1 |
| `terminal.cursor.shape` | `block`, `underline` or `bar` | `underline` |
| `terminal.cursor.blink` | boolean | false |
| `terminal.focus.ring` | `neutral` or `accent` | `accent` |
| `terminal.focus.strength` | number 0–1, used with `accent` | 0.25 |
| `terminal.mouse.copy_on_select` | boolean | false |
| `terminal.env.term` | `[a-z0-9-]{1,64}`; new tabs and panes | `xterm-256color` |

Apply and reset take each path, or `terminal` for the whole group. The
summary carries `terminal` when any value is set.

## Topics and storage

Publish retained `settingsd.desktop.changed.<profile>` (the snapshot in schema
1), then retained `settingsd.desktop.compact.<profile>` (schema 2), then
retained `settingsd.desktop.summary.<profile>` (its `Summary`), all owned by
the registered `settingsd` service. The unscoped base names are reserved too.
A revision is published once all three topics are; a failure retries all three. All clients may
subscribe; ordinary publishers/clearers cannot replace its canonical state.
Noded strips inner routing headers and stamps broker_service independently of
caller input. The publisher repopulates retained state at startup and reconnect,
even without a settings mutation. Generic props-prefix ownership is deliberately
not used: embedding a profile in that prefix changes its matched service owner.
Failed publication starts a single pending retry job, with exponential backoff
from 250 ms capped at 30 seconds. Success removes the job and every timer.
Reconnection or a new revision restarts the backoff. There is no idle heartbeat;
publication_pending remains visible throughout a failed pending job.

**Following from an app.** An app on a plain Bus connection (no owner
stamps) subscribes to the profile's summary topic, treats a delivery only as
a hint, and reads the look with `settings.get`'s `summary` view, never the
complete snapshot: `settings::follow::Follower` keeps one read in
flight (hints during it fold into one more), ignores an answer older than one
already seen (same incarnation, lower or equal revision), adopts the instance
from `wrong_target` once (never the profile), and reports settingsd missing so
the app keeps its theme file. `toolkit::session_look` turns the profile's
appearance into the app's session theme; an appearance naming its own design
package (`source`) or a name the app does not know keeps the theme file's.

Default root: resolved MixOS Etc directory / `settings/<profile>/`. Explicit
test roots are supported. One retained writer.lock inode provides a process
flock; it is never removed on normal exit. The root must be an owned directory
not writable by other users. `desktop.conf.mix` holds schema, binding,
incarnation, revisions, authored desktop, pinned package source, receipts and
a verified BLAKE3 content digest and effective interpretation digest. These
digests detect corruption and interpretation drift; they are not an
authentication signature. A synced
`desktop.previous.conf.mix` is written before replacing the accepted generation.
Files are private, never evaluated as Mix source.
Reads, lock acquisition, replacements and syncs are relative to the same held
directory descriptor. Replacing/detaching the profile directory or writer-lock
inode fences the existing writer. Newly created directory entries are synced in
their parents before initial acceptance.

Replacement uses exclusive temporary create, write, file sync, directory-relative
rename and directory sync. Pre-rename errors leave accepted state unchanged.
Post-rename sync errors report outcome_unknown and fence further mutations until
recovery; they cannot be reported as a known uncommitted failure. Corrupt input
is preserved before a valid backup is restored with a new incarnation. Newer
schemas or mismatched target bindings are not overwritten by a fallback.
Corruption evidence is hard-linked and synced before the atomic replacement;
recovery never removes the primary before its replacement is ready.
A missing established primary fails visibly even with a backup; automatic
recovery applies only to a present corrupt primary.
I/O errors, strict shape changes and intact documents requiring a changed
compiler interpretation fail without an automatic backup rollback.

`settingsd init --instance example` explicitly creates a profile and refuses
existing accepted/backup data. `settingsd serve --instance example` never
materialises defaults for a missing established store. Plain `settingsd seed
--instance example` validates an existing profile without rewriting valid state;
it refuses a wholly missing directory. First installation explicitly uses
`settingsd seed --allow-create --instance example` as the service account.
A retained writer.lock is establishment evidence: even --allow-create refuses
a missing established primary without a backup. Existing-store
corruption uses the same validated, evidence-preserving recovery as serve.
The unit validates with plain seed before serving, binds the instance to the machine hostname, and
the session target wants/upholds it. Settings readiness never blocks application
or compositor startup. The image provisions the authority account's writable
MixOS settings parent and seeds once explicitly. Automatic unit startup never
uses --allow-create; missing mounts/directories fail visibly rather than resetting
preferences. Isolated native image adoption still needs runtime evidence.

## Validation and remaining scope

Machine fixtures: [authority.spec.mix](authority.spec.mix). Rust tests cover
precision, patches, projection round-trip, writer locking, changed/no-op receipts,
lost replies, conflicts, digest reuse, eviction, backup restore and future schemas.
`tests/settings/authority_test.mix` runs real ABP publication, unrelated operator
mutation, forged publish/clear refusal, authority restart and cold broker restart
against isolated noded instances. Broker loss keeps the authority alive and its
writer exclusive; the shared consumer reconnects through the same client and
the authority repopulates the empty retained broker without a semantic edit.
The broker-restart fixture also starts a headless cold consumer from persisted
cache while offline, then promotes it to current with no redundant stage after
fresh ABP readback. Resource readiness is a fixture inventory, not GUI proof.
Another native fixture keeps an authority registered but deliberately withholds
read replies, exercising the combined bootstrap deadline and expired work.
OS process lifecycle here belongs to the test fixture; application calls
and observations remain native ABP.

This slice does not claim GUI propagation, renderer acknowledgements, presentation,
GUI offline-fallback/first-map timing, candidate import/watch, immutable artifacts,
full field provenance, named-profile management, compatibility, scheduled policy,
preview, routed observation or replication. Every deferred feature must extend
the same authority and shared contracts, with appropriate contract versions and
migration. Native VT/image presentation and latency gates remain outstanding.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/dopus/ (source: https://mixos.dev/dopus/README.md) -->

# DOpus

DOpus is MixOS's file manager: two panes side by side, each a folder
tree, with a Places sidebar on the left and a Properties sidebar on the
right. The name is a nod to Directory Opus on the Amiga, whose twin panes
it keeps.

## The window

- **Two panes.** Each shows one folder as a tree with Name, Size and
  Modified columns; columns that do not fit are hidden, Modified first. One
  pane is active; Switch Pane (F6 or Tab) moves between them, and copy and
  move always go to the other pane. Drag the divider to change the split.
- **The path field** at the top of each pane always shows where it is. Click
  it, type a path and press Enter to go there; `~` is your home, and a file
  path opens the folder that holds it.
- **The tree.** A chevron or a double-click opens a folder in place;
  another collapses it. Double-click a file to open it in its default
  application.
- **Selecting.** Click a row to select it, Ctrl-click to add or remove one,
  Shift-click for a range. The arrow keys, Home and End move the selection.
- **Sorting.** Click a column header to sort by it, ascending first; click
  it again to reverse.
- **Places** lists Home, the filesystem root and your Desktop, Documents,
  Downloads, Music, Pictures and Videos folders, where they exist. Its
  toggle sits left of the left pane's path field.
- **Properties** shows the selected item: kind, size, dates, permissions,
  owner and path, under a preview of a file when one can be made. Its
  toggle sits right of the right pane's path field.
- **Previews** (View › Previews, per pane, on by default) are thumbnails
  from the desktop's shared thumbnail cache, made by the thumbnailers
  installed on the system (the same ones GNOME and COSMIC use). A type
  with no thumbnailer keeps its icon. Files on network, FUSE and automounted filesystems (NFS, SMB,
  sshfs, ntfs-3g and the like) keep their icons too, unless
  `remote_previews: true` is set in the configuration (below). A file
  whose filesystem stops answering keeps its icon rather than holding up
  the previews of the others.
- **Icons** show what a folder or file holds: your well-known folders have
  their own, and files are grouped by their MIME type (document, code,
  image, audio, video, archive, spreadsheet, presentation, font, disk
  image, program, shell script).
- **Drag and drop.** Drag rows from one pane onto the other, or onto a
  folder in it, and choose Move Here, Copy Here or Cancel.
- **Right-click** a row or a pane's background for the actions that apply
  there.

Deleting asks first, and naming a new folder or a rename is checked before
anything happens. Copies, moves and deletes run in the background, and the
status line says how they ended.

## Menus and keys

The menus hold every action except moving the selection (the arrow keys,
Home and End) and the quick theme keys (Ctrl+Alt+D for light or dark,
Ctrl+Alt+1 to 6 for a scheme; View › Theme has the full choice). Help ›
Keyboard Shortcuts lists every key in force.

| Menu | Action | Keys |
|---|---|---|
| File | Open | Enter |
| | New Folder | Ctrl+Shift+N |
| | Rename | F2, Ctrl+E |
| | Copy to Other Pane | Ctrl+C |
| | Move to Other Pane | Ctrl+X |
| | Delete | Delete |
| | Quit | Ctrl+Q |
| View | Places, Properties | Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I |
| | Hidden Files | Ctrl+H |
| | Refresh | F5, Ctrl+R |
| | Sort by Name, Size, Modified | Ctrl+1, Ctrl+2, Ctrl+3 |
| | Theme | (this window's look; the session's by default) |
| Go | Back, Forward | Alt+ArrowLeft, Alt+ArrowRight |
| | Parent Folder | Backspace |
| | Home | Alt+Home |
| | Location… | Ctrl+L |
| | Switch Pane | F6, Tab |
| Help | Keyboard Shortcuts | F1 |

To change a key, set it in the desktop profile: the binding applies at once,
and DOpus's defaults stay for every action you leave alone. For example,
`settings.apply` with `keymaps.dopus.nav.parent: ["Ctrl+U"]` makes Ctrl+U
the parent-folder key, an empty list leaves an action without a key, and a
reset of `keymaps.dopus` restores the defaults. See [key bindings are desktop
settings](../docs/decisions/2026-10-11-keymaps-in-settings.md).

## What it remembers

The two panes' folders, sorting and hidden-files setting, which pane was
active, the split, and the sidebars' state and widths are kept in
`config.conf.mix` in DOpus's own directory (by default
`~/.local/state/mixos/apps/dopus/config/`). `dopus --print-config` shows the
configuration it would use. One setting lives only there:
`remote_previews` (default `false`) makes previews of files on network,
FUSE and automounted filesystems too.

## For agents

DOpus answers on the Bus as `dopus` (schema `dopus.v1`).

| Verb | Arguments | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `dopus.ping`, `dopus.describe`, `dopus.info` | | liveness, the control surface, version and build |
| `dopus.state` | | both panes (path, sort, hidden files, previews, selection, rows, status) and the sidebars |
| `dopus.open` | `paths` (one per pane), or one path and `pane` | goes there |
| `dopus.action` | `id`, `pane` (`left`, `right` or `active`) | runs one action |
| `dopus.actions.list` | | every action, its keys in force and whether it can run now |
| `dopus.theme.set` | `scheme`, `mode` | this window's look |
| `dopus.quit` | | closes the window |

**File operations are keyboard-only.** `dopus.action` refuses every `file.*`
action (`FORBIDDEN`). Input played through the drive verbs (`dopus.ui.*`)
is held to the same rule: while it runs, file actions and opening files are
refused, and a delete, name or drop dialog can be dismissed but not
accepted. The rule holds for the whole time drive input runs, so a key you
press yourself in that moment is refused too; press it again after. An agent reads, navigates, sorts and selects through DOpus, but
never creates, renames, moves, copies, deletes or opens files through it.

The window is drivable like every MixOS app, including its menus: see
[driving an app](../docs/drive.md) (`dopus.ui.*`, `dopus.window`). The verbs are
registered in `docs/docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix`.

Each command run from a menu, a key, a sidebar button or an accepted
`dopus.action` is published on `dopus.command.executed`, with how it was
reached (`menu`, `shortcut`, `ui` or `bus`;
[executed commands](../docs/decisions/2026-10-11-executed-commands.md)). A refused
action is not published.

`dopus --headless` runs the core and the Bus port without a window, for
tests: the same verbs, minus those that need a window. It publishes its
accepted `dopus.action` runs on `<service>.command.executed` too.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/edit/ (source: https://mixos.dev/edit/README.md) -->

# Edit

Shared headless text buffers used by [editd](../editd/README.md) and
[Ced](../ced/README.md). This promotion has two external owners: the
service is the authoritative buffer store; the app uses the same revision,
operation, anchor and position contracts for local echo and rebasing. No
Bus connection, clock, renderer or async runtime is required by this
library.

The Microsoft Edit buffer implementation remains in
[`vendor/msedit`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/vendor/msedit),
with its licence, upstream revision and retained commit-failure, Unicode
and convergence tests. This library supplies the revision CAS,
transactions, single-authority OT, per-origin undo, anchors and search API
above it.

Source: frozen cosmix revision `e0297242305f3a3c3de09f1ca01e8faa771768da`.
The source is [`libs/edit`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/libs/edit).

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/editd/ (source: https://mixos.dev/editd/README.md) -->

# Edit service

`editd` registers the `edit` service and serves the `edit.v1` contract.
[Ced](../ced/README.md) and agents share its buffers through native ABP.
The service is headless and requires no compositor or D-Bus session.

`edit.open`, `edit.list` and `edit.get` discover buffers and page their
contents. `edit.insert`, `edit.delete`, `edit.replace` and `edit.apply` change
text. `edit.save`, `edit.reload` and `edit.close` manage disk state.
`edit.undo`, `edit.redo` and `edit.history` expose history; selection, cursor
and anchor verbs retain positions across edits. Properties have get, list,
describe and watch ports. Ask `HELP` for the complete manifest.

Mutations can carry origin, operation identity and expected revision.
Buffer identities include a daemon epoch, so a restarted service does not
silently reinterpret an old identifier. Paged snapshots remain tied to their
captured revision while later edits arrive. Slow work on one buffer does not
block operations on another.

## Buffers and recovery

The buffer model is the [edit](../edit/README.md) library, shared with Ced:
revision CAS, per-origin undo, anchors, atomic save, external-change
detection and a recoverable change feed. This service owns its actors,
filesystem watching and the recovery writer.

Discovery uses the shared node configuration. Recovery defaults beneath
`MIXOS_VAR/edit/recovery`, following the MixOS Var directory rule.
`MIXOS_EDIT_RECOVERY_DIR` selects an absolute recovery directory, and
`MIXOS_EDIT_RECOVERY=0` disables durable recovery. The session supplies its
own state root.

## Tests

The retained integration tests exercise dispatch, recovery and the actual
service over a private native noded, rather than a substitute control
socket.

The source is
[`services/editd`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/services/editd).

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/editor-model/ (source: https://mixos.dev/editor-model/README.md) -->

# editor-model

`editor-model` is the frontend side of the [edit service](../editd/README.md):
everything an editor needs that is not drawing. It has no UI toolkit, needs
no async runtime and does no Bus I/O. The transport stays in the consumer;
the mirror only produces requests (`types::Outgoing`) and consumes replies
and events.

Used by:

- [editor](../editor/README.md), the shared egui editor widget, which turns
  keys and pointer events into `EditCommand`s;
- [ced](../ced/README.md) and its `documents` crate, including
  `ced --headless`, which drive the mirror against `editd`.

It builds on the [edit](../edit/README.md) library (`Text`, `ot`, `view`,
`wire`, origins) and the [`syntax`](../syntax/README.md) crate (lsh highlighting).

The source is [`libs/editor-model`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/libs/editor-model).

## Modules

| Module | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `model` | `EditorModel`: selection, preferred column, scroll, overwrite, remote carets, change markers and the input-method composition range. `command()` turns an `EditCommand` into a `LocalEdit`. |
| `mirror` | `Mirror`: one buffer's view text (confirmed rev + in-flight + queue) with local echo and single-authority OT rebase against `editd`. Pure: no Bus, no clock; every method returns a `Step`. |
| `highlight` | `Highlight`: per-view highlighting state, lsh languages through `syntax::cache`, Mix through the Mix lexer. |
| `diag` | `Diagnostics`: per-source diagnostic sets (`mix lint --json` output, or external sets) mapped through edits. |
| `types` | Shared types every frontend speaks: `Intent`, `LocalEdit`, `ViewDelta`, `Outgoing`, `Incoming`, `Conflict`, `Notice`, `OpIdGen`, `bus_lane_label`. |
| `fake` | `FakeEditd`, a fake `edit` daemon over the real `edit::Buffer`, for tests (feature `fake`). |

## The editor model

`EditorModel::command(&text, &cfg, command)` applies an `EditCommand` to the
current view text and returns the `LocalEdit` to send, or `None` for a pure
motion. Commands: insert, newline, backspace, delete, delete word left or
right, tab, outdent, duplicate line, delete line, move line up or down,
toggle comment, `Move { to, extend }`, select all, select word
(double-click), select line (triple-click) and set selection. Motions are
left and right, word left and right, up and down, smart Home, End, page up
and down, document start and end, and `To(offset)`.

The contracts, from the module docs:

- Every motion is grapheme-correct through `edit::view`; Up and Down keep
  `preferred_cells`.
- A multi-line Tab or Outdent is one multi-item `LocalEdit`: one
  `edit.apply`, one undo group. `coalesce` is set only for single-grapheme
  typing and backspace/delete runs.
- Newline copies the line's leading whitespace and uses the buffer's line
  ending. ToggleComment uses the language's line-comment token
  (`line_comment_for`: `--` for Mix, `//` for Rust, C, C++, Go and
  JavaScript, `#` for shell, Python, TOML and YAML; other languages get
  nothing).
- `apply_delta` maps the selection, remote carets and markers through a
  `ViewDelta`. A delta that overlaps the composition range cancels it.
- Lines are 1-based, cells 0-based.

```rust
use edit::text::Text;
use edit::view::MeasureCfg;
use editor_model::model::{EditCfg, EditCommand, EditorModel};

let cfg = EditCfg {
    measure: MeasureCfg { tab_size: 4, ambiguous_wide: false },
    insert_spaces: true,
    eol: "\n",
    line_comment: Some("--"),
};
let text = Text::from_text("hello\n").unwrap();
let mut m = EditorModel::default();
let edit = m.command(&text, &cfg, EditCommand::Insert("> ".into()));
// `edit` is Some(LocalEdit { items, coalesce, caret_after }) for the mirror.
```

## The mirror

`Mirror::bootstrap` starts from an `edit.open` reply. The host then feeds it
`local_edit`, `server_op` (undo, redo, save, reload, apply at a revision),
`on_event` (`edit.changed`), `on_reply`, `on_deadline`, `on_page` and
`on_history`, and after every call drains `next_outgoing`,
`take_retry_timer`, `take_echo_timer` and `take_outcomes`. The deltas it
produces are `ViewDelta`s, the one thing the editor side consumes: how the
view text changed, with its kind (`Local`, `Remote`, `Undo`, `Redo`,
`Reload`, `Revert`, `Resync`), revision and view generation.

The rules are binding and written out in the module docs of
[`src/mirror.rs`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/blob/main/libs/editor-model/src/mirror.rs):
one request in flight per buffer; how a server edit is folded (duplicate,
gap, own ack, or a remote fold that rebases pending ops and reports a
`Conflict`); how replies, `busy` backoff and refusals are handled; what
happens at a deadline; recovery from an event gap, a reconnect or an epoch
change (history first, then a paged snapshot); and the keep-mine transfer
of a detached copy, staged over 1 MiB.

## Highlighting and diagnostics

- **Highlight**: lsh languages are checkpointed every 1024 lines and seek
  under a per-frame `SliceBudget`; a line not reached yet draws plain. Mix
  languages (`mix`, `scene`, `mix-data`) are relexed whole off the UI
  thread, 150 ms after the last delta (the caller debounces and runs the
  worker); buffers over 2 MiB stay plain. A result tagged for another
  epoch, buffer, language or config is discarded; an older result is used
  only above the first line touched since.
- **Diagnostics**: one set per source. `LINT_SOURCE` is the frontend's own
  `mix lint --json -` run (schema version 2 only); any other source is an
  external set (`ced.diagnostics`). A diagnostic whose line was touched
  since its tagged generation is dropped; the rest map through the deltas.

## Features

- `mix` (the crate default; the workspace dependency turns default
  features off, and ced and editor enable it): Mix highlighting through the
  Mix lexer. Without it, Mix buffers draw plain.
- `fake`: the `fake` module, for consumers' tests. ced's tests enable it.

## Testing

Unit tests sit beside each module (`src/model/tests.rs`,
`src/highlight/tests.rs`, `src/diag/tests.rs`). The mirror is tested end to
end against `FakeEditd`:

- `tests/fixture_server_side.rs` runs the server side of every scripted
  scenario in
  [`tests/fixtures/mirror/`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/libs/editor-model/tests/fixtures/mirror)
  (format in its README), so a contradictory fixture fails there first.
- `tests/mirror_convergence.rs` replays every fixture through a real
  `Mirror`, checking the exact requests sent and the declared client
  expectations, then runs proptest properties over random interleavings of
  typing, agent edits, undo, reordered or dropped events and replies, lost
  requests, deadlines and dedup eviction. The emitted deltas are replayed
  onto a shadow string that must match the mirror's text.

On an authorised build worker:

```
cargo test --locked -p editor-model
```

A vertical-motion benchmark is `#[ignore]`d; run it in release on a build
node.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/editor/ (source: https://mixos.dev/editor/README.md) -->

# editor

The shared plain-text editor for MixOS egui applications: a monospace,
virtualised view over the headless editing model (`editor-model`,
[edit](../edit/README.md)). [Ced](../ced/README.md) is built on it, and so
is any application that needs a text editor: a Markdown editor, a notes
pane, a config field.

- **Only visible rows are measured and drawn.** A multi-megabyte file, or a
  multi-megabyte line, costs about the same per frame as a short one.
- **Soft wrap is a view option** (`Wrap::Words`): rows break after
  whitespace, inside a word only when it is longer than a row.
- **The widget never edits text.** It turns keys, pointer, clipboard and
  input-method events into `Event`s (mostly `EditCommand`s) for the
  document's owner to apply.
- **Colours come from the theme**, through the toolkit's chrome roles, with
  every highlight class kept at 3:1 contrast or better.

The source is [`libs/editor`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/libs/editor).

## A local document

`local::Document` is the editor without a daemon: an `edit::buffer::Buffer`
with open and save (byte-order mark and line endings kept), undo and redo,
and highlighting for the 25 lsh languages, Markdown included.

```rust
let mut doc = editor::local::Document::open("notes.md")?;
let palette = editor::Palette::from_theme(&theme);
let view = editor::View::prose(); // soft wrap, no line numbers

// each frame
doc.show(ui, &palette, &view);
if doc.is_dirty() { /* offer to save: doc.save()? */ }
```

## A shared buffer

Ced applies the same events to a buffer shared through the edit service
(`editor_model::mirror`) and passes other origins' carets, selections and
change markers through the same `Doc`. Any application can move from a
local document to a shared one without changing its UI code.

## Saving

`save` writes a new temporary file beside the real one (created
exclusively, so no existing file or link is followed), gives it the
original's permissions, flushes it and renames it into place. Saving
through a symbolic link writes the link's target; the link stays a link.
Edits the buffer refuses (a paste over the 1 MiB request limit) are kept
for `take_refusal`. `set_contents` is a reload: it has no request limit,
and Undo does not take it back.

## Tests

`cargo test -p editor`: measurement, rows and wrapping, geometry, keys, the
input-method guard, palettes in every scheme, the local document, and
`tests/snapshot.rs`, which drives a real document through egui (typing,
selection, undo, read-only) and keeps offscreen snapshots. Regenerate the
snapshots with `UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1` and look at them before committing.

## Known limits

- One monospace grid: proportional text is a separate, larger piece of work.
- With soft wrap, the scrollbar counts visual rows for documents up to
  256 KiB and lines beyond that.
- In lines over 64 KiB, which break every row width, a tab wider than a
  whole row can leave an empty row before it.
- A text area under two cells wide wraps at two cells (the widest cluster
  but a tab), so its second cell is clipped.
- A row's end and the next row's start are the same offset, and a caret has
  no affinity yet: Up or Down onto a row that breaks inside a word stops
  before its last character, so the caret stays on that row.
- Glyphs come from the theme's faces; scripts they do not cover (CJK, for
  one) draw as boxes until the font set gains a fallback.
- Without wrap, Home and End are logical; with wrap, Up and Down move by
  rows and Home and End stay logical.
- Mix-family buffers are highlighted by the Mix lexer only when the `mix`
  feature is on and the owner runs the relex (Ced does).

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/email/ (source: https://mixos.dev/email/README.md) -->

# email — the MixOS JMAP mail client

`email` (`dev.mixos.email`) is the reserved MixOS mail client: a **pure
JMAP client** speaking HTTPS to any RFC 8620/8621-shaped server — the
mesh's own maild, or anyone else's server. Mail is listed, read, composed
and sent; calendars and address books are listed and shown.

## Running it

```
email [--noded-url URL] [--service NAME]
```

A second launch raises the first window. The first run shows the account
form:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| Server URL | The JMAP server base (`https://…`). maild directly, or a webd vhost that proxies `/jmap`. |
| Email address | The login; the Basic username at the token exchange. |
| Password | Spent once per token lifetime; held in the config file (mode 0600) afterwards. |
| CA bundle path | Optional. A PEM bundle to trust for a server whose certificate is self-issued. |

The account persists in the app's config directory
(`~/.local/state/mixos/apps/email/config/config.conf.mix`); a malformed
file loads defaults and is never overwritten.

## What it does

- **Mail** — mailboxes with unread counts; the newest 100 emails per
  mailbox; read in the reader pane (plain text first, HTML source when
  there is no plain text); opening an email marks it read; compose (To, Cc,
  Bcc, Subject, body) and reply, sent through the proven recipe: build the
  message, upload it, create the Email in Sent, submit. **Sending requires
  maild:** the create step uses maild's extension of a top-level `blobId` on
  `Email/set`. A strict RFC 8621 server builds an Email from uploaded MIME
  with `Email/import` instead, and refuses the send; `Email/import` is
  future work. Reading, calendars and contacts use standard methods only.
- **Calendar** — calendars, their events by start, the open event's
  detail.
- **Contacts** — address books, contacts with a server-side text filter
  over name, email and company, the open contact's detail.

## How it talks to the server

One HTTPS session per account. On connect: the password is exchanged for a
Bearer token (`POST /auth/tokens/issue`) and the Session is discovered
(`GET /.well-known/jmap`); every method call after that carries the token.
A server without the token endpoint falls back to Basic auth on every
request. Requests batch their methodCalls and chain `Email/query` into
`Email/get` through a ResultReference — one round trip per list.

The engine (`apps/email/crates/jmap`) is ported from the retired Dioxus
mail client, with its faults fixed: session discovery and URL templates
instead of hardcoded paths, real pagination, Bcc carried through,
`In-Reply-To` wrapped exactly once, CR/LF stripped from header inputs
(header injection), typed method-error handling, and attachment download
wired (the UI for it is a later slice).

## Keyboard

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| Ctrl+R | Refresh |
| Ctrl+Q | Quit |
| Ctrl+N | Compose |
| Ctrl+Shift+R | Reply |
| Ctrl+1 / 2 / 3 | Mail / Calendar / Contacts |

## Performance workload

The recorded workload for future profiling: a 10,000-email mailbox — the
list renders 100 rows from one query+get round trip, and the reader fetches
one email's bodies on open. Nothing else scales with mailbox size.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/expr/ (source: https://mixos.dev/expr/README.md) -->

# expr

The pure expression language of Mix Scenes bindings. A scene binds a port
to an expression such as `= $model.rows`, `= not $model.volume.has_icon` or
`= $model.prefix .. $item.cells[0]`; this crate compiles the expression,
reports which globals it reads, and evaluates it over `serde_json::Value`
globals under size and time limits.

The language is the expression subset of [Mix](../mix/README.md) with every
builtin denied: literals, `$name` globals with field and index access,
arithmetic, `..` concatenation, comparisons, `and`/`or`/`??`, the ternary
and the `if … then … else … end` expression. Calls, assignments, statements
and shell or Bus forms are refused at compile time with
`ErrorKind::NotAllowed`. The crate does not depend on the Mix interpreter.

```rust
let model = serde_json::json!({"prefix": "live ", "rows": [{"cells": ["one"]}]});
let binding = expr::compile("$model.prefix .. $model.rows[0].cells[0]")?;
assert_eq!(binding.roots().iter().collect::<Vec<_>>(), ["model"]);
let text = binding.eval(&[("model", &model)], &expr::Limits::default())?;
assert_eq!(text, "live one");
```

Test: `cargo test -p expr`. The semantics are pinned in
`tests/semantics.rs`; the crate documentation in `src/lib.rs` lists what is
accepted, refused and how errors are classified.

The source is [`libs/expr`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/libs/expr).

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/hostd/ (source: https://mixos.dev/hostd/README.md) -->

# The host service

`hostd` is the one MixOS service that runs as root on a host. It does two
jobs:

- **It describes the host:** hardware, OS, the MixOS mode, and who manages
  the network.
- **It makes privileged changes** through a short list of closed, typed
  verbs. Each change is checked, recorded, and reversed if it doesn't work.

Agents and session code ask hostd instead of running `sudo`. The rules
behind it are in the
[hostd decision](../docs/decisions/2026-10-12-hostd.md).

## Calling it

Locally, hostd listens on `/run/hostd/hostd.sock` (mode 0660, group
`hostd`). Frames are JSON, each ended by a NUL byte, many per connection:

```text
-> {"verb":"net.state","body":{}}\0
<- {"rc":0,"body":{...}}\0
```

`rc` is 0 on success and 10 on refusal, with `body.status` saying why. From
a shell:

```text
hostd call host.info
hostd call net.link.apply '{"link":"eth1","config":{"mode":"dhcp"}}'
```

Read verbs are also on the Bus, owned by `hostd`. Changes are never taken
from the Bus.

There is one hostd per host, run as root and socket-activated:

```text
hostd serve                      # local socket, plus the Bus when noded is up
hostd serve --no-bus             # local socket only
```

`hostd serve` refuses to take over a socket another hostd is serving.

## Verbs

| Verb | Tier | What |
|---|---|---|
| `host.info` | read | hostname, kernel, OS, MixOS mode, container, uptime, CPU, memory |
| `net.state` | read | which network managers run, networkd links and files, resolved DNS, iwd stations, hostd's own files |
| `hostd.status` | read | frozen or not, the policy's state, the caller's identity, and the grants it holds: `held` (names) and `held_grants` (each in full: verbs, limits, expiry, rate) |
| `hostd.receipt` | read | one change's receipt: what it changed, under which grant, how it ended (never file contents) |
| `hostd.freeze` | control | refuse every change until thawed: root on the host, or a grant naming it |
| `hostd.thaw` | control | accept changes again and lift grant suspensions: root on the host only |
| `net.link.apply` | write | configure one link through networkd, rolled back unless it comes up |
| `hostd.undo` | write | put back what an applied change replaced; needs no grant of its own (see below) |
| `net.wg.apply` | write | configure a WireGuard link through networkd, rolled back unless it comes up and its peers complete a handshake |
| `desk.restart` | write | restart the desk machine that the caller's grant names, session and console included (starts `desk-restart@DESK.service`); the host stays up; no undo |
| `desk.stop` | write | power off the desk machine that the caller's grant names and give the console back (starts `desk-stop@DESK.service`); the host stays up; no undo |

The desk verbs take no machine name. A grant gives the caller one desk through
its `desks` limit, which must name exactly one machine. A grant with no desk,
or with two, is refused.

A desk power action is a cycle that outlives the caller: a restart stops the
desk's session, reboots the machine, starts the session again and switches
the console back to the desk's VT if it was in front (returning it to the
previous VT if the compositor does not come up); a stop returns the console
to the VT that was in front, stops the session and powers the machine off.
hostd runs none of these steps. It starts the host's template unit for the
action with `systemctl start --no-block`, records a receipt that the cycle
started, and answers. The host installs `desk-restart@.service` and
`desk-stop@.service`; the unit's journal says how the cycle ended. If either
unit is missing, the verb is refused `unit_failed`.

Only hostd on the host can do this. A hostd running inside a desk refuses
both verbs `in_container`. The desk reaches the host's hostd through its
socket bound into the machine, so the grant names the caller by its cgroup as
the host sees it, under the machine's payload:
`/machine.slice/systemd-nspawn@DESK.service/payload/system.slice/system-scenes.slice/scenes@VT.service/*`.
Every refusal is logged at warn under `hostd::audit`.
| `net.wifi.scan` | write | scan for Wi-Fi networks on one device (iwd). It changes nothing durable, but it drives the radio, so it needs a grant |
| `net.wifi.connect` | write | connect a Wi-Fi device to a network (iwd), put back unless connected in time |

`host.info` is also published as the retained topic `hostd.info`.

## Who may change what

Reads are open to anyone who can reach hostd. Changes need a **standing
grant** in `/etc/hostd/policy.mx`, a strict-data document that only root
can change:

```text
{
  schema: 1,
  grants: [
    {name: "desk-network",
     caller: {cgroup: "/machine.slice/systemd-nspawn@desk.service/*"},
     verbs: ["net.link.apply"],
     limits: {links: ["eth0", "wlan0"]},
     expires: "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z",
     rate: {count: 3, per_s: 600}}
  ]
}
```

- **The caller is matched by what the kernel says,** never by what it
  sends: its uid and its cgroup. A cgroup only counts when hostd holds a
  pidfd for the caller and the caller was alive after the cgroup was read.
  Both are read again for every request.
- **`X/*` matches the cgroup `X` and everything below it.** Name a subtree
  the caller can't move itself into, such as one under `machine.slice`.
- **Verbs** are exact names or a family such as `net.*`. No grant can name
  `hostd.thaw`.
- **Limits** are allow-lists the verb checks its arguments against
  (`links` for `net.link.apply`). A key the grant doesn't list is
  unrestricted.
- **Rate** applies per caller, with a grant-wide cap of four callers' worth.
- **Default deny.** No policy file means no grants.

The policy is read for every change, so an edit takes effect at once. A
file that anyone but root could change, or that sits in a directory anyone
but root could change, is refused.

## What a change does

Every write follows the same pattern:

1. **Check:** the request is typed and validated (no free text reaches a
   file), then the grant, limits, rate and freeze state.
2. **Record:** a receipt keeps the previous content of every file the change
   replaces.
3. **Apply:** hostd writes only files it names itself, and never edits a file
   it didn't write.
4. **Prove:** a health check runs within the change's window (5 to 60
   seconds, 20 by default).
5. **Keep or revert:** a change that doesn't pass is rolled back
   automatically.

One change runs at a time, host-wide. A change waits at most 15 seconds
behind others (`busy` after that), and the whole gate runs again once it
holds the lock, so a freeze, a suspension, an expiry or a policy edit that
lands while it waits is obeyed. A change runs to the end, rollback
included, even if the caller hangs up.

**A stop waits for a running change** (up to 80 seconds), and a change that
a crash or a forced kill cuts short is rolled back when hostd next starts,
before it accepts any change.

Recovery looks at what each file holds before it acts. It puts back the
backup only over content hostd itself installed. A file someone else has
changed since is left alone, and the receipt is marked `abandoned`. A
rollback, undo or recovery that can't finish, or a receipt that can't be
recorded, blocks all changes (`recovery_pending`). Every later change
retries it first, and changes resume once it finishes.

**Undo puts back exactly what a receipt replaced,** and only while the file
still holds what that change installed. If a later change, or anyone's
edit, has replaced it since, undo is refused (`superseded`): undo the later
change first.

**Two rollbacks in a row** under one grant suspend that grant until root on
the host thaws hostd.

## Network links

`net.link.apply` gives one link a networkd configuration:

```text
{"link": "eth1", "config": {"mode": "dhcp"}}
{"link": "eth1", "config": {"mode": "static",
  "addresses": ["192.0.2.10/24"], "gateway": "192.0.2.1", "dns": ["192.0.2.53"]},
 "window_s": 30}
```

- hostd writes `/etc/systemd/network/50-hostd-<link>.network`, reloads
  networkd and reconfigures the link.
- **`route_metric`** (static with a gateway, or DHCP) sets the metric of
  the default route the link installs. A higher metric loses to a lower
  one, so a second uplink with a high metric never takes over the host's
  default route.
- **It passes** when networkd reports the link configured from hostd's file,
  carrying every requested address with its prefix length. With DHCP or a
  gateway, the default route must also be installed (through the requested
  gateway, if static) and **the gateway must answer**: hostd sends it one UDP
  datagram and reads the kernel's neighbour table until the gateway's
  address resolves. A gateway that doesn't exist fails the change, even one
  inside the link's own subnet.
- **A link another file already configures is refused** (`foreign_config`),
  and so is a link that carries addresses nobody's networkd file set, by
  hand or by another manager such as NetworkManager
  (`unmanaged_configured`). hostd's rollback restores files, so it can't
  give such a link its old runtime configuration back, and it doesn't take
  it over.

The reply to a change that passed (`rc` 0):

```text
{"receipt": "<id>", "outcome": "applied", "reason": null, "grant": "<grant>",
 "grant_suspended": false, "link": {"admin": "configured", "operational": "routable"}}
```

A change that failed and was reversed comes back with `rc` 10, as
`{"status": "rolled_back", "detail": {...}}`, where `detail` has the same
keys. Keep the `receipt` id to undo the change later, or to look it up with
`hostd.receipt`.

**Undo needs no grant of its own.** `hostd.undo {receipt}` is allowed to
whoever holds a grant that covers the original change: its verb and its
limits (for `net.link.apply`, that link). A grant that may configure `hd0`
may undo its own changes to `hd0`. Naming `hostd.undo` in a grant adds
nothing.

## WireGuard links

`net.wg.apply` gives one WireGuard link its networkd configuration:

```text
{"name": "wg-home", "addresses": ["10.99.0.1/24"], "listen_port": 51820,
 "peers": [{"public_key": "<base64>", "endpoint": "vpn.example.com:51820",
            "allowed_ips": ["10.99.0.0/24"], "keepalive_s": 25}],
 "window_s": 25}
```

- hostd writes `50-hostd-<name>.netdev`, `50-hostd-<name>.network` and the
  private key `50-hostd-<name>.key` in `/etc/systemd/network`.
- **The key never leaves the host.** hostd makes it the first time,
  readable only by root and group `systemd-network` (mode 0640), and keeps
  it across later applies. Replies carry only the `public_key`, for the
  peers' side.
- **It passes** when the link comes up configured from hostd's file with
  every address, and **every peer with an endpoint completes a handshake**
  within the window. A peer that never answers puts the change back.
- `require_handshake: false` skips the handshake wait. Use it for the first
  side of a new pair, whose peer doesn't exist yet.
- A link of that name hostd didn't create is refused (`foreign_config`).
- A changed `.netdev` takes effect because hostd deletes its own link and
  networkd creates it again. Peers reconnect within a keepalive.
- Grants limit WireGuard links by `links`, like other links.

hostd's unit has two capabilities, both for this verb:
- `CAP_CHOWN`, to give the key file to group `systemd-network`;
- `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, to read peer handshakes over WireGuard netlink and to
  delete its own WireGuard link.

## Wi-Fi

Wi-Fi goes through iwd. hostd never starts iwd: if it isn't running, the
Wi-Fi verbs answer `no_iwd`.

```text
{"device": "wlan0"}                                         net.wifi.scan
{"device": "wlan0", "ssid": "home", "passphrase": "…"}      net.wifi.connect
{"device": "wlan0", "ssid": "cafe-open", "window_s": 30}    net.wifi.connect
```

- **`net.wifi.scan`** replies with each network's SSID, security
  (`open`, `psk`), signal in dBm, and whether iwd already knows it.
- **`net.wifi.connect`** writes no files.
  - **The passphrase never leaves hostd except to iwd.** It reaches iwd
    through an agent that hostd registers for that one connect. The agent
    answers only the process that owns iwd's bus name, and only for the
    network being connected. iwd saves the network itself, after a
    successful connect. Receipts and the audit never hold the passphrase.
  - **It passes** when the device is connected to that SSID within the
    window.
  - **If it doesn't,** hostd forgets the network (if this change made it
    known) and reconnects the network the device was on before, or
    disconnects if it was on none.
  - **A known network takes no passphrase.** To change one, forget it
    first. An open network takes none, and 802.1X networks are
    `unsupported`.
- **Undo** puts the device back the same way. It is refused (`superseded`)
  once the device has moved to another network since. If someone else
  moved the device during a change, the put-back leaves it alone.
- Grants limit Wi-Fi by `links` (the device) and `ssids`.

## Stopping it

`hostd.freeze` stops every change at once and survives restarts and
reboots. An unreadable freeze record counts as frozen. Only root on the
host itself thaws it, never root inside a container.

## Refusals

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `not_served` | no such verb |
| `bad_request` | the body doesn't fit the verb's schema |
| `local_only` | a control or write verb arrived over the Bus |
| `caller_unverified` | hostd couldn't prove the caller's cgroup |
| `no_grant` | no unexpired grant covers this caller and verb |
| `outside_grant` | a grant covers the verb but not these arguments |
| `grant_suspended` | the circuit breaker suspended the grant |
| `rate_limited` | the grant's rate is used up |
| `frozen` | hostd is frozen |
| `policy_invalid` | the policy can't be loaded; changes are refused |
| `root_only` | only root on the host may do this |
| `foreign_config`, `unmanaged_configured`, `no_such_link` | `net.link.apply` or `net.wg.apply` won't touch this link |
| `no_iwd`, `no_such_station`, `no_such_network`, `unsupported` | Wi-Fi: iwd isn't running, the device isn't an iwd station, the SSID isn't in range, or the security type isn't handled |
| `rolled_back` | the change failed its health check and was reversed |
| `superseded` | undo refused: the file no longer holds what that change installed |
| `not_applied` | undo refused: the change was rolled back or already undone |
| `rollback_failed`, `undo_incomplete` | a rollback or undo couldn't finish; it is retried, and writes wait |
| `recovery_pending` | an unfinished change is being retried and hasn't finished yet; writes wait |
| `timeout`, `busy` | too slow, or too many requests at once |

## Source layout

The source is
[`services/hostd`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/services/hostd):

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `src/local.rs` | the local socket: NUL-framed JSON, per-uid and per-connection limits |
| `src/caller.rs` | caller identity from `SO_PEERCRED`, a held pidfd, cgroup and namespaces, read per request |
| `src/service.rs` | the verb table, tiers, dispatch and the `authorise` gate |
| `src/policy.rs` | grants: loading (one `O_NOFOLLOW` open, root-only), matching, rate limits |
| `src/freeze.rs` | the kill switch, failing closed |
| `src/receipt.rs` | receipts, durable atomic writes, restore, the circuit breaker |
| `src/txn.rs` | the transaction every write runs through: receipt first, conclude (keep or put back, breaker, durable outcome), recovery, undo |
| `src/link.rs` | `net.link.apply`: validation, rendering, the change, its proof |
| `src/wg.rs` | `net.wg.apply`: WireGuard netdev, network and key files, the handshake proof |
| `src/wgnl.rs` | WireGuard generic netlink (peer handshakes) and deleting a link |
| `src/wifi.rs` | `net.wifi.scan` and `net.wifi.connect` through iwd: the one-connect passphrase agent, runtime put-back |
| `src/networkd.rs` | networkd over D-Bus and Varlink, the event-driven health wait |
| `src/net.rs`, `src/info.rs` | the read verbs |
| `units/` | `hostd.socket`, `hostd.service` (sandboxed), `sysusers.conf` |

## Adding a write verb

1. A typed request with `deny_unknown_fields`, validated into a plan before
   anything else happens. Anything the plan reads from the host (a key, a
   file) is read inside the writer lock.
2. `service::write(host, origin, peer, verb, limits, ...)` with the
   allow-list keys the verb checks: it gates the call, takes the writer
   lock, gates it again and runs the change in its own task.
3. The change through `txn`: `FileChange::backup` for every file (with the
   mode and group a new file needs), `txn::begin`, the change and its proof,
   then `txn::conclude`. Never order the breaker or the receipt by hand.
4. A `reapply` for the verb in `txn::put_back`, so rollback, recovery and
   undo can make the host use the restored files. Without it the verb
   doesn't ship.
5. The paths it writes added to `ReadWritePaths=`, and any capability it
   needs to `CapabilityBoundingSet=`, in `units/hostd.service`, with the
   reason beside it.
6. Registered in `docs/docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix` (class `intent`), in
   this page, and reviewed on its own.

## Tests

`cargo test -p hostd`: no test needs root. The live gate for network writes
runs as root on a disposable networkd host, on dummy links only, and
removes everything it made.

# logging

Shared tracing, sink selection, reload handles and process statistics for

use the directory rule in [config](../config/README.md), including isolated
session roots.

Transplanted from `cosmix-lib-log` at cosmix
`e0297242305f3a3c3de09f1ca01e8faa771768da`. Production callers are Mix and
[noded](../noded/README.md).
