<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/releasesd/ (source: https://mixos.dev/releasesd/README.md) -->

# Application releases

Many good Linux applications ship as a GitHub release: a tarball per
platform, a checksum file, release notes. `releasesd` makes those first-class
on MixOS. You list the repositories you follow; it tells you when a new
release is out, installs it for you (never system-wide), checks it against
the checksums the release publishes, and keeps the previous version so you
can step back.

It works the same from the command line, from the Bus (so agents and the
settings panel can drive it), and on any Linux, not only MixOS.

## The catalogue

Your catalogue is `~/.config/mixos/releases.mx`. Until you write one,
releasesd follows MixOS itself: `mixos-desktop` (the compositor and the
apps) and `mixos-server` (`mix` and the headless services), both built by
the MixOS release workflow. Your own catalogue replaces that list, so keep
those two entries at the top to keep MixOS current:

```text
{
  schema: 1,
  apps: [
    {name: "mixos-desktop", repo: "markc/mixos"},
    {name: "mixos-server", repo: "markc/mixos"},
    {name: "example", repo: "owner/example"}
  ]
}
```

`name` is how you refer to the app and the directory it installs into;
`repo` is the GitHub `owner/name`. If a release has several Linux tarballs,
add `asset:` with a regular expression that picks the right one. To start an
app through a launcher of your own, give `exec_wrapper:` its command as a
list, for example `["/usr/local/bin/launch", "example"]`. The app's menu
entry then runs `launch example -- <the app's own command>`. The full schema
is in the [releases contract](../docs/spec/releases/README.md).

## Everyday use

```sh
mix releases.mix check            # ask GitHub what's new
mix releases.mix                  # installed vs latest, no network
mix releases.mix install example  # latest release; or: install example v1.2.0
mix releases.mix notes example    # what changed
mix releases.mix update           # every installed app that has a newer release
mix releases.mix rollback example # back to the previous version
mix releases.mix remove example
```

(`releases.mix` lives with the service in `/opt/mixos/lib/releasesd/`;
`mix tools/component_install.mix releasesd` puts it there from a checkout.)

`check` uses conditional requests, so asking again costs almost nothing. It
uses `GITHUB_TOKEN`, or your `gh` login if you have one; without either,
GitHub allows 60 requests an hour.

## What an install does

1. Picks the release's `linux-<arch>.tar.gz` (not the AppImage, Flatpak,
   deb or rpm: the tarball needs nothing from the system and unpacks as a
   ready prefix).
2. Verifies it. Every checksum the release publishes must match: GitHub's
   own digest of the file, and the release's `SHA256SUMS` file if there is
   one. If the release publishes neither, or anything differs, nothing is
   installed.
3. Unpacks it to `~/.local/opt/<name>/<version>` and points
   `~/.local/opt/<name>/current` at it.
4. Links its programs into `~/.local/bin`, and its desktop entry, icons and
   file types into `~/.local/share`, so it appears in the launcher and opens
   its files. The entry's command is rewritten to run the installed binary
   through `current`, so an update or rollback needs no relinking.
5. Keeps the previous version for `rollback`; older ones are removed.

It never overwrites a file it didn't create. If something of yours is
already at `~/.local/bin/example`, the install leaves it alone and says so.

## On the Bus

The session runs the service as `releases`:

```sh
send releases releases.check
send releases releases.install body='{"app": "example"}' timeout=600
```

The verbs, bodies and replies are in the [releases contract](../docs/spec/releases/README.md).
After any change it asks the application registry to rescan, so the
launcher updates by itself.

## Sharing one install with a container

An install can be linked into a second place, such as a MixOS session in a
container that sees your `~/.local/opt` through a read-only bind mount at
the same path. `releases.mix link` writes only the desktop entries, icons and
file types into that session's data directory (`MIXOS_RELEASES_SHARE`), with
its own record of what it made. Nothing is downloaded twice, and an update on
the host reaches the container at once. When the container sees the files at
another path, `MIXOS_RELEASES_VIEW` says where.

## Source and tests

`releasesd` is a Mix component
([decision](../docs/decisions/2026-10-10-mix-components.md)): no Cargo
package, identity in `component.mx`. The source is
[`services/releasesd`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/services/releasesd):

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `scripts/lib/releases.mix` | all of the logic, as a module |
| `scripts/releasesd.mix` | the Bus service (`mix --serve … --name releases`) |
| `scripts/releases.mix` | the command line, same logic in-process |
| `units/releasesd@.service` | the session unit |
| `tests/releases_test.mix` | offline: validation, verification, install, rollback, links |
| `tests/releasesd_test.mix` | every verb over a private broker and a stand-in API |

Run the tests from the checkout root. They need `bsdtar`; the Bus test
needs a `noded`, by default `/opt/mixos/bin/noded`, or `--noded <path>`:

```sh
mix services/releasesd/tests/releases_test.mix
mix services/releasesd/tests/releasesd_test.mix
```

The verbs are registered in `docs/docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix`.

# scene

The Mix Scenes document core, with no renderer and no interpreter. A scene
is a `---` envelope of headers followed by one ```` ```mix ```` fence
holding a strict-data map of nodes:

````text
---
scene: 1
name: about-panel
citizen: about-citizen
model: {"title":"About"}
---
```mix
root: {widget: "column", gap: 8, children: ["title"]}
title: {widget: "text", text: "= $model.title", size: 18, bold: true}
```
````

The crate provides:

- `parse` to a `SceneDocument`, `lint` for every diagnostic (codes in
  `ALL_CODES`), `resolve` to a `ResolvedScene` with defaults filled and
  bindings evaluated, `diff` between two resolved trees, `describe` for a
  family's ports, and `to_source` to write a document back out;
- `bindings`: `= expression` ports compiled once (`compile`), re-evaluated
  on a model patch (`reevaluate`) and instantiated per list row
  (`template_instantiate_with`);
- `evaluator`: the `Evaluator` trait the bindings go through, implemented
  by `ExprEvaluator` over the [expr](../expr/README.md) crate and used by
  default;
- `fixtures`: the test documents, exported for hosts' tests.

The node fence is parsed by [strict](../strict/README.md) and never
executed. A binding may read `$model` anywhere and `$item` inside a list
template; calls, assignments, statements and shell or Bus forms are refused
at compile time with `binding-policy`.

Window declarations accept `kind:"edge"`, `kind:"dialog"` and
`kind:"toast"`. Toasts are pointer-only overlays in compd, with optional
`w`, `h`, `title` and `chrome` (false by default). The host clamps their
geometry and manages visibility through its
[toast verbs](../compd/README.md#toast-scenes).

Test: `cargo test -p scene`.

The source is [`libs/scene`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/libs/scene).

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/screenshot/ (source: https://mixos.dev/screenshot/README.md) -->

# Screenshot

Screenshot takes a picture of the screen, a window or a region you drag
out, lets you mark it up, and saves it where you and your agents can find
it. Every mark stays editable until you save: the captured pixels are never
changed, and what is saved is exactly what you see.

## Taking a screenshot

| Key | Takes |
|---|---|
| **Print** | a region: drag out a rectangle with the crosshair; a click or Enter takes the whole screen, Escape cancels |
| **Shift+Print** | the whole screen |
| **Alt+Print** | the window you were working in |

The keys work everywhere on the desktop. They open Screenshot, or hand the
shot to the one already open, and Screenshot hides itself while it takes the
picture. If the window holds annotations you have not saved, it comes
forward and asks first. Nothing you drew is ever thrown away by a key press.

In the window, **Take screenshot** (Ctrl+N) takes another shot in the mode
the toolbar shows: region, full screen or window. For a window shot, choose
the window from the list beside the mode buttons; opening the list reads
the windows again. With more than one display, the same place offers the
**output**: the one under the pointer, or a named one (also
**Capture › Output**). The **Capture** menu also has a delay (3, 5 or 10
seconds) and **Include pointer**, which is off unless you turn it on.
For a region, the status line says "Drag to select an area · Esc to
cancel" as the window hides; compd then outlines the screen until you
drag. A left drag selects, Escape or the right button cancels, and a click
without a drag keeps the selection waiting. If you select nothing before
compd's limit, the window comes back saying "Nothing was selected".
Whatever happens, a shot you asked for brings the window back on top and
focused.
Escape or **Capture › Cancel** stops a shot that is waiting out its delay.
A second Print while a shot is being taken is answered "already being
taken" in the window's status line.

## Marking it up

The tool bar on the left holds the tools. Each has a key you press with
nothing else held:

| Tool | Key | Does |
|---|---|---|
| Select and move | V | click an annotation to select it; drag it to move it |
| Crop | C | drag out the part to keep (Edit › Reset crop undoes it) |
| Arrow | A | drag from the tail to the point |
| Line | L | drag |
| Rectangle | R | drag a box |
| Ellipse | E | drag a box |
| Pen | P | draw freehand |
| Highlighter | H | draw a translucent stroke |
| Redact | X | drag a box; it is filled solid, so nothing shows through |
| Text | T | type the text in the bar at the top, then click or drag |
| Numbered marker | N | click; markers count up 1, 2, 3… |

The bar at the top sets the **ink** (red, amber, green, teal, black or
white), the **stroke width**, and for text and markers the **text size**.
Changing the ink or width while an annotation is selected changes that
annotation too. In a narrow window, the controls that don't fit are left
out of the bar; **Annotate** still has them all.

Widths and text sizes are what you see: a Medium line is the same
thickness on screen whether the shot is a 4K screen shown scaled down or a
small region shown full size. Each annotation keeps the size it was drawn
at in the image's own pixels, so zooming later makes it bigger or smaller
with the picture, and changing only the ink never changes its width. To
an agent, `width` and `size` are in the image's pixels (up to 512 and 1024).

Delete or Backspace removes the selected annotation, and Escape deselects
it. Undo is Ctrl+Z and
Redo is Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y. Ctrl with + and − zooms, Ctrl+0 fits the
picture to the window, the wheel scrolls, and a middle-button drag pans.

## Saving

Once there is a picture, **Copy** and **Save** buttons sit at the right
end of the bar at the top; Save's tip names the folder it saves to.

- **Save** (Ctrl+S) writes the picture straight into
  **Pictures/Screenshots**, no questions asked, as
  `20261012_193927.png` (the local date and time you saved, as
  `YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS`, the form KDE's Spectacle can be set to use). If that
  name is taken, the new file gets `_2`, `_3` and so on
  (`20261012_193927_2.png`).
  Screenshot never overwrites a file. The status line then says
  "Saved to ~/Pictures/Screenshots/…" with the file's name.
- **Save As…** (Ctrl+Shift+S) asks for a path, proposing the name Save
  would use in Pictures/Screenshots (created if missing). It refuses one
  that already exists.
- **Copy image** (Ctrl+C) puts the marked-up picture on the clipboard.

The Pictures folder is the one your desktop names
(`XDG_PICTURES_DIR` in `~/.config/user-dirs.dirs`), or `~/Pictures`.
Saved PNGs are created like any file an application saves: your umask
decides who else may read them.

The raw shot compd takes is kept, until you save, in Screenshot's own
private folder (`~/.local/state/mixos/apps/screenshot/captures`, readable
only by you). It is deleted once the shot is saved, replaced by another,
or closed, and when a capture is cancelled or fails. On start, Screenshot
also prunes that folder to the newest 20 raw shots and nothing older than
7 days. The window and headless instances share that folder.

## Handing a shot to an agent

You don't need to tell an agent where a shot is. Press Print, mark it up,
press Ctrl+S, and ask the agent to look at your latest screenshot. The
agent finds it in two ways:

- **`screenshot.recent`** lists the newest saved shots: path, size,
  whether they carry annotations, and when each was saved.
- **`screenshot.saved`** is published on every save with the same fields,
  for an agent that is listening.

```mix
-- The newest saved screenshot's path.
$body = json_encode({limit: 1})
send screenshot screenshot.recent body=$body
if $rc != 0 then raise("SCREENSHOT", to_string($result)) end
$recent = if type($result) == "string" then json_parse($result) else $result end
print $recent.shots[0].path
```

The answer names the folder too:
`{folder, shots: [{path, width, height, annotated, saved_at}]}`, newest
first.

## For agents

Screenshot answers on the Bus as `screenshot` (schema `screenshot.v1`).

| Verb | Arguments | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `screenshot.ping`, `screenshot.info` | | liveness and the compositor served (`comp`); the document, its source and last save, the capture, the job and the UI state |
| `screenshot.capture` | `mode` (`screen`, `window`, `region`), `output`, `window` `{id, generation}`, `cursor`, `delay` (0–10) | a new document, once it is ready; any answer, refusals included, carries `restore_failed: true` if the window could not be shown again; refused while unsaved annotations exist |
| `screenshot.take` | `mode`, `window`, `comp` | as Print Screen: starts at once, or brings the window forward and asks about unsaved work at once; refused (`COMPOSITOR`) when `comp` names another compositor |
| `screenshot.cancel` | | cancels a capture during its delay |
| `screenshot.open` | `path` | opens an image; refused while unsaved annotations exist |
| `screenshot.annotate` | `kind`, `points`, `colour`, `width`, and `text`, `size`, `number` for text and markers | the new annotation's id |
| `screenshot.move`, `screenshot.delete` | `id` (and `dx`, `dy`) | the document |
| `screenshot.crop` | `crop` `{x, y, width, height}`, or null | the document |
| `screenshot.undo`, `screenshot.redo` | | the document |
| `screenshot.save` | | saves into the screenshots folder as `YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.png` (`_2`, `_3`… when taken); publishes `screenshot.saved` |
| `screenshot.export` | `path` | Save As to a new file |
| `screenshot.recent` | `limit` (1–100) | the newest saved shots |
| `screenshot.select` | `tool`, `mode`, `window`, `output` | the UI state |
| `screenshot.commands`, `screenshot.execute` | `id` | every command, or runs one as its menu item would |
| `screenshot.theme` | `scheme`, `mode` | this window's look |
| `screenshot.show`, `screenshot.quit` | | brings the window forward; closes it (refused with unsaved work) |

Coordinates are pixels of the captured image, whatever the zoom. Like any
program you run, an agent on the Bus acts as you: `screenshot.open` reads
any image you can read, and `screenshot.export` writes a new PNG wherever
you can write (never over an existing file). An agent
is refused rather than allowed to discard a person's unsaved annotations
(`UNSAVED`), and is refused while a dialog is open (`DIALOG`) or another job
runs (`BUSY`).

The window is drivable like every MixOS app, including its menus: see
[driving an app](../docs/drive.md) (`screenshot.ui.*`, `screenshot.window`). The
verbs are registered in `docs/docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix`. Each command run
from a menu, a key, the toolbar or `screenshot.execute` is published on
`screenshot.command.executed`
([executed commands](../docs/decisions/2026-10-11-executed-commands.md)).

`screenshot --headless` runs the same verbs with no window, for agents and
tests, registered under the headless names above so Print Screen never
lands in an instance nobody can see. It never asks anything: work that would need a
question is refused.

## From the command line

```
screenshot [IMAGE]                 open the window (or bring it forward)
screenshot --capture region        take a shot, as Print does
screenshot --capture window --window ID:GEN
screenshot --headless              the Bus service alone (screenshot-headless)
screenshot --comp comp-nested      capture through another compositor
```

There is one window, and one headless instance, per compositor:

| Compositor | Window | Headless |
|---|---|---|
| `comp` (the desktop's own) | `screenshot` | `screenshot-headless` |
| another, e.g. `comp-nested` | `screenshot-comp-nested` | `screenshot-headless-comp-nested` |
| a name too long to fit | `screenshot--<8 hex>` | `screenshot-headless--<8 hex>` |

The hex is a stable hash of the compositor's name; a service name is at
most 31 bytes, and a window name never starts with `screenshot-headless`.
A second launch, or Print Screen in a compositor, hands its request to
that compositor's window, so a shot is always taken through the
compositor whose key was pressed; before handing over, the launch checks
that the running instance serves the same compositor (`comp` in
`screenshot.ping`) and refuses otherwise, and the request itself names the
compositor so the receiver refuses it too. A running window from an older
build that does not report `comp` refuses every hand-over: close it and
launch again. `--comp` and `--service` take Bus
service names: 2 to 31 of a-z, 0-9 and `-`, starting with a letter.

An agent's capture (`screenshot.capture`) hides the window and shows it
again without taking the focus or switching workspace; a person's capture
brings the window forward. Showing the window again is retried for a few
seconds; if it still fails, the shot is kept, the answer carries
`restore_failed: true` and the status line says so. Bring the window back
with Print Screen, `screenshot.show` or the taskbar; nothing restores it
later on its own.

## Source and tests

The source is
[`apps/screenshot`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/apps/screenshot)
(app id `dev.mixos.screenshot`):

- `crates/annotation`: the headless engine (document, painter, viewport,
  screenshots folder, ledger).
- `src/`: the egui shell (`app` state and rules, `commands` registry,
  `capture` over compd, `jobs`, `view`, `shell`, `headless`). The instance
  names per compositor are in `src/names.rs`.

Test it on a build worker:

```
cargo test -p screenshot -p annotation
```

`tests/native_bus.rs` runs the headless binary against an in-process
broker and a fixture compositor; `tests/snapshot.rs` renders the window
offscreen (regenerate with `UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1` and look at the images);
`tests/registry.rs` checks the verb registry.

## Notes

- Copy image goes through the desktop's X11 clipboard (XWayland), so
  native Wayland applications may not see it yet. Save, then paste the
  file, is the reliable path for now.
- Screenshot replaces Cap, the earlier screenshot app; see the
  [decision](../docs/decisions/2026-10-12-screenshot.md).

## Changes from Cap

- Print, Shift+Print and Alt+Print take shots from anywhere.
- Ctrl+S saves straight into Pictures/Screenshots; agents find saves with
  `screenshot.recent` and `screenshot.saved`.
- Stroke width and text size are steps (thin to heavy, small to huge)
  rather than free values; numbered markers are discs.
- Open and Save As take a typed path rather than a file browser.
- The pointer is left out of shots unless you include it, for people and
  agents alike.
- A region selection may take up to 70 seconds (Cap allowed 38).
- Raw shots are deleted when no longer needed, and the folder is pruned.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/settings/ (source: https://mixos.dev/settings/README.md) -->

# settings

Headless desktop settings types, validation and resolution, and the shared
consumer. Shared by the authority ([settingsd](../settingsd/README.md)) and
the app and compositor adapters. Library API: 0.3.0; the authority wire and
schema contract remains 0.1.0, schema 1.

See [the settings contract](../docs/spec/settings/README.md). The source is
[`libs/settings`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/libs/settings).

## The consumer

`consumer::Consumer` owns ordering, bounded bootstrap buffering, one active
subscribe/read job, pending-only recovery and fenced staged/application
state. `domains::ChangePlan` compares one effective context for paint,
text, layout, resource and motion work; shell hosts opt into shell
geometry. Provenance and source/revision metadata alone do not cause
rendering work. Construct apps with `Consumer::for_app(binding, "ced")` and
shell hosts with `Consumer::for_shell(binding)`. `context()` returns the
canonical projection key (`app:ced` or `desktop`); adapters use it without
repeating key construction.

## Native execution

The optional `native` feature executes actions over an **existing**
`bus::native_client::SupervisedClient`. It does not connect, spawn a task or
take the incoming receiver. The host multiplexes work futures with its
current incoming lane and connection state, feeding the sampled connection
generation even when a state watch coalesces a disconnect/reconnect. Feed
queue loss through `lost()` before using further queued data. There is one
pending retry deadline, from 250 ms capped at 30 seconds; remove it after
success/disconnect and never arm an idle timer. Unsupported, wrong-target
and protocol refusals await a new event or explicit refresh rather than
automatically retrying unchanged bad data. `retry_deadline()` is absolute
and remains fixed during malformed-event storms; `retry_delay()` returns
its remaining duration, not a new per-event delay. Inspect `is_confirmed()`
to distinguish fresh authority evidence from preserved usable data during
loss/recovery. Captured read baselines expose same-incarnation rollback
while allowing an older read that legitimately raced a newer event. Cancel
an old executor future when `current_work()` changes or disappears;
superseded work must not become a second active host job. Reconcile the
pending timer from `retry_deadline()` after every engine input and
completion, including successful RPC replies: a delivery anomaly may have
scheduled recovery while that otherwise successful read was in flight.
Timer scheduling follows engine state, not just the last RPC result.

## Bootstrap and fallback

Each native call has a one-second bound. Pass the same initial deadline to
`native::execute_until` for subscribe and read to bound their combined
bootstrap to one second before presenting a labelled fallback; complete
cancelled work as a timeout so the engine can recover. After that deadline
the host may capture `fallback_request()` and run `Request::prepare` on its
worker, passing a loaded cache candidate and a resource readiness callback.
Retained bootstrap data is tried first, then cache, then embedded defaults.
Every candidate must pass the callback for all references used by its
context/host. If none is usable, preparation returns diagnostics.
`complete_fallback` fences the completion before producing the usual UI
stage; the usual synchronous pre-swap check and acknowledgement still
apply. Resource loading and real renderer integration remain host work.

## Applying a change

Readback advances `current()`, not `applied()`. Prepare every changed
resource before entering the renderer loop. Check `is_current(update)`
immediately before the synchronous swap, then activate and
`acknowledge(update)` with no intervening await; a stale completion must
never mutate the renderer. Failed activation preserves last-good applied
data. Identical render inputs advance evidence without a swap. Neither
readback nor application proves a presented frame. Profiles and contexts
are immutable for one consumer lifetime. A host rebind cancels its old
work, retires the old subscription via `unsubscribe_topic`, and creates a
new consumer; unique consumer tickets reject completions from retired
hosts.

`presentation_kind()` labels installed data as Current, Retained, Cached,
LastGood or Embedded. Fallback never enters `current()` or supplies
mutation fences. Embedded/cached fallback cannot be saved as
authority-derived data. An unchanged fresh authority projection promotes
evidence without a swap. `fault()` reports authority/current-resource
faults; `fallback_fault()` reports fallback preparation/activation failure.
A usable fallback clears its own fault while preserving an ongoing
authority outage or unavailable live resources.

## The presentation cache

The optional `cache` feature provides bounded presentation-cache I/O over
`config::atomic` ([config](../config/README.md)). The caller supplies an
existing absolute directory inside its isolated session; no paths are
created and no host preferences are touched. Reads reject symlinks in every
path component, non-regular files and oversized data. A versioned,
digest-bound envelope also binds instance/profile, context, shell
capability and interpretation; the whole projection must match a current
recompilation. An unavailable old pinned package source is refused
visibly. JSON parsing preserves floating-point round trips for exact
projection checks. Digests detect corruption; they do not authenticate
local files. Local cache never supplies authority evidence, even when its
data is valid.

`cache_target()` captures the immutable producer/binding/context/capability
descriptor for `load_for` and `Writer::open_for`; the private producer fence
does not enter the persistent filename. `Save::same_capture` allows bounded
worker deduplication. `Request::prepare_with_cache` loads lazily after
retained resource validation and preserves load failures in its prepared
diagnostics.

Capture `cache_save()` only after activation (or unchanged evidence
advancement), then submit it to the host's one serial `cache::Writer` off
the UI loop. Captures carry immutable applied data and an activation
serial. A stable advisory lock excludes duplicate writers; superseded saves
cannot replace newer attempts. The latest failed save can retry, while
post-rename sync failure reports `cache_write_ambiguous`. Do not delete
corrupt or ambiguous data automatically. Retire the writer when retiring
its producer consumer. The held directory inode is the I/O boundary;
renaming it cannot redirect a write elsewhere, but may make the cache
unavailable under the new path. That is a fallback/cache miss, never an
authority rollback. Cache failure does not change applied renderer state.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/settingsd/ (source: https://mixos.dev/settingsd/README.md) -->

# settingsd

The headless native ABP desktop settings authority, contract 0.1.0. An
established profile has one writer and durable whole-document settings and
operation receipts. Native publication is retained and owner-stamped by
[noded](../noded/README.md). [Ced](../ced/README.md) and
[compd](../compd/README.md)'s scene-host consume shared appearance jobs on
their existing Bus lifetimes. Full desktop integration, panel geometry and
native frame acceptance remain in development.

See [the settings contract](../docs/spec/settings/README.md). Clients use
the [settings](../settings/README.md) library. The source is
[`services/settingsd`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/services/settingsd).

## Running it

```text
settingsd init --instance example
settingsd seed --allow-create --instance example
settingsd serve --instance example
```

Init explicitly initialises new state. An installer can explicitly seed a
first-run session profile with `--allow-create`. Plain seed validates an
existing profile unchanged and refuses a wholly missing root; a retained
writer lock prevents seed from recreating an established missing primary,
including without a backup. Serve fails for a missing or unsupported
established store. Both accept `--profile` and `--root` for an explicit
binding or test directory. Use an isolated broker when testing.

## Profiles and upgrades

Profiles pin their initial package design source. Reload checks a content
digest; a binary upgrade cannot change effective settings within the same
revision. An effective interpretation digest fences compiler drift for
explicit migration. The accepted record's format (`store::FORMAT`, now 2)
is that migration: an older record whose seal verifies as stored is
re-derived and re-sealed on open by `Accepted::upgrade`, whose doc comment
says how to add the next field.

Present corrupt primary data can restore a validated backup under a new
incarnation. A missing primary fails visibly, including when a backup
exists. I/O faults and intact unsupported documents fail without automatic
rollback.

## The unit

The packaged unit binds the instance to its machine hostname; its
session/VT number is a supervision attribute and never a second instance
identity. The session target wants and upholds the authority. The unit
validates with plain seed before serving, and application and compositor
startup does not wait for settings readiness. An image must provision its
service account's writable `MIXOS_ETC/settings` root and explicitly seed
once during first installation. Automatic startup never receives
`--allow-create`, so lost mounts or directories do not silently become new
default profiles.

## Tests

Worker tests: `cargo test -p settingsd`. The native ABP gate and the
compositor fixtures arrive with the desktop test harness.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/strict/ (source: https://mixos.dev/strict/README.md) -->

# strict

The MixOS strict-data format: the grammar of `*.conf.mix` and `*.data.mix`
files. A document is a JSON-shaped tree (nil, bool, number, string, list,
map) with bare keys, optional top-level braces, `#` / `--` comments and
trailing commas. It is loaded as data and never executed: anything that
could run (a variable, a call, a command substitution, interpolation, a
semicolon) is refused with a line-numbered error naming the construct.

The crate has no dependency on the Mix language. It provides:

- `parse` / `parse_file` to a `Value` tree;
- `from_str` / `from_value` / `from_file` into a `#[derive(Deserialize)]`
  type, and `to_string` / `to_string_pretty` / `to_value` back out;
- `encode` / `encode_pretty` for a `Value`, in text that reads back
  unchanged;
- `to_json` / `from_json` for consumers that work on `serde_json::Value`.

Build and test with `cargo test -p strict`. The grammar tests live in
`tests/grammar.rs`, the serde bridge in `tests/serde_bridge.rs`.

The source is [`libs/strict`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/libs/strict).

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/syntax/ (source: https://mixos.dev/syntax/README.md) -->

# syntax

Deterministic syntax highlighting for MixOS text editors. It wraps `lsh`
from Microsoft Edit (msedit): a small compiler from `*.lsh` language
definitions to bytecode, and a line-oriented runtime that turns each line
into highlight spans. The two upstream crates, `lsh` and `stdext`, are
vendored with documented patches under
[`vendor/msedit`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/vendor/msedit)
(MIT, from microsoft/edit at `826b4c0`).

It is a core library (`kind = "lib"`, `layer = "core"`) with no Bus
contract. Its one direct user is [`editor-model`](../editor-model/README.md)
([`libs/editor-model/src/highlight.rs`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/blob/main/libs/editor-model/src/highlight.rs)),
which maps its highlight kinds to colour classes for the
[editor](../editor/README.md) widget, and so for [ced](../ced/README.md).
Mix source is highlighted by the Mix lexer, not by this crate.

The source is [`libs/syntax`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/libs/syntax).

## Concepts

- **Bytes, not graphemes.** lsh works on bytes, so a text store may hand
  over chunks that split a grapheme cluster.
- **Line numbers are 1-based** everywhere in the API.
- **Lines of 32 KiB or more are left plain** (`MAX_LINE_LEN`, as upstream).
  Unlike upstream, the highlighter still advances to the real end of such a
  line, so later line numbers stay correct.
- **A checkpoint every 1024 lines** (`cache::INTERVAL`, pinned in every
  build profile; upstream uses 16 in debug builds). A random seek costs at
  most one interval of parsing.
- **No build script and no mutable statics.** The compiled definitions in
  `src/defs.rs` are generated once and committed.

## API

- `language_for_path(&Path)`, `language_by_id("rust")`,
  `language_by_name("Markdown")` (ASCII-case-insensitive): look up a
  `&'static Language`.
- `LineSource`: the trait a text store implements. `read_forward(offset)`
  returns the contiguous bytes from `offset` to some chunk boundary (empty at
  the end); the highlighter assembles lines that span chunks. The optional
  `indexed_line_end(line)` lets a store with a line index skip over-long
  lines without reading them. `&[u8]` and `str` implement it.
- `highlighter::Highlighter`: parses one line at a time from the top.
  `parse_next_line(&mut Vec<Span>)` fills the spans of the next line;
  `snapshot()` and `restore()` save and resume a `HighlighterState`.
- `highlighter::Span { start, kind }`: `kind` applies from `start` (an
  absolute byte offset in the source) to the next span or the end of the
  line.
- `cache::Cache`: checkpointed random access. `parse_line(h, line, out)`
  resumes from the nearest checkpoint; `invalidate_from(line)` drops the
  states an edit at `line` makes stale; `advance(h, target, max_lines)`
  time-slices a cold seek with a per-call line budget and returns true once
  `target` is reachable; `reach()` is the furthest line reachable without
  parsing. The cache also keeps a frontier, so a budget below one interval
  still makes progress from frame to frame.
- `defs::HighlightKind`: `Comment`, `String`, `KeywordControl`,
  `StorageType`, the `Markup*` kinds and the rest. `defs::LANGUAGES` and
  `defs::FILE_ASSOCIATIONS` are the generated tables. `syntax::runtime`
  re-exports the vendored `Language` and `Highlight` types.

## Languages

C, C++, C#, Diff, F#, Git commit and rebase messages, Go, ignore files,
Java, JavaScript, JSON, LSH, Lua, Markdown, Odin, PowerShell, properties,
Python, Ruby, Rust, shell script, TOML, XML and YAML: one per definition
file in
[`vendor/msedit/lsh/definitions`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/vendor/msedit/lsh/definitions).

## Example

From the tests:

```rust
use syntax::highlighter::Highlighter;

let text = "fn main() {\n    // hello\n}\n";
let src = text.as_bytes();
let rust = syntax::language_by_id("rust").expect("lsh defines rust");
let mut h = Highlighter::new(&src, rust);
let mut spans = Vec::new();
h.parse_next_line(&mut spans); // line 1
h.parse_next_line(&mut spans); // line 2: a Comment span starts at the "//"
```

An editor keeps one `Cache` per buffer, builds a fresh `Highlighter` over
its text each frame (a highlighter borrows the text), calls `cache.advance`
with a line budget for lines not yet reached, and calls
`cache.invalidate_from(line)` after each edit.

## Regenerating the definitions

`src/defs.rs` is written by the `gen` example, the same generator msedit
runs from its build script, with two changes: the compiler's IR dump is left
out (it prints node addresses, so it differs on every run) and
`HighlightKind` also derives `Hash`.

```sh
cargo run --release -p syntax --example gen            # writes src/defs.rs
cargo run --release -p syntax --example gen -- --stdout
```

The lsh compiler panics on patterns it does not support, so it runs only
here and in the tests (`syntax::compiler`, hidden from the docs), never
inside an editor. The crate has no features.

## Source layout

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `src/lib.rs` | Language lookup, `LineSource`, the hidden `compiler` module |
| `src/highlighter.rs` | `Highlighter`, `HighlighterState`, `Span`, `MAX_LINE_LEN` |
| `src/cache.rs` | `Cache` and `INTERVAL` |
| `src/defs.rs` | Generated bytecode, strings, charsets and language tables |
| `examples/gen.rs` | The generator for `src/defs.rs` |

## Tests

- `tests/defs_fresh.rs`: the committed `src/defs.rs` matches a fresh
  generation byte for byte; two generations in one process agree; every
  file association points into `LANGUAGES`, and the lookups work.
- `tests/highlighter.rs`: spans are absolute and ordered; any chunk size
  gives the same spans as one slice; `INTERVAL` stays 1024; over-long lines
  are plain and keep later line numbers, with and without a line index;
  reading past the end is empty; `advance` makes progress below one interval
  per call; and a proptest checks that random seeks, also after an edit and
  `invalidate_from`, equal a linear parse. An ignored benchmark times
  over-long lines with and without a line index.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/system/ (source: https://mixos.dev/system/README.md) -->

# system

The system binary, `mix`: the Mix shell and every headless MixOS daemon in
one file ([decision](../docs/decisions/2026-10-12-one-system-binary.md)).

The binary picks a personality from the basename of argv[0]. Started as
`mix` it is the shell ([mix-shell](../mix-shell/README.md),
`mix_shell::main`); started through a symlink named `noded` it is the node
daemon ([noded](../noded/README.md), `noded::main`). Each daemon still runs
as its own process, under its own unit and journal identity. This package
holds only the dispatcher and the global allocator (mimalloc); each
component keeps its own crate, tests, version and units.

```text
cargo build --profile release-fast -p system   # target/release-fast/mix
mix --personalities                            # each personality and its component version
ln -s mix noded                                # noded, as its own process
```

An unknown name exits 2 and prints the personalities. A login shell's
`-mix` is the shell.

The Mix language is documented in the [Mix manual](../mix/README.md).

## Tests

`cargo test -p system` runs the identity test (`tests/personalities.rs`) and
the shell's process-level tests, which moved here from `cli/mix-shell` so
they test the shipped binary. Their scripts moved with them
(`tests/scripts`); the manual they check is the site source
([`docs/mix`](../mix/README.md)), and the source guards read
`cli/mix-shell/src`.

The source is [`cli/system`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/cli/system).

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/term/ (source: https://mixos.dev/term/README.md) -->

# Terminal

`term` is the MixOS terminal (app id `dev.mixos.term`): tabs, split panes,
and a grid drawn on the GPU. It is an egui shell (see
[AGENTS.md](https://github.com/markc/mixos/blob/main/AGENTS.md) §4.1) around
two private crates:

- `crates/term-core`: the engine. PTYs, the VT grid, tabs and panes,
  selection, mouse reporting, configuration, the native session and the
  `term.*` Bus verbs.
- `crates/term-render`: the grid on the GPU. A glyph atlas and instanced
  cells drawn by an egui-wgpu paint callback per pane. The CPU raster in
  term-core is its test oracle.

The shell adds the window: the toolkit title bar and menus, the tab strip,
pane borders on whole physical pixels, the keyboard and input method, the
pointer (selection, mouse reporting, middle-click paste of the primary
selection), the clipboard, and font zoom. Every action is a command on the
toolkit registry, published on `term.command.executed`.

The source is [`apps/term`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/apps/term).

## Bus

The window registers `term` (or `term-<pid>` when another instance holds
it) and answers:

- the terminal's verbs, served by term-core (`HELP` lists them):
  `term.session`, `term.tabs`, `term.tab.*`, `term.panes`, `term.pane.*`,
  `term.snapshot`, `term.scroll`, `term.type`, `term.props.watch`;
- the window's own: `term.commands`, `term.execute`, `app.describe`, and the
  toolkit drive verbs (`term.ui.*`, `term.window`, `term.window.state`).

`term --headless` serves the terminal's verbs with no window.

## Configuration

The desktop profile's `terminal.*` settings, held by
[settingsd](../settingsd/README.md) and edited in [Prefs](../prefs/README.md):
font family, size and weight, padding, border width, history lines, scroll
speed, cursor shape and blink, the focus ring, copy on select, and `TERM`.
The window follows them as they change; Ctrl+plus and minus write
`terminal.font.size` back 400 ms after the last zoom key. Ctrl+0 returns to
the profile size without writing, except to correct a write already in
flight. An unsaved zoom stays pending in memory until another zoom key or a
successful settings read; a validation refusal discards it. Failures
schedule no retry timers. History lines and `TERM` apply to tabs and panes
opened afterwards. Without settingsd the defaults stand, and zoom stays the
window's own. `TERM_FONT_PX` sets the size until settingsd answers, and
`TERM_SPIKE_FONT` overrides the font file; `term --print-config` prints the
startup values.

## Keys

`term --help` lists them. Tabs: Ctrl+Shift+T/W, Ctrl+PageUp/PageDown.
Panes: Ctrl+Shift+E/O split, Ctrl+Shift+X close, Ctrl+Shift+arrows,
Tab/Shift+Tab or Ctrl+Tab between split panes. Clipboard: Ctrl+Shift+C/V,
Shift+Insert. Font: Ctrl+plus/minus/0 and Ctrl+wheel. History:
Shift+PageUp/PageDown/Home/End. Alt is Meta (ESC before the key; Alt+cursor
keys send xterm's CSI 1;3 sequences). Right-hand modifier chords are the
person's own on MixOS and are not bound.

## Building and testing

On an authorised build worker at a pushed commit:

```
cargo test --locked -p term-core -p term-render -p term
cargo build --locked --profile release-fast -p term
```

`tests/window.rs` takes an offscreen snapshot of the window with two tabs
and a split; regenerate it with `UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1` and look at it. The
PTY tests need the Mix binary at `/opt/mixos/bin/mix`.

Development fixture for the Term-to-Mix native session acceptance tests.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/thumbs/ (source: https://mixos.dev/thumbs/README.md) -->

# thumbs

File thumbnails the way the freedesktop desktops make them. A thumbnail
lives in the shared cache (`$XDG_CACHE_HOME/thumbnails`, the Thumbnail
Managing Standard), so one made by another file manager shows at once, and
the reverse. A missing one is made by a thumbnailer installed on the system
(a `.thumbnailer` entry, the contract GNOME, COSMIC and glycin share). It
runs as a plain argv in its own process group under a timeout, and its
output is checked before it is cached. Thumbnailers reach every format the
system knows, and keep decoders MixOS cannot ship under its licences
(FFmpeg-backed video, for one) in their own process.

The crate is headless: no toolkit, no pixels. Showing a cached thumbnail is
`toolkit::thumbnail`'s part.

- `Pool<K>` makes thumbnails off the caller's thread. Each `Request` has a
  `lane` (a new request replaces the one waiting in its lane) and a
  `Ticket` (a shared generation counter: bump it when the view moves on,
  and its requests are dropped or their runs killed). Replies go to the
  callback given to `Pool::new`, which also names the app the cache is
  written as.
- `generate::Generator` makes one thumbnail. Everything that touches the
  file before its thumbnailer runs happens on a probe thread under a
  deadline, so a hung filesystem strands a thread, never a worker.
- `mounts` refuses network, FUSE and automounted files from the mount table
  before anything touches them.
- `cache`, `png` and `registry` are the cache, the few PNG facts it needs,
  and the installed thumbnailers.

Users: [DOpus](../dopus/README.md) (the Properties preview). Build and test
with `cargo test -p thumbs`.

The source is [`libs/thumbs`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/libs/thumbs).

## Known limits

- Output is checked structurally, never decoded (no decoders here), so a
  well-formed PNG with corrupt image data is cached as ready. The display
  side shows the type icon for it until the file changes.
- There is no way to withdraw one lane's waiting request short of making
  its ticket stale. A folder view that scrolls will want one; it can be
  added without changing what exists.
- The PNG and mountinfo parsers have unit tests but no fuzz targets yet.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/toolkit/ (source: https://mixos.dev/toolkit/README.md) -->

# Toolkit

`toolkit` is the library every MixOS egui application is built on. It is
the shell layer of the
[egui applications decision](../docs/decisions/2026-10-09-egui-applications.md)
(see [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/markc/mixos/blob/main/AGENTS.md) §4.1).
An app keeps its behaviour in a headless engine and its UI state in one
serialisable struct. The toolkit draws the window around that state and
routes every action through one command registry.

It gives each app:

- the resolved [design](../design/README.md) as an egui style, plus the
  embedded Inter and JetBrains Mono faces and the Lucide icons;
- the client-side title bar, menu bars and menus, and the View › Theme
  submenu;
- the chrome components (bars, buttons, panels, tabs, fields, toggles,
  combos, sliders, canvas scrollbars, tooltips, dialogs), drawn to the
  chrome specification in each chrome scheme;
- the command registry, which generates menus, shortcuts, the palette and
  the Bus surface, and records every executed command;
- the drive verbs, the UI-level Bus verbs that every app shares;
- Fluent string catalogues, a key-chord grammar, and thumbnail decoding.

The source is
[`libs/toolkit`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/tree/main/libs/toolkit).

## Who uses it

The apps [term](../term/README.md), [ced](../ced/README.md),
[dopus](../dopus/README.md), [prefs](../prefs/README.md),
[screenshot](../screenshot/README.md), [backdrop](../backdrop/README.md)
and busviewer; the [editor](../editor/README.md) library; and four of
[compd](../compd/README.md)'s crates (`decor`, `ui`, `scene-host`,
`world`). backdrop is the only one that turns on the `layer` feature.

## Starting an app

Call `toolkit::install(ctx, &theme)` once on the egui context. It installs
the image loaders the icons need and applies the theme's style and fonts.
`Theme::load()` reads the shared `theme.conf.mix` from the MixOS etc
directory (`$MIXOS_ETC`, else `$MIXOS/etc`, else `/etc/mixos` for root,
else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/mixos`). It falls back to the embedded design, and
says why on stderr, when the file is missing or unusable.

A minimal window, condensed from `tests/snapshot.rs`:

```rust
use toolkit::command::{Command, Registry, always};
use toolkit::{Icon, Strings, Theme, icons};

#[derive(Default)]
struct Demo { refreshed: u32 }

let mut commands = Registry::new();
commands.add(Command {
    id: "bus.refresh",           // stable, never reused once published
    label: "cmd-refresh",        // Fluent key
    menu: Some("menu-bus"),      // Fluent key of the top-level menu
    submenu: None,
    group: 0,
    shortcut: Some(egui::KeyboardShortcut::new(egui::Modifiers::COMMAND, egui::Key::R)),
    icon: Some(Icon::RefreshCw),
    enabled: always,
    run: |s: &mut Demo| s.refreshed += 1,
});

let theme = Theme::load();
toolkit::install(ctx, &theme);
let strings = Strings::new(include_str!("../i18n/en/demo.ftl"));
let stroke = icons::stroke_width(&theme);

// each frame:
let _ = toolkit::titlebar::show(ui, "Demo", Some(Icon::Server), stroke,
                                &commands, &state, &strings);
```

## Main pieces

### Theme and look

- `theme`: `Theme` holds a resolved design together with the context it
  was compiled for (scheme, style, mode, contrast) and its framing
  (server- or client-side decorations, caption side). Build one with
  `Theme::embedded()`, `for_context`, `from_source` (a full design
  document or a selection-only file) or `load()`. Then adjust it with
  `with_choice`, `framed` and `with_overlay`.
- `session_look`: turns the desktop profile's appearance, as
  [settingsd](../settingsd/README.md) holds it, into a `Theme`. It is pure,
  with no Bus and no I/O. An appearance that names a design this build
  does not know leaves the app's session theme in place.
- `theme_menu`: the View › Theme submenu, added with
  `Registry::theme_menu`. It covers the hue schemes (Ocean, Crimson, Stone,
  Forest, Sunset, Mono), the chrome schemes (Pro, Studio, Classic), modes,
  styles and framing. Command ids are `view.theme.<scheme>`,
  `view.mode.*`, `view.style.*`, `view.decorations.*` and
  `view.captions.*`, and each axis can follow the session.
- `style`: maps a hue scheme's design onto egui's `Style`. The module docs
  give the field-by-field mapping table.
- `chrome`: the colours and geometry of the title bar and menus. For the
  chrome schemes (`pro`, `studio`, `classic`) it supplies the whole egui
  style, taken from the design's chrome family. Components read
  `Chrome::style` and `Chrome::metrics` and never ask which scheme they are
  drawing, so a new style needs only design data. See the
  [chrome family decision](../docs/decisions/2026-10-09-chrome-family-and-schemes.md).
- `fonts`: the embedded faces. Weight is a design token: each typography
  role names a weight, and the static Inter file of that weight is the one
  installed. Monospace is JetBrains Mono.
- `icons`: Lucide icons, from unmodified upstream SVGs. The `Icon` enum
  names them. Stroke width comes from the design metric
  `icon.stroke_width`, and colour comes from the widget's text colour at
  draw time. See the
  [icons and type decision](../docs/decisions/2026-10-09-icons-and-type.md).

### Window chrome and components

- `titlebar`: the client-side title bar. From the left it holds the app
  mark, the registry's menus, the centred title, an optional right-hand
  group of controls, and the minimize, maximize and close buttons. Captions
  can be on the left instead. A window opened with `titlebar::viewport` is
  undecorated. Only the free gap between the menus and the buttons drags
  the window. Call `titlebar::edges` last in the frame to add the resize
  zones. Under server-side decorations the row becomes a plain menu bar.
- `menu`: menu bars and menus drawn by the toolkit, not by egui's
  `MenuBar`. One highlight is shared by pointer and keyboard, a menu opens
  on press, and press-drag-release runs an item. `Nav` holds the open menu
  and its highlights as pure data and is tested without egui.
- `bars`, `button`, `panel`, `tabs`, `field`, `toggle`, `combo`, `slider`,
  `canvas`, `tooltip`, `dialog`: the chrome components (options, status
  and tool bars, icon rail, push and icon buttons, dock panel groups,
  document tabs, value, text and search fields, checkboxes and switches,
  combo boxes, sliders, canvas scrollbars, tooltip wording, and modal
  dialogs).

### Commands

- `command`: `Command<S>` is one action, with an id, a label key, a menu
  and submenu, a group, a shortcut, an icon, an `enabled` rule and a `run`
  handler over the app's state `S`. A handler only changes state. Work that
  leaves the process, such as a Bus call or a file write, is queued on the
  state for the app's effect loop. `Registry<S>` provides `add`,
  `add_choice`, `add_toggle`, `execute(id, state, origin)`, `describe`,
  `menus` and `model`, `shortcuts`, `search`, `shortcut_grid` and `rebind`.
  The UI, the command line and Bus verbs all dispatch by id.
- `executed`: every run is recorded with its `Origin` (`menu`, `shortcut`,
  `palette`, `ui`, `bus`, `macro`) and given a per-process sequence number.
  It goes into a bounded `Journal` that counts the runs it drops.
  `Registry::take_executed` hands the records to the app's Bus connection,
  which publishes them on `<app>.command.executed`
  ([decision](../docs/decisions/2026-10-11-executed-commands.md)).
- `keymap`: the chord grammar (`Ctrl`, `Alt`, `Shift`, then one key, joined
  by `+`). `Registry::rebind` applies the person's bindings from the
  desktop profile.

### Drive verbs

`drive` lets an agent do in the window anything a person can.
`drive::install(ctx, app)` turns on AccessKit, keeps each pass's widget
tree, and injects queued pointer and key events through egui's input hook,
the same path real input takes. The app registers these verbs under its own
prefix (`<app>.ui.tree` and so on):

`ui.tree`, `ui.click`, `ui.pointer`, `ui.scroll`, `ui.key`, `ui.type`,
`ui.menu`, `ui.menu.list`, `ui.menu.open`, `ui.menu.close`, `ui.capture`,
`window`, `window.state`

The app forwards each request, with the prefix removed, to
`drive::request` from inside a frame. It sends back whatever `request`, or
`drive::logic` (called once per frame), returns. It holds later commands
while `drive::pending` is true, and calls `drive::finish` before closing.
Reads answer at once. Input verbs run one at a time, one step per pass,
and answer one pass after their last step. At most 32 input requests can
be queued. The [driving guide](../docs/drive.md) shows them in use.

### Strings, thumbnails, layer surfaces

- `strings`: `Strings::new(ftl)` wraps an app's Fluent catalogue
  (`i18n/en/<app>.ftl`). It provides `get`, `with` (with arguments) and
  `has`. A missing key renders as the key itself, so a gap shows on screen
  instead of a blank. The toolkit's own labels, such as window buttons and
  the Theme menu, are in `i18n/en/toolkit.ftl`.
- `thumbnail`: decodes cached thumbnail PNGs within explicit size limits
  on a `Decoder` thread, ready to upload as textures. Making the
  thumbnails is the job of [thumbs](../thumbs/README.md).
- `layer` (feature `layer`): egui programs on wlr-layer-shell surfaces,
  such as wallpapers, desktops and docks. `layer::run(options, program)`
  creates one surface per output (`Outputs::Each`), or a single surface
  the compositor places. Each surface has its own egui context and draws
  through wgpu's GL backend on its `wl_surface`. It follows fractional
  scale and takes pointer, scroll and optional keyboard input. It redraws
  only when something changes, so an idle surface costs nothing.

## Features and dependencies

The default build has no features. `layer` adds smithay-client-toolkit
0.19.2 (the version eframe's winit already links), wayland-backend, wgpu,
egui-wgpu and xkbcommon. Workspace dependencies: `assets`, `config`,
`design`, `settings` (data types only, no Bus) and `thumbs`.

## Assets and licences

`assets/fonts/` holds static Inter (Light, Regular, Medium, SemiBold) and
JetBrains Mono (Light, Regular, Medium) faces with their OFL texts.
`assets/icons/` holds the Lucide SVGs with `LICENSE-lucide.txt`, and
mixos.dev uses the same icons. `assets/licenses.conf.mix` pins each notice
by SHA-256. This includes the notices for egui's own fallback fonts, which
are in `assets/fonts/fallbacks/`.
`scripts/install_licenses.mix` installs them under
`<share>/licenses/toolkit` (default share `/opt/mixos/share`). `--check`
validates only the sources, and `--verify` checks an installed tree. See
the [bundled font licences decision](../docs/decisions/2026-10-13-bundled-font-licences.md).

## Source layout

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `src/lib.rs` | module list and `install` |
| `src/theme.rs`, `theme_menu.rs`, `session_look.rs`, `style.rs`, `chrome.rs` | the look |
| `src/fonts.rs`, `icons.rs` | embedded faces and Lucide icons |
| `src/titlebar.rs`, `menu.rs` | window chrome |
| `src/bars.rs` … `src/dialog.rs` | chrome components |
| `src/command.rs`, `executed.rs`, `keymap.rs` | commands, executed records, chords |
| `src/drive.rs` | the drive verbs |
| `src/strings.rs`, `thumbnail.rs` | Fluent strings, thumbnail decoding |
| `src/layer.rs`, `src/layer/` | layer-shell surfaces (feature `layer`) |
| `i18n/en/toolkit.ftl` | the toolkit's own strings |
| `assets/`, `scripts/install_licenses.mix` | fonts, icons, licence notices |

## Testing

Unit tests sit in the modules; for example `menu::Nav` is tested as plain
data. The integration tests in `tests/` drive real frames through
`egui_kittest`:

- `components.rs`, `menu.rs`, `titlebar.rs`, `chrome.rs`: component, menu
  and title-bar behaviour under pointer and keyboard;
- `drive.rs`: the drive verbs, requested inside frames the way an app's
  shell requests them;
- `snapshot.rs`, `components_snapshot.rs`: offscreen wgpu snapshots across
  schemes and modes, compared with `tests/snapshots/*.png`. Regenerate them
  with `UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1`, and look at the images before committing;
- `spec_renders.rs`: when `CHROME_RENDER_DIR` is set, it renders the
  chrome scenes for an out-of-tree comparison against the chrome
  specification's evidence. When it is unset, it does nothing;
- `asset_licenses_test.mix`: install, drift and verify checks for the
  licence installer.

On an authorised build worker at a pushed commit:

```
cargo test --locked -p toolkit
cargo test --locked -p toolkit --features layer
```

# bridged Bus contract

> Mirrored from [`services/bridged/CHANGELOG.md`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/blob/main/services/bridged/CHANGELOG.md), where releases update it. The component's page is [bridged](README.md). This page describes the current `main` branch of MixOS.

## 0.2.0

- Additive: `auth: "key"` (instance config 0.2.0). The first line is
  `params.key`, the secret is the 64-hex content of `token_file`, read on every
  connect before any bytes are sent. A missing, unreadable or unusable key is
  rc 11 with no connection; the retry after `backoff_s` reads it again.
  `status` works before the key exists and never shows it. Token and none
  modes are unchanged. Bus verbs and registry classes are unchanged.

## 0.1.0

First version. A Bus bridge to an external application's line-delimited JSON
control channel, one instance per application (`bridged@<app>`), answering
`<app>.call`, `.commands`, `.execute`, `.inspect`, `.screenshot` and
`.status` with rc 0 (the app's result), 10 (the app's error), 11 (connect,
auth, transport or timeout) or 12 (a bad request).

- Instance config 0.1.0 (`docs/spec/bridge/`): `<etc>/bridge/<app>.conf.mix`,
  `<etc>` = `$MIXOS_ETC` or `/etc/mixos`, or `$BRIDGED_CONFIG`; keys `host`
  (loopback only), `port`, `auth` (`token` or `none`), `token_file`,
  `timeout_s`, `connect_timeout_s`, `backoff_s`, `max_line`, `instance`.
- Start checks, also as `mix bridged.mix --check <app>`: the Bus service-name
  rule, and no name that a registered verb already starts with (read from the
  installed verb registry, failing closed). A refusal exits 2 with
  `RUNTIME`, `NAME_INVALID`, `NAME_RESERVED`, `REGISTRY`, `CONFIG` or
  `TOKEN`.
- The name may not start with `mixos-` (mix --serve strips it) or be one of
  the broker's (`noded`, `noded-*`, the session-name shape).
- The token is redacted from every error, result and `last_error`; the token
  file must be `0600`. `localhost` connects as `127.0.0.1`.
- A reply without a boolean `ok` drops the connection (rc 11, then backoff).
- The unit runs `bridged.mix --start <app>`: the start checks in process,
  then `mix --serve` as a child (Mix has no exec), exiting with the child's
  code. A documented refusal exits 2 and is never restarted
  (`RestartPreventExitStatus=2`); an unexpected start error exits 3, and it,
  a crash or a broken install is a rate-limited failure. A clean stop exits
  143 (`SuccessExitStatus=143`). Run `--start` under the unit: outside
  systemd it has no parent-death protection. `BRIDGED_MIX` and the `.env`
  file must be administrator-controlled.
- Writes draw on the same transport budget as connect and reads
  (`timeout_s`): every `tcp_send` gets the time left as `{timeout}`, and a
  send that runs out is rc 11 with the connection dropped. Local encoding
  and scheduling cannot be interrupted and can run past it. Requires Mix >=
  0.112.1; an older Mix is refused at start
  (`RUNTIME`).
- `max_line` bounds both directions exactly: an encoded request over it is
  refused with rc 12 before the connection is touched; a reply line over it
  is rc 11 with the connection dropped, even when it arrives whole in one
  read.
- The unit is sandboxed (no capabilities or new privileges, read-only file
  system with private `/tmp`, loopback-only IP by `IPAddressAllow=localhost`
  and `IPAddressDeny=any`; a non-loopback Bus needs a drop-in).
  `systemd-analyze security` exposure 4.0 (OK).
- Documented residuals: loopback port squatting after the app dies (a
  unix-socket channel would close it), a direct `mix --serve` briefly holding
  a refused name, and the reverse name collision being the verb-registry
  gate's to refuse.
- The six verbs are declared in `docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix` as the
  `bridged` instance family (`<app>.<verb>`, `members: "instances"`), in the
  registry's schema 3. Installing the registry is a separate deployed
  prerequisite, and this entry does not claim a live installation.
- The bridge tests run in `tools/mix_tests.mix`. Their mix binary is
  `BRIDGED_MIX`, else `MIXOS_TEST_MIX`, else `/opt/mixos/bin/mix`; the Bus
  test's noded is `--noded`, else `MIXOS_TEST_NODED`, else the installed one.
- The over-`max_line` reply test asserts rc 11 and the `transport:` prefix,
  not the wording of Mix's line-limit error, which the current Mix changed.

Ported from a private prototype (a serve citizen and its core, version
0.3.0), with the instance-config path rule, the serve-name guard and the
`--check` mode added, and its tests moved from a socat stand-in to one
written in Mix on `tcp_listen`.

# Changelog

> Mirrored from [`services/compd/CHANGELOG.md`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/blob/main/services/compd/CHANGELOG.md), where releases update it. The component's page is [compd](README.md). This page describes the current `main` branch of MixOS.

## 0.2.0

- `comp.region.select` 0.2.0: a click (under 4 logical px of travel, with
  no drag on the way) and Enter or keypad Enter now select the whole output
  under the pointer, answering exactly as a drag from corner to corner does;
  a click used to re-arm the selection. A drag stays a drag even if it
  returns to its start. The overlay dims the output (clear inside a drag),
  outlines the selection in the theme's focus-ring colour and shows a hint
  ("Drag to select an area · Click or Enter for the whole screen · Esc to
  cancel"), only on the selected output, in the session look (followed on
  every change); a selected reply waits for a frame of that output without
  the overlay.
- While a `comp.region.select` run holds the seat the cursor is a
  crosshair (the theme's `crosshair`, else `cross` or `tcross`, else the
  arrow); the normal cursor is back on the frame that ends the run, however
  it ends, so the clean frame never shows the crosshair. A cursor's hotspot
  is now read after its shape is chosen, so a change of shape lands in place
  on its first frame.
- The capture panels (the setup chooser, region border and dim, Stop
  buttons and the Continue, Save, Encoding and error dialogs) draw in the
  session theme, followed on every change like the region overlay, with
  the embedded theme until the shell delivers one. Open panels repaint at
  once.
- Workspaces: `comp.workspaces.list`, `comp.workspaces.set_count {count,
  persist}` and `comp.workspace.rename {index, name, persist}`, and the
  `comp.workspace.changed` topic. The count and names persist in
  `preferences.json` (`workspaces_count`, `workspace_names`) and compd
  starts with them. `workspaces.list` rows carry `name`.
- The pointer moves at the same logical speed at every output scale: a
  relative delta is multiplied by the output scale as well as
  `cursor_sensitivity`, so a scale-2.5 output no longer needs a sensitivity
  of 2.5.

- compd's own UI is egui: capture overlays and dialogs, the frame-rate
  overlay, notifications and the Mix Scenes shell are egui programs painted
  with egui-wgpu into textures on compd's own EGL context, on the same MixOS
  look the apps draw with (`toolkit`).
- Mix Scenes are laid out as flexbox with taffy, as Quoin lays them out;
  `shell.scene.layout` reports the rectangles each node was drawn and
  hit-tested at.
- The session look follows settingsd through the shared consumer on the scene
  host's own connection (compact schema-2 deliveries, offline cache), and
  window decorations take their themes from the same look.
- A UI surface off screen is suspended: its animations stop waking the
  compositor until it is shown again.
- The whole `comp.*` verb catalogue is registered, and a registry test keeps
  it exact.
- Window titles are shaped with cosmic-text over the apps' embedded faces, so
  they match the apps' type and need no fonts installed.

# hostd contract changes

> Mirrored from [`services/hostd/CHANGELOG.md`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/blob/main/services/hostd/CHANGELOG.md), where releases update it. The component's page is [hostd](README.md). This page describes the current `main` branch of MixOS.

## 0.1.0 (draft)

- Read verbs `host.info`, `net.state`, `hostd.status`, `hostd.receipt` on the
  local socket and the Bus; retained `hostd.info` topic.
- Control verbs `hostd.freeze` (root on the host, or a grant) and
  `hostd.thaw` (root on the host only; also lifts grant suspensions), local
  only.
- Write verbs `net.link.apply` and `hostd.undo`, local only, behind standing
  grants in `/etc/hostd/policy.mx` (schema 1): caller by uid and verified
  cgroup, verb families, argument allow-lists, expiry, per-caller rate with a
  grant-wide cap. Receipts, health-checked rollback, and a circuit breaker
  that suspends a grant after two rollbacks in a row.
- Local socket: NUL-framed JSON, kernel caller identity read per request,
  per-uid connection cap, connection lifetime, read and write deadlines.
- `hostd.status` adds `held_grants`: each grant the caller holds, in full.
- Write verb `net.wg.apply`: networkd-native WireGuard, key made and kept by
  hostd (0640 root:systemd-network, never returned), the handshake dead-man
  check. The unit gains `CAP_CHOWN` and `CAP_NET_ADMIN` for it.
- Write verbs `net.wifi.scan` and `net.wifi.connect` through iwd: no files,
  the passphrase only through a one-connect agent, put back by forgetting
  and reconnecting.

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/mix/changelog/ (source: https://mixos.dev/mix/changelog.md) -->

# Changelog

> Mirrored from [`libs/mix/CHANGELOG.md`](https://github.com/markc/mixos/blob/main/libs/mix/CHANGELOG.md), where releases update it. The component's page is [mix](README.md). This page describes the current `main` branch of MixOS.

## Unreleased

### Added

- Add the `archive` feature with the `tar_list`, `tar_unpack` and `tar_pack`
  builtins. Archives use zstd (default), gzip or no codec. `tar_unpack`
  validates every member, extracts into a staging directory and renames it
  into place only after the stream verifies. See `mix man tar`.
- Harden archive builtins: count trailing padding against the shared decoded
  stream budget, reject oversized declared files before creation and bound
  copying, cap GNU/PAX metadata payloads before buffering, and refuse unread
  gzip input or additional members. Packing captures capabilities only with
  `keep_special_bits:true` and walks pinned directory/file descriptors without
  following replacement symlinks. Rollback restores directory access and
  reports cleanup failures. Empty/truncated zstd headers now raise
  `ARCHIVE_STREAM_CORRUPT`. GNU sparse entries are refused; `tar_list` also
  accepts `max_entries`. Each fix has targeted archive regression coverage.
- Archive review fixes. `tar_unpack` restores only `user.*` xattrs by
  default: `security.capability` needs `keep_special_bits:true`, and
  `trusted.*`, POSIX ACLs (`system.*`) and the rest of `security.*` need the
  new `privileged_xattrs:true`. Retained xattr bytes are bounded across the
  archive by the new `max_xattr_bytes` (16 MiB). Staging has an unpredictable
  name and is held by descriptor; members are created one O_NOFOLLOW
  component at a time relative to it, and the commit refuses to replace
  anything that appeared at `dest` (RENAME_NOREPLACE). Owner, mode and mtime
  failures are no longer discarded: an owner that cannot be applied is listed
  in the receipt's new `warnings`, and then its setuid/setgid bits and
  capability are dropped; mode and mtime failures raise. PAX global headers
  (`git archive`) are accepted as metadata (receipt `metadata`, list kind
  `"metadata"`). A bare relative dest or output name means the current
  directory. `tar_pack` refuses an output inside its source and raises when
  a file changes size while it is packed.
- Archive review, round 2. `tar_unpack` refuses a dest parent that another
  user could write (group/other-writable without the sticky bit, or owned by
  neither the caller nor root) before creating anything, and checks the new
  staging directory is the caller's, `0700` and empty. Without
  `RENAME_NOREPLACE` the commit now fails closed and rolls back. Implicitly
  created parent directories count against `max_entries` (receipt
  `implicit_dirs`). zstd content checksums are verified on unpack and list,
  and `tar_pack` now writes one.
- `analyzer::Analysis` carries `handlers`: one `HandlerDeclaration` (`command`,
  `file`, `line`) per `on <command>` statement in the parsed AST, in source
  order, with duplicates kept. `analyze()` collects them with the existing
  statement walker. Remote `ssh_mix` bodies are not included. `mix lint --json`
  and `--data` report the same list as an additive `handlers` field. The data
  is structural: it does not prove that a handler runs or is reachable.

### Fixed

- `mix lint` MIX-W2307 (send result never checked) now counts a status read
  inside an `if` condition, a map value, a nested call argument or a string
  interpolation. A correctly checked send no longer warns.
- MIX-W2307 treats every writer of `$rc`, `$result` and `$reply` as an
  overwrite: `publish()`, `sh`, `$(...)`, pipes to external commands, user
  assignments, address-block calls and calls to functions that send. A send
  followed by one of these, and no read before it, now warns.
- MIX-W2307 is conservative by construction: a construct whose effect on the
  status the analyser cannot prove absent counts as an overwrite. A call is
  proven non-writing only for a function defined in the file whose body and
  parameter defaults do not write, or for one of the pure builtins (no I/O,
  process, bus, network, clock or function-valued argument). Any other builtin,
  value call (`$f()`), method call, `include` or `source`, and any name
  defined nowhere in the file, now overwrites. A name that is also bound as a
  variable or parameter is a barrier, because a callable binding runs before a
  named function. A bare word that names a function is a call. A function that
  can `exit`, `panic`, `die` or fail uncaught ends its caller's path, so a read
  after that call does not discharge a send. String and heredoc `${...}`
  fallbacks (`${x ?? sh "..."}`) are analysed as the program they are, and an
  index is evaluated before its object. This can add warnings for code that is
  correct but calls a non-pure builtin between a send and its check.

## 0.116.0

### Added

- The remote mix binary is configurable. Every builtin that drives a
  remote mix (`ssh_mix`, `ssh_mix_many`, `ssh_exec`, `ssh_run`'s
  `env_transport: "mix"`, `send_mail`'s `host` hop) resolves it in one
  place: the `mix_bin` option, else the local env var `MIX_REMOTE_BIN`
  (empty counts as unset), else `/opt/cosmix/bin/mix`, the unchanged
  default. The value is interpolated into the remote command string, so
  it must be an absolute path or a bare name using only `[A-Za-z0-9_./+-]`;
  anything else raises `OPTION_INVALID` locally before ssh runs. A host with
  mix only at `/opt/mixos/bin/mix` used to fail with exit 127.

### Changed

- `ssh_exec`'s `remote_mix` option is now validated the same way (it was
  interpolated unchecked) and is an alias of `mix_bin`; passing both
  raises.

## 0.115.0

### Added

- `unix_connect(path[, {timeout, frame}])`: a client for a local
  unix-domain stream socket, in `tcp_connect`'s handle space, so
  `tcp_send`, `tcp_recv`, `tcp_recv_line`, `tcp_on` and `tcp_close` take it.
  The connect is bounded by `timeout` and fails at once on a full backlog
  (`UNIX_CONNECT_BUSY`). `frame: "nul"` makes a line a NUL-terminated
  frame, the framing of systemd's Varlink services and of hostd, for
  `tcp_recv_line` and `tcp_on {frame: "line"}` alike. Refusals carry
  `UNIX_CONNECT_*` codes. `mix man system` documents it.

### Changed

- One frame splitter serves `tcp_recv_line` (blocking and Class C) and
  `tcp_on` line mode, keyed to the connection's delimiter. One trailing CR
  is still stripped from an LF line.

### Fixed

- `max` now caps a complete line too. A line longer than `max` whose
  terminator arrived in the same read used to be delivered, so whether it
  was refused depended on packet timing. All three paths (`tcp_recv_line`
  blocking and Class C, `tcp_on` line mode) now refuse it the same way.

## 0.114.0

### Changed

- Released with mix-shell 0.114.0, whose usage-statistics store is now an
  append-only JSONL store (`mix man stats`). The language and its builtins
  are unchanged.

## 0.113.1

### Fixed

- An `on` header reads a hyphenated name whole, like a `send` target:
  `on dopus-test.command.executed` handles that topic. Before, the header
  stopped at the hyphen, so the handler registered as `dopus` with
  `-test.command.executed` as its body: it parsed, linted clean and never
  fired. Leading-zero segments (`on svc-01.ping`) lex as part of the name,
  as they do after `send`.

## 0.113.0

### Added

- `mime_type(path[, {content}])`: a file's type from the freedesktop
  shared-mime-info database, decided by GLib's rules, so it agrees with
  `gio info` and the file manager (checked against GIO on 5,047 files).
  Returns `{mime, by, uncertain, exists, parents}`. Behind the new `mime`
  feature, through the new `mimedb` crate. `mix man io` documents it.

## 0.112.1

### Added

- `tcp_send(handle, payload[, {timeout}])`: one deadline bounds the whole
  send, however many partial writes a slow reader forces (seconds, 0 = wait
  forever). On expiry it raises `TCP_SEND_TIMEOUT` with
  `details: {written, total}` and retires the handle; bytes already written
  stay written. The wait honours SIGTERM and Ctrl-C. On a `tcp_on` handle
  the timeout is the receipt deadline. Without the option `tcp_send` is
  unchanged.

### Fixed

- SIGTERM now ends a blocking `tcp_accept`, `tcp_recv`, `tcp_recv_line` or
  `ws_recv` at once, as it ends `sleep()`. On unix these numeric waits now
  wait on the async runtime instead of blocking the evaluator's thread, so
  the shell's SIGTERM and Ctrl-C handling can cancel them. Before, a script
  looping on `tcp_accept($l, {timeout: 0.05})` ignored SIGTERM until the
  15 s backstop forced it out. Options, results and error messages are
  unchanged.
- A receive returns data already buffered before it judges the deadline, so
  a very short timeout no longer returns nil while a line sits in the buffer.
  Traffic that delivers nothing (a WebSocket Pong flood, a line trickled with
  no newline) now counts against the deadline and the interrupt flag, so a
  finite timeout ends on time and SIGTERM still ends an untimed wait.
- A very large receive timeout in a Class C `tcp_recv`/`ws_recv` waits
  forever instead of overflowing the deadline.

## 0.112.0

### Added

- Server-side TCP. `tcp_listen(host, port[, {backlog}])` binds and listens
  and returns a listener handle; `host` is required (`"127.0.0.1"` is the
  normal choice) and port 0 takes an ephemeral port. `tcp_local_addr(handle)`
  returns `{host, port}` for a listener or connection.
  `tcp_accept(listener[, {timeout}])` returns an ordinary connected handle,
  or nil on timeout; in a Class C body it waits on native readiness.
  `tcp_on` on a listener delivers one `accepted: {handle, peer}` event per
  connection, and `tcp_accept(source)` reads that source outside serve mode.
  `tcp_close` closes a listener. Listeners and the connections they accept
  belong to the evaluator generation and close when it retires. Errors
  carry stable codes (`TCP_LISTEN_ADDR_IN_USE`, `TCP_LISTEN_PERMISSION`,
  `TCP_LISTEN_ADDR_UNAVAILABLE`, `TCP_LISTEN_ADDRESS`, `TCP_LISTEN_ARGUMENT`,
  `TCP_ACCEPT_HANDLE`, `TCP_HANDLE_LIMIT`, `TCP_LISTENER`).
- The handle limit is server-side: at most 1024 listeners and accepted
  connections are live at once, each holding a slot until it closes, and
  `tcp_listen` and `tcp_accept` refuse with `TCP_HANDLE_LIMIT` past it.
  `tcp_connect` is not limited and behaves as before.
- A blocking `tcp_accept` wakes promptly on Ctrl-C through a SIGINT wake
  socket that `interrupt::init` installs, and rechecks the interrupt flag at
  least every 250 ms, so no waiter misses it.
- `on @.verb` registers a handler under the serve name: the unquoted `@` is
  replaced by the `--serve` name (the value `serve_name()` returns) when the
  handler registers, so one generic script run as `--name photo` answers
  `photo.verb` and a second instance as `--name other` answers `other.verb`.
  Dispatch, HELP and handler listings show the resolved name; the AST keeps
  `@.verb`. Outside `mix --serve` the statement raises
  `SERVE_PREFIX_OUTSIDE_SERVE`. Each segment after `@.` must be a bare name,
  quoted or not. `on a.@.b`, `on @`, `on @x.y`, a quoted `on "@.x"`, a quoted
  segment that isn't a bare name (`on @."a.b"`) and `@` in an expression are
  parse errors (an unquoted `@` was a lexer error before). Positions that read
  raw source text now accept `@` as an ordinary character where it used to
  fail lexing: a bareword `source`/`include` path (`source ./foo@bar.mix`) and
  the command after `|` (`print(1) | cat @foo`).

### Fixed

- HTTP 1xx, 204 and 304 responses are bodyless on every method, not only
  HEAD. A conditional GET answered 304 with `Content-Encoding: gzip` no longer
  fails with `HTTP_BODY`, so ETag polling works.

## 0.111.0

### Added

- `script_path()` returns the entry script's absolute, symlink-resolved path,
  the same answer as `realpath($0)`, fixed when the script starts (a later
  `chdir()`, including one in the prelude, does not move it). It is nil under
  `mix -c`, in the REPL, for `mix -` and when the path cannot be resolved at
  start. A `require`d module, even during its top-level init, gets the entry
  script's path.

### Fixed

- Lambdas created inside a served `on` handler keep the handler's local
  variables when they run later (they faulted with `undefined variable`). A
  module first required inside a handler still reads its globals live.
- `password_hash` sha512-crypt output is now verifiable by glibc `crypt(3)` and
  Dovecot.
- `chr()` and `ord()` structured error codes are pinned by tests.

## 0.109.1

Initial MixOS transplant of the current language library and regression corpus.
Language syntax, builtin contracts and evaluator behaviour retain the source
version. Environment and project roots use MixOS names. SSH helpers retain the
installed Mix path used by existing Cosmix nodes during the migration.
